records.set: NSO model with standard Elo win probability, mG = mH = 1; proofs in Section G.2

records.t: Predicted NSO success at a 400-point general Elo gap: 51.7% Debate, 9.4% Wargames
records.x: Assuming all Guards and Houdinis lie on the fitted Elo lines with no saturation, the paper predicts oversight success at a 400-point general Elo gap ranging from 9.4% for Wargames to 51.7% for Debate, noting that a random judge already gets 50% in Debate so its curve converges to about 50%. Win probability generally falls as Delta_general grows, n* increases with Delta_general where mG > mH (Mafia, Debate, Wargames), and Backdoor Code has a zone where two steps are optimal.
records.q:
In this subsection, we apply NSO to each of the games we study in Section 3 and obtain quantitative
predictions for the oversight success probability pwin and the optimal number of oversight steps
n∗ . We assume that all Guard and Houdinis lie along the empirical slope and intercept estimates
we arrive at in Section 3 and assume no Elo-rating saturation. Fig. 8 shows the optimal number
of oversight steps (n∗ ) and win rate estimate (p∗win ) for each oversight game as we vary ∆general
using the numerical strategy described in Eq. (5). Our oversight success rate estimates at a 400-point
general Elo difference range from 9.4% for Wargames to 51.7% for Debate. Note that in Debate,
a judge who chooses a random side achieves 50% success rate – whereas in other games, random
players almost never win. Hence, the win probability curve of Debate converges to ≈ 50%.
We find that win probability is generally decreasing with ∆general , and that for games where mG >
mH (Mafia, Debate, and Wargames), n∗ is a monotonically increasing function of ∆general . Finally,
we observe that Backdoor Code has a “Goldilocks zone” where two steps of oversight is optimal.
records.set: NSO model applied to the fitted Section 3 Elo slopes and intercepts of Mafia, Debate (Fig. 3 shows TruthfulQA), Backdoor Code and Wargames

records.t: Debate game assumes debaters faithfully compete; collusion and side bias out of scope
records.x: The authors state their simple debate assumes both debaters faithfully engage adversarially, whereas advanced agents might collaborate to deceive the judge, and that agents may argue some perspectives more effectively regardless of truth; they treat these incentive and systematic problems as out of scope.
records.q:
Limitations: The simple form of debate presented here assumes that both debaters will faithfully
engage in an adversarial debate. However, advanced agents might collaborate to deceive the judge.
Another limitation is that agents may be more effective at arguing for certain perspectives in a way
independent of which perspectives are true. We consider these incentive and systematic problems out
of scope; see Section B for a discussion of other debate protocols that fix some of these issues.
records.set: Prompted 3-round LLM debate on TruthfulQA, BoolQ, QuALITY, PrOntoQA

records.t: Single-step games, prompted deception, and Chatbot Arena Elo as intelligence proxy
records.x: The authors state their oversight settings remain simplified: they simulate only single-step oversight, which may not capture dependencies between steps that compound or attenuate errors; deception is induced by prompting rather than adversarial fine-tuning, since many tested models are proprietary; and Chatbot Arena Elo is a reasonably reliable but imperfect proxy for general intelligence.
records.q:
Limitations: While our oversight settings aim to be as realistic as possible, they remain simplified.
For instance, we simulate only single-step oversight in Section 3, which might not generalize to
real-world oversight games that involve dependencies between steps that could compound or attenuate
errors. Another limitation is our modeling of deceptive behavior via prompting. A more realistic
testbed might fine-tune models to behave adversarially (we do not do this because many models
we test are proprietary and cannot be fine-tuned). Lastly, although Chatbot Arena Elo ratings are a
reasonably reliable proxy for model general intelligence, they are not perfect (Singh et al., 2025).
records.set: All four oversight games and the NSO analysis built on them

records.t: What is the probability that ASI escapes control (Compton constant) in realistic settings?
records.x: The authors propose applying the framework to more realistic settings such as RLHF, supervised fine-tuning and AI control environments, where the framework's win probability from Eq. (5) would estimate p, the probability that artificial superintelligence escapes human control, which they call the Compton constant for ASI; they also propose generalizing the work to estimate risk over time.
records.q:
Future directions: Future work should apply our framework to more realistic settings, such as
RLHF, supervised fine-tuning, and AI control environments. In these more realistic settings, the win
probability of our framework from Eq. (5) serves as an estimate for p, the probability that artificial
super intelligence (ASI) will escape human control. We refer to p as the Compton constant for ASI
and denote it pc (ASI) because of the apocryphal story of Arthur Compton and colleagues estimating
the probability to be less than 3 × 10−5 that the first nuclear explosion would ignite the atmosphere.
Another future direction is to generalize our work to estimate risk over time. Suppose that NSO
records.set: Future application of the NSO framework to real training and control pipelines

records.t: Scalable oversight benchmark based on agent score difference (ASD), with a Debate demo
records.x: The paper argues that recent empirical studies of scalable oversight protocols, especially Debate, use experiments that do not generalize to other protocols, and introduces a scalable oversight benchmark built on the agent score difference (ASD) metric, which measures how much a mechanism advantages truth-telling over deception. It supplies a Python package for evaluating protocols on the benchmark and runs a demonstrative experiment benchmarking Debate.
records.q:
effectively supplying human feedback to potentially superhuman AI models – becomes increasingly critical to ensure alignment. While numerous scalable oversight protocols have been proposed, they lack a systematic empirical framework
to evaluate and compare them. While recent works have tried to empirically
study scalable oversight protocols – particularly Debate – we argue that the experiments they conduct are not generalizable to other protocols. We introduce
the scalable oversight benchmark, a principled framework for evaluating human
feedback mechanisms based on our agent score difference (ASD) metric, a measure of how effectively a mechanism advantages truth-telling over deception. We
supply a Python package to facilitate rapid and competitive evaluation of scalable
oversight protocols on our benchmark, and conduct a demonstrative experiment
benchmarking Debate.
records.set: Benchmark framework for scalable oversight protocols; demo on 100 GSM8K questions with gpt-4o-mini judge

records.t: Scalable oversight as a training method or as an inference-time oversight mechanism
records.x: The authors describe scalable oversight (citing Bowman et al. 2022) as the problem of developing a human feedback mechanism that scales to superhuman intelligences, and give two framings: a training method that makes honesty (or alignment) the best policy for the model, extending RLHF to the superhuman realm, or an inference-time mechanism that catches a model when it says something false or does something bad, framed as mechanism design.
records.q:
The problem of developing a human feedback mechanism that scales to superhuman intelligences is
known as scalable oversight (Bowman et al., 2022). Broadly speaking, there are two ways to think
about the scalable oversight problem:
1. The problem of developing a training method that makes honesty (or more generally
“alignment”) the best policy for the model; i.e. something to replace or extend RLHF
to the superhuman realm.
2. An inference-time oversight mechanism to catch a model when it says something false
or does something bad; i.e. a mechanism design problem to get AIs to be truthful or useful.
records.set: Conceptual definition; no specific task

records.t: Agent score difference (ASD) replaces judge accuracy as the protocol metric
records.x: The authors argue judge accuracy relative to a Consultancy baseline is the wrong metric for evaluating scalable oversight protocols from an alignment perspective, and define ASD as the difference between the score an agent earns arguing for the true answer and for the false answer (e.g. judge belief 0.8 for a truthful agent and 0.6 for a lying one gives log 0.8 minus log 0.6, about 0.29). They state ASD is equivalent to judge accuracy for simultaneous debate but not for Consultancy, so the baseline comparison in previous debate experiments is incorrect.
records.q:
1) Principled metrics for evaluating scalable oversight protocols. In previous debate experiments, protocols were evaluated based on “judge accuracy” – i.e. they looked at how much Debate
improved a (human or weak model) judge’s accuracy at answering questions relative to a baseline
“Consultancy” protocol. In Section 2, we argue that this is the wrong metric to evaluate scalable
oversight protocols on from an alignment perspective. Instead, we introduce the agent score difference (ASD) metric, which measures how much the protocol “advantages truth over falsehood”, by
taking the difference in the score earned by an agent arguing for the true answer vs. for the false
answer. For example, if under some scalable oversight protocol, a judge believes a truthful agent
with probability 0.8 and a lying agent with probability 0.6, the ASD is log(0.8) − log(0.6) ≈ 0.29.
This measure is equivalent to judge accuracy for Simultaneous Debate; however it is not equivalent
for Consultancy, hence the baseline comparison in previous debate experiments is incorrect.
records.set: Binary-answer questions; judge reports probabilities after a protocol run in two worlds (agent argues true vs false answer)

records.t: Expected Agent Score (EAS) as a capability measure generalizing debater Elo
records.x: The authors note that ASD measured on current models estimates a protocol's present training signal, and to ask whether it will hold as capabilities grow they generalize the debater Elo used in earlier debate experiments to any protocol by defining Expected Agent Score, EAS = (log p_true, log p_false) dotted with q, as a pure measure of the agent's capabilities.
records.q:
Calculating ASD for a scalable oversight protocol with currently existing models gives us an estimate of how effective that protocol is now, i.e. how good of an alignment training signal they
provide to current-day models. However, we would like to know if they will continue to provide a
useful training signal as models’ capabilities improve.
Previous debate experiments used debaters’ ELO ratings as a measure of their capabilities (or “persuasiveness” as it is called in Khan et al. (2024)), and correlated them with judge accuracy. We
generalize this to other scalable oversight protocols by defining “Expected Agent Score” as a pure
measure of the agent’s capabilities:
EAS = (log p⊤ , log p⊥ ) · q,
records.set: Any scalable oversight protocol evaluated in SOlib; q is the agent's propensity to argue for each answer

records.t: Protocols benchmarked: Propaganda (RLHF), NaiveJudge, Consultancy and Debate variants
records.x: The authors benchmark Propaganda, which simulates RLHF (the judge's probability for the answer an agent argues for is the preference signal); NaiveJudge, which simulates supervised learning (the judge answers without the agent and the agent is scored by agreement); Consultancy, like Propaganda but with judge-consultant interaction, in four versions (2 or 4 turns, consultant or judge starts); and Debate in four versions (2 or 4 turns, simultaneous or sequential).
records.q:
• Propaganda – this simulates a “reinforcement learning from human feedback” setting.
Here, the judge reports probabilities by looking at the response of an agent arguing for that
answer. The probability it reports for the answer the agent is arguing for can be interpreted
as a human preference signal for the agent AI.
• NaiveJudge – this simulates a “supervised learning” setting. Here, the judge does not
give feedback based on the agent’s response, but reports its probability independently. The
agent is scored based on its agreement with the judge.
• Consultancy – similar to Propaganda, but the judge can interact with the Consultant.
Four different versions of the consultancy protocol are tested, depending on the number
of turns ( n2 or n4) and whether the Consultant ( t1) or the judge ( t0) initiates the
interaction.
• Debate – Four different versions of the debate protocol are tested, depending on the number of turns ( n2 or n4) and whether the debate is simultaneous ( t1) or sequential ( t0).
records.set: 100 GSM8K questions with Claude-generated plausible wrong answers; judge gpt-4o-mini; agents claude-3-5-sonnet and claude-3-5-haiku (with and without a calculator tool) and deepseek-v3 (no tools)

records.t: Debate outperforms all other tested protocols on inducing alignment and Expected Judge Score
records.x: The paper reports that Debate outperforms all other tested protocols both on inducing alignment (Figure 1) and on the combined capability-and-alignment measure Expected Judge Score (Figure 3).
records.q:
Our main insights from the results are summarized as follows:
1. Debate outperforms all other tested protocols, both on inducing alignment (Figure 1) as
well as on the “combined” capabilities and alignment measure of Expected Judge Score
(Figure 3).
records.set: 100 GSM8K questions; gpt-4o-mini judge; Claude 3.5 Sonnet/Haiku and DeepSeek-V3 agents, calculator tool for agents only; negative Brier scores

records.t: No significant effect of debate turns or simultaneous vs sequential debate
records.x: The paper reports no significant effect of changing the number of turns or of switching between simultaneous and sequential debate.
records.q:
2. There is no significant effect of changing the number of turns or changing between
simultaneous and sequential debate. This finding has been consistently replicated in

records.t: In Debate, more capable (higher-EAS) agents give higher ASD
records.x: The paper reports reproducing Khan et al. (2024) with its new metrics: in Debate, higher Expected Agent Score is associated with higher ASD, which the authors take to suggest Debate will keep incentivizing alignment as capabilities scale, while noting this is not a formal guarantee for the superhuman regime.
records.q:
3. Debating with more persuasive debaters incentivizes more truthful answers. We reproduce the finding in Khan et al. (2024) with our new, more general metrics, observing
that in Debate, higher EAS is associated with higher ASD. This suggests that Debate will
continue to incentivize alignment as capabilities scale, though it is not a formal guarantee
that this will remain true in the superhuman regime.
records.set: GSM8K; fixed gpt-4o-mini judge; five agent configurations (Claude 3.5 Sonnet/Haiku with and without calculator, DeepSeek-V3)

records.t: Consultancy underperforms NaiveJudge and Propaganda; Propaganda does not beat NaiveJudge
records.x: The paper reports that Consultancy significantly underperforms both NaiveJudge and Propaganda on ASD and shows no significant EAS-ASD trend, with consistently high EAS that the authors read as judge-consultant interaction making a gpt-4o-mini judge more vulnerable to manipulation; Propaganda (RLHF) does not beat NaiveJudge (supervised learning) on inducing alignment but does show the same positive association between EAS and ASD.
records.q:
4. Judge interaction with the agent AI makes it especially vulnerable to manipulation.
Consultancy significantly underperforms both the NaiveJudge and Propaganda baselines for ASD, and also does not exhibit any significant trends between EAS and ASD.
We observe that EAS is particularly consistently high for Consultancy, suggesting that the
judge interaction that differentiates Consultancy from Propaganda makes the judge (or at
least a gpt-4o-mini judge) systematically more vulnerable to manipulation.
5. Propaganda (RLHF) does not beat a NaiveJudge (supervised learning) baseline
on inducing alignment. However, Propaganda does show the same positive association
between EAS and ASD.
records.set: GSM8K, gpt-4o-mini judge; Consultancy with 2 or 4 turns and either party starting; Propaganda single-argument protocol

records.t: Benchmark relies on prompted LLMs simulating aligned and misaligned behaviour
records.x: The authors state that an empirical benchmark is no substitute for formal guarantees and that it, like previous debate experiments, only compares reward for simulated aligned versus misaligned behaviour, so results assume current language models can simulate both reasonably well when instructed. They add that only current models can be tested, extrapolating ASD versus EAS trends is not a formal guarantee, and protocols that do well may only work where ground truth is available.
records.q:
It is worth stressing that an empirical benchmark is not a substitute for formal or mathematical
guarantees. The explicit description in Section 3 reveals a key limitation of our benchmark, as well
as of previous debate experiments: it only computes and compares the reward given to simulated
aligned versus mis-aligned behaviour – i.e. it only works because existing language models follow
instructions and act truthfully or untruthfully when we tell them to. Thus all the results obtained
from experiments such as these are predicated on the assumption that current language models can
simulate aligned and misaligned behaviour “reasonably well”.
Secondly, a fundamental limitation of such empirical research is that we can only experiment with
currently-existing models. As discussed in Section 2.1, we may observe and extrapolate trends in
ASD vs EAS to predict ASD in the superhuman regime – however, this is not a formal guarantee.
Similarly, it is possible that mechanisms that do well on our experiments only work so well on
domains where ground truth is available.
records.set: SOlib benchmark and prompted-agent debate experiments generally

records.t: Demonstration uses 100 questions, one judge (gpt-4o-mini), five agent configurations
records.x: The authors state the main contribution is the benchmark and the experiments are small and demonstrative, with 100 questions, one judge model (gpt-4o-mini) and five agent configurations, and that future work should cover more agent and judge models and more questions for statistical significance, with reasoning models such as deepseek-r1 and o3 as agents.
records.q:
Our main contribution as of this workshop is a benchmark; the experiments themselves are small
and demonstrative, conducted with only 100 questions, one judge model (gpt-4o-mini) and five
agent models (claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022, and claude-3-5-haiku-20241022
with and without tools, and deepseek-v3 without). The results of our preliminary experiments
with Debate are promising: apart from benchmarking more protocols, future work should extend
our experiments to a wider range of agent models and judge models, as well as with larger numbers
of questions to increase statistical significance. Using reasoning models like deepseek-r1 and
o3 for the agent AI would be particularly novel and valuable.
records.set: GSM8K demonstration experiment

records.t: Do protocols that raise worst-case ASD resist rare catastrophic failures?
records.x: The authors name as an important direction measuring worst-case rather than average-case ASD, since superhuman AI oversight must prevent rare catastrophic actions (e.g. one piece of vulnerable code enabling weight exfiltration), and suggest protocols that raise worst-case ASD should be more robust to such failures.
records.q:
One important direction for future work will be to look at the “worst-case” ASD, as opposed to the
average case ASD, as we’ve used here. For superhuman AIs, it will be imperative that our scalable
oversight protocol prevents AIs from taking rare, catastrophic actions. For example, even one piece
of vulnerable code slipping through the filter may allow the AI to exfiltrate its weights. One reasonable thing to do might be to look at the worst ASD’s that your protocol results in. Protocols that
raise the worst case ASD should be more robust to the types of rare, catastrophic failures that we
care about.
records.set: Future benchmark metric for scalable oversight protocols

records.t: Iterated Amplification: training signal built by combining solutions to easier subproblems
records.x: The authors propose Iterated Amplification, a training strategy that progressively builds up a training signal for problems too complicated for a human to evaluate directly by combining solutions to easier subproblems. They describe it as closely related to Expert Iteration but using no external reward function, and present results in algorithmic environments showing it can efficiently learn complex behaviors.
records.q:
Many real world learning tasks involve complex or hard-to-specify objectives, and
using an easier-to-specify proxy can lead to poor performance or misaligned behavior. One solution is to have humans provide a training signal by demonstrating
or judging performance, but this approach fails if the task is too complicated for a
human to directly evaluate. We propose Iterated Amplification, an alternative training strategy which progressively builds up a training signal for difficult problems
by combining solutions to easier subproblems. Iterated Amplification is closely
related to Expert Iteration (Anthony et al., 2017; Silver et al., 2017b), except that it
uses no external reward function. We present results in algorithmic environments,
showing that Iterated Amplification can efficiently learn complex behaviors.
records.set: Proposal plus experiments on 5 toy algorithmic tasks; human replaced by a hard-coded decomposition algorithm

records.t: Amplify_H(X): human expert plus copies of the current agent as the training target
records.x: The authors define Amplify_H(X) as the composite system in which a human expert H invokes several copies of the current agent X to help solve a problem; X then learns from Amplify_H(X) the same way it would traditionally learn from H alone. In this paper the task set is question answering.
records.q:
We propose a new method, Iterated Amplification, for a human expert H to train an ML agent X.
Rather than having H demonstrate or evaluate the target behavior on their own, we allow them to
invoke several copies of the current agent X to help them. We write AmplifyH (X) for the composite
system, consisting of H and several copies of X working together to solve a problem. The agent X
then learns from AmplifyH (X) in the same way that it would traditionally learn from H alone.
To instantiate this framework we make three design decisions:
• What set of tasks do we train X to solve? In order for X to be a useful assistant, we need to
choose a sufficiently broad set of tasks. In this article, we will focus on question-answering.
records.set: Iterated Amplification framework, question-answering tasks

records.t: Amplification by delegation to subquestions with supervised distillation
records.x: The paper instantiates Amplify_H(X) by delegation: H identifies a sequence of subquestions, X computes a subanswer to each, and H decides how to answer the original question after seeing the subanswers. X is an autoregressive model trained by supervised learning to predict Amplify_H(X)'s output; the authors note future work could instead use imitation learning or use Amplify_H(X) to define a reward for RL.
records.q:
• How do we construct AmplifyH (X)? In this article, we focus on delegation: AmplifyH (X)
answers a question Q by having H identify a sequence of useful subquestions, using X
to compute a subanswer to each subquestion, and having H decide how to answer Q after
seeing the subanswers.
• How does X learn from AmplifyH (X)? In this article, we focus on supervised learning:
X is an autoregressive model trained to predict AmplifyH (X)’s output. Future work could
instead use imitation learning, or use AmplifyH (X) to define a reward function that X
maximizes with RL.
records.set: Iterated Amplification design choices: delegation-based amplification, supervised distillation

records.t: Learned human predictor H' replaces direct calls to the human decomposer
records.x: To reduce the burden on the expert, the authors train a human predictor H' to imitate H's role (identifying subquestions and combining subanswers) and train X from Amplify_H'(X) instead of consulting H directly. Because X keeps changing, H' faces a non-stationary distribution and must be updated continuously during training.
records.q:
In order to reduce the burden on the human expert H, we train a “human predictor” H 0 , and use
this predictor to generate training data rather than consulting H directly. That is, we train H 0 to
0
imitate the role of H when computing AmplifyH (X), and we train X using AmplifyH (X) rather
H
than using Amplify (X) directly.
Because H 0 is only learning how to identify subquestions and combine subanswers, rather than
solving an entire task, we expect to train it with much less data.
Note that H 0 needs to predict how H will respond to subanswers provided by X. Because X is
changing, this distribution is non-stationary, and so we need to continuously update H 0 throughout
the training process.
records.set: Iterated Amplification implementation detail; H' is a Transformer decoder that never sees the full context

records.t: Decomposing questions over contexts too large for the expert to observe
records.x: The paper states that a question may be decomposable without looking at the whole context, which lets Iterated Amplification apply to tasks whose context is too large for a human expert to observe directly. H is given the ability to look at small parts of the context, ideally decomposing until subquestions depend only on isolated facts.
records.q:
In practice, questions often take the form of a very large context (e.g. a hundred-page design
document) and a relatively small context-conditional question (e.g. “what are the largest risks when
implementing this design?”). In particular, this is the case in the experiments reported in Section 4.
Answering a question requires understanding the entire context, but it may be possible to decompose
a question without looking at the entire context. This allows us to apply Iterated Amplification to
tasks where the context is too large for a human expert to observe directly. Instead, we can give H
the ability to look at small parts of the context as needed. Hopefully, H can decompose a question
into pieces that depend on smaller and smaller parts of the context, until arriving at questions that
depend on only isolated facts from the context.
records.set: Questions posed over a large context (e.g. a long design document); used in the paper's Section 4 experiments

records.t: Amplification learns almost as quickly as supervised learning from ground truth
records.x: The paper compares Iterated Amplification against supervised learning from ground-truth data and reports that amplification solves the tasks effectively with at worst a modest slowdown. The authors state they do not expect amplification to be as fast as supervised learning, so learning almost as quickly counts as achieving their main goal.
records.q:
In order to evaluate Iterated Amplification, we compare it to supervised learning from the ground
truth data. The results are presented in Fig. 2. Iterated Amplification is able to solve these tasks
effectively with at worst a modest slowdown, achieving our main goal.
The purpose of amplification is to handle tasks where an expert can perform decomposition but can’t
solve the task directly. We don’t expect amplification to solve those tasks as quickly as supervised
learning. Because we can learn these tasks almost as quickly as supervised learning from the ground
truth, we have achieved our main goal.
records.set: 5 toy algorithmic tasks (permutation powering, sequential assignments, wildcard search, shortest path, union find); hard-coded decomposer H; Transformer agent

records.t: Decomposition oracle: tens of thousands of examples vs tens of millions for supervised
records.x: The paper reports that supervised learning needed tens of millions of examples to learn these algorithms, while Iterated Amplification needed tens of thousands of examples to learn the much simpler decompositions (numbers for each task are in Table 2 in Appendix A). The authors expect sample complexity to be much larger for realistic tasks where modelling H may need a high-quality language model, but believe learning decompositions can be much cheaper than learning complex behaviors directly.
records.q:
Supervised learning required tens of millions of examples in order to learn these algorithms. This
would be a prohibitive cost if the examples were provided by an external expert. In contrast,
Iterated Amplification required tens of thousands of examples in order to learn the much simpler
decompositions (numbers for each task are in Table 2 in Appendix A). The sample complexity will be
much larger for realistic tasks, where modeling H might require (for example) a high-quality language
model. But the general phenomenon, that learning decompositions can be much cheaper than learning
complex behaviors directly, is likely to hold for realistic tasks, since performing decomposition is
strictly easier than solving the task without the aid of X.
records.set: 5 toy algorithmic tasks; examples are queries to a hard-coded decomposition oracle H

records.t: Key assumption: a human can coordinate copies of X to beat a single copy
records.x: The authors state that the key assumption underlying Iterated Amplification is that a human can coordinate multiple copies of X to perform better than a single copy of X. They discuss this assumption in the context of whether amplification can be applied to complex real-world tasks beyond human scale.
records.q:
Having successfully applied Iterated Amplification to synthetic algorithmic problems, the natural
question is whether it can actually be applied to complex real-world tasks that are “beyond human
scale.” We leave a convincing demonstration to future work, but we discuss here why we think this is
likely.
The key assumption underlying Iterated Amplification is that a human can coordinate multiple copies
of X to perform better than a single copy of X.
records.set: Conceptual discussion of applying amplification to realistic, beyond-human-scale tasks

records.t: Experiments use hand-coded algorithmic decompositions, not humans
records.x: The authors state that in their experiments questions are algorithmically decomposable and the human is replaced with a hand-coded algorithm, so the experiments shed no light on whether humans can decompose interesting real-world tasks or whether messy real-world decompositions can be learned. They also note the combinatorial domains admit an algorithmic training signal, unlike the tasks they ultimately care about.
records.q:
These experiments make several important simplifications:
• In our experiments questions can be algorithmically decomposed into subquestions, and we
replace the human with a hand-coded algorithm. These experiments don’t shed any light on
whether humans can decompose interesting real world tasks, nor on whether it would be
feasible to learn messy real world decompositions.
• We work in combinatorial domains where it it is possible to construct an algorithmic training
signal. This makes it possible for us to cheaply run experiments and easily evaluate our
performance, but in the long run we care about tasks where it is not possible to construct an
algorithmic or even human training signal.
records.set: Section 4.3 simplifications of the algorithmic-task experiments

records.t: Question distribution must cover all subquestions; supervised rather than reward learning
records.x: The authors note X is trained by supervised learning from Amplify_H(X), whereas many important applications would likely learn a reward function from it and train X with RL. They also state the question distribution D must be broad enough to cover all subquestions asked during amplification, and that in the experiments D was usable directly whereas realistically the designer would have to construct it.
records.q:
• In our experiments X is trained by supervised learning from AmplifyH (X). In many
important applications we suspect that we would learn a reward function from AmplifyH (X)
and then train X to maximize that reward function.
• In order for Iterated Amplification to succeed, the question distribution D needs to be broad
enough to cover not only the questions we care about, but also all of the subquestions asked
during the computation of AmplifyH (X). The distribution also determines how the model
will allocate its capacity, and so must be carefully chosen. In our experiments, we started
with a distribution D that could be used directly. In a more realistic setting, we might start
with some distribution D0 of questions that have intrinsic interest, and it would be the system
designer’s responsibility to construct D appropriately.
records.set: Section 4.3 simplifications of the algorithmic-task experiments

records.t: Can Iterated Amplification be applied to complex real-world tasks?
records.x: The authors state that removing their simplifications is a task for future work, which will ultimately test the hypothesis that Iterated Amplification can be usefully applied to complex real-world tasks for which no other training strategy is available.
records.q:
Removing these simplifications is a task for future work, which will ultimately test the hypothesis
that Iterated Amplification can be usefully applied to complex real-world tasks for which no other
training strategy is available.
records.set: Future work stated after the algorithmic-task experiments

records.t: Iterated Amplification vs debate: shared recursive structure
records.x: The authors describe debate (Irving et al., 2018) as another possible approach to training question-answering systems where a human expert cannot evaluate answers directly, and state that both debate and Iterated Amplification involve a recursive structure where AI systems help humans address relevant subquestions.
records.q:
Debate: training AI systems to debate each other (Irving et al., 2018) is another possible approach
to training question-answering systems where a human expert cannot evaluate answers directly.
Both debate and Iterated Amplification involve a recursive structure where AI systems help humans
address relevant subquestions. The largest conceptual difference is that in Iterated Amplification each
records.set: Related-work comparison of Iterated Amplification and AI safety via debate

records.t: Research direction: agent alignment via reward modeling
records.x: The authors outline a high-level research direction for the agent alignment problem centred on reward modeling: learning a reward function from interaction with the user and optimising the learned reward function with reinforcement learning. The paper discusses the key challenges expected when scaling reward modeling to complex and general domains, concrete approaches to mitigate them, and ways to establish trust in the resulting agents.
records.q:
One obstacle to applying reinforcement learning algorithms to real-world problems
is the lack of suitable reward functions. Designing such reward functions is difficult
in part because the user only has an implicit understanding of the task objective.
This gives rise to the agent alignment problem: how do we create agents that behave
in accordance with the user’s intentions? We outline a high-level research direction
to solve the agent alignment problem centered around reward modeling: learning a
reward function from interaction with the user and optimizing the learned reward
function with reinforcement learning. We discuss the key challenges we expect
to face when scaling reward modeling to complex and general domains, concrete
approaches to mitigate these challenges, and ways to establish trust in the resulting
agents.
records.set: Position/agenda paper; single agent aligned to a single user; deep RL framing

records.t: Reward modeling: separate learning what to achieve from learning how to achieve it
records.x: The authors split the alignment problem into (1) learning a reward function from user feedback that captures the user's intentions and (2) training a policy with RL to optimise the learned reward function, separating the 'What?' from the 'How?'. They call this approach reward modeling.
records.q:
Alignment via reward modeling. Section 3 presents our approach to the agent alignment problem,
cast in the reinforcement learning framework (Sutton & Barto, 2018). We break the problem into
two parts: (1) learning a reward function from the feedback of the user that captures their intentions
and (2) training a policy with reinforcement learning to optimize the learned reward function. In
other words, we separate learning what to achieve (the ‘What?’) from learning how to achieve it (the
‘How?’). We call this approach reward modeling. Figure 1 illustrates this setup schematically.
records.set: Reinforcement learning framing; reward model trained from user feedback provides rewards to an RL agent

records.t: Recursive reward modeling: agent A(k-1) assists the user in evaluating agent A(k)
records.x: The authors define recursive reward modeling: agent A1 is trained with reward modeling from user feedback, and at step k agent A(k-1) assists the user in evaluating outcomes when training agent A(k), for example by giving auxiliary information, summarising large data, interpreting A(k)'s internals, or solving sub-problems the user has carved off. They note the assisting task differs from the task A(k) is trained on.
records.q:
Setup. Imagine repeating the following procedure. In step 1, we train agent A1 with reward
modeling from user feedback as described in the previous section. In step k we use the agent Ak−1 to
assist the user in evaluating outcomes when training agent Ak . This assistance can take various forms:
providing relevant auxiliary information, summarizing large quantities of data, interpreting agent
Ak ’s internals, solving sub-problems that the user has carved off, and so on. With this assistance the
user is then able provide feedback to train the next agent Ak (see Figure 2). Note that the task agent
Ak−1 is trained to solve, assisting in the evaluation of outcomes on the task of Ak , is different from
the task that Ak is trained to solve.
records.set: Proposed protocol for domains too complex for unaided humans to evaluate; no experiments

records.t: Assumption 1: user intentions can be learned to sufficiently high accuracy
records.x: The authors state their research direction rests on Assumption 1, that user intentions can be learned to a sufficiently high accuracy, i.e. that with enough model capacity and the right training algorithms the user's intentions can be extracted from data. They acknowledge adversarial vulnerability and poor out-of-distribution performance as relevant but not contradictory.
records.q:
Assumption 1 We can learn user intentions to a sufficiently high accuracy.
When phrased in terms of AI safety problems, this assumption states that we can learn to avoid
various specification problems (Leike et al., 2017; Ortega et al., 2018) in practice. In other words,
we assume that with enough model capacity and the right training algorithms we can extract the
user’s intentions from data. Needless to say, there are many problems with current scalable machine
learning techniques such as vulnerability to adversarially perturbed inputs (Szegedy et al., 2013) and
poor performance outside of the training distribution, which are relevant but not contradictory to this
claim.
records.set: Foundational assumption of the reward-modeling agenda

records.t: Assumption 2: evaluating outcomes is easier than producing correct behavior
records.x: The authors' Assumption 2 is that for many tasks we want to solve, evaluating outcomes is easier than producing the correct behaviour, with 'easier' read as labour, effort or insights, or by analogy to computational complexity. They note it fails for tasks with a low-dimensional outcome space such as yes/no questions, but argue it is recovered when the user also wants an explanation, since evaluating an explanation is typically easier than producing it.
records.q:
Assumption 2 For many tasks we want to solve, evaluation of outcomes is easier
than producing the correct behavior.
The notion of easier we employ here could be understood in terms of amount of labor, effort, or the
number of insights required. We could also understand this term analogous to more formal notions of
difficulty in computational complexity theory (see e.g. Arora & Barak, 2009).
There are examples where Assumption 2 is not true: for instance, tasks that have a low-dimensional
outcome space (such as in the case of yes & no questions). However, this assumption is recovered as
soon as the user also desires an explanation for the answer since the evaluation of an explanation is
typically easier than producing it.
records.set: Foundational assumption of the reward-modeling agenda; underpins bootstrapping via recursion

records.t: Recursion scales only if assisting tasks are simpler; RRM as an instance of amplification
records.x: The authors state that for recursive reward modeling to scale, agent A(k-1)'s task must be simpler and in a narrower domain than A(k)'s; if Assumption 2 holds, the recursion builds a hierarchy of increasingly capable agents. They describe recursive reward modeling as an instance of iterated amplification using reward modeling instead of supervised or imitation learning.
records.q:
Discussion. In order for this recursive training procedure to scale, the task of agent Ak−1 needs
to be a simpler task in a more narrow domain compared to the task of agent Ak . If evaluating
outcomes is easier than producing behavior (Assumption 2), then recursive reward modeling would
build up a hierarchy of agents that become increasingly more capable and can perform increasingly
general tasks. As such, recursive reward modeling can be thought of as an instance of iterated
amplification (Christiano et al., 2018) with reward modeling instead of supervised learning or
imitation learning.
records.set: Recursive reward modeling, conceptual discussion

records.t: Evaluation decomposition must be exhaustive
records.x: The authors state that the user's decomposition of task evaluation into simpler assistance tasks, combined into an aggregated evaluation, must be exhaustive, because if one aspect of the task outcome is neglected the new agent may optimise it in an arbitrary, undesirable direction. They add that this is another problem they hope to solve with recursive reward modeling.
records.q:
How should the user decompose task evaluation? They need to assign evaluation assistance tasks
that are simpler to the previous agent, and combine the result into an aggregated evaluation. This
decomposition needs to be exhaustive: if we neglect to assess one aspect of the task outcome, then
the new agent Ak might optimize it in an arbitrary (i.e. undesirable) direction. This is another
problem that we hope to solve with recursive reward modeling: We can have an agent A2 propose a
records.set: Recursive reward modeling, conceptual discussion

records.t: Do errors accumulate across levels of recursive reward modeling?
records.x: The authors pose as an important open question whether the mistakes of the narrower agent A(k-1) lead to larger mistakes in training A(k), or whether training can be made self-correcting so small mistakes are dampened (e.g. via ensembles or agents trained to find and counteract mistakes). They argue that if error accumulation can be bounded and reward modeling yields aligned agents, the hierarchy could be argued aligned by analogy to induction.
records.q:
An important open question is whether errors accumulate: do the mistakes of the more narrow agent
Ak−1 lead to larger mistakes in the training of agent Ak ? Or can we set up the training process to be
self-correcting such that smaller mistakes get dampened (e.g. using ensembles of agents, training
agents to actively look for and counteract these mistakes, etc.)? If error accumulation can be bounded
and reward modeling yields aligned agents, then the hierarchy of agents trained with recursive reward
modeling can be argued to be aligned analogously to proving a statement about natural numbers by
induction.
records.set: Recursive reward modeling, conceptual discussion

records.t: Complexity analogy: reward modeling ~ NP, recursion depth k ~ k alternating quantifiers
records.x: The authors argue, via an analogy to complexity theory first introduced by Irving et al. (2018), that recursive reward modeling at depth k targets problems with k alternating quantifiers, e.g. A2 proposes behavior x, A1 responds with assisting behavior y, and the user evaluates both. With polynomially bounded quantifiers and a polynomial-time formula, reward modeling is analogous to solving NP-complete problems.
records.q:
logic formulas that involve alternating quantifiers. For example, ∃x∀y. ϕ(x, y) corresponds to the
next level of the recursion: agent A2 proposes a behavior x and agent A1 responds with an assisting
behavior y. The user then evaluates the assistance y with respect to x (training agent A1 ) and the
outcome x with help of the assistance y (training agent A2 ). At recursion depth k increases, we can
target problems that involve k alternating quantifiers.
When using polynomially bounded quantifiers and a formula ϕ that can be evaluated in polynomial time, reward modeling is analogous to solving NP-complete problems: a nondeterministic
execution (analogous to the agent) proposes a solution which can be ‘evaluated’ for correctness in
deterministic polynomial time (by the user).
For example, finding a round trip in a given graph that visits every vertex exactly once (the Hamiltonian cycle problem) is NP-complete (Karp, 1972): it can take exponential time in the worst case
with known algorithms to find a cycle, but given a cycle it can be verified quickly that every vertex is
visited exactly once.

records.set: Informal complexity-theory analogy; user's evaluation assumed binary; no theorem proved

records.t: Reward gaming as possibly the greatest weakness of reward modeling
records.x: The authors state that reward gaming is in principle solvable by improving the reward model, but whether it can be overcome in practice is arguably one of the biggest open questions and possibly the greatest weakness of reward modeling. They cite RL from learned rewards succeeding in gridworlds, Atari and continuous control as evidence it can be avoided in practice.
records.q:
Reward gaming problems are in principle solvable by improving the reward model. Whether this
means that reward gaming problems can also be overcome in practice is arguably one of the biggest
open questions and possibly the greatest weakness of reward modeling. Yet there are a few examples
from the literature indicating that reward gaming can be avoided in practice. Reinforcement learning
from a learned reward function has been successful in gridworlds (Bahdanau et al., 2018), Atari
games (Christiano et al., 2017; Ibarz et al., 2018), and continuous motor control tasks (Ho & Ermon,
2016; Christiano et al., 2017).
records.set: Reward hacking challenge for scaling reward modeling; Figure 4 shows a frozen reward model being exploited in Atari (from Ibarz et al., 2018)

records.t: Scope excludes the preference payload; one agent aligned to one user
records.x: The authors state they do not address the preference payload: whose preferences the agent should be aligned to, how to aggregate and trade off different users' preferences, or when the agent should be disobedient. They treat these as out of scope and restrict the paper to a technical treatment of aligning a single agent to a single user.
records.q:
We are not considering questions regarding the preference payload: whose preferences should the
agent be aligned to? How should the preferences of different users be aggregated and traded off
against each other (Baum, 2017; Prasad, 2018)? When should the agent be disobedient (Milli
et al., 2017)? We claim that the approach described is agnostic to the ethical paradigm, the user’s
preferences, and the legal or social framework, provided we can supply enough feedback (though the
preference payload might influence the amount of feedback required). These questions are treated as
outside of the scope of this paper, despite their obvious importance. Instead, the aim of this document
is to discuss the agent alignment problem from a technical perspective in the context of aligning a
single agent to a single user.
records.set: Stated scope of the agenda

records.t: Does debate's honesty assumption hold beyond fact-checkable claims; can humans judge?
records.x: Discussing debate, the authors say that initial MNIST experiments, in which debating agents boost the accuracy of a sparse classifier, are promising but more research is needed to determine whether debate is a scalable alignment approach. They pose two questions: does debate's central assumption (that it is easier for the agent to tell the truth than to lie) hold outside domains of easily fact-checkable statements, and can humans accurately judge the debate even if the debaters have superior persuasion and deception ability?

game. In order to become aligned, this agent needs to be trained in a way that it converges to a Nash
equilibrium in which both instances of the agent try to be helpful to the user. The central assumption
of debate is that it is easier for the agent to tell the truth than it is to lie. If this assumption holds, then
the dynamics of the game should incentivize the agent to provide true and useful statements.
The authors provide initial experiments on the MNIST dataset in which the debating agents manage
to boost the accuracy of a sparse classifier that only has access to a few of the image’s pixels. While
these initial experiments are promising, more research is needed in order to determine whether debate
is a scalable alignment approach. We need more empirical evidence to clarify, among others, the

records.t: Recursive task decomposition plus human feedback for summarizing entire books
records.x: The paper combines learning from human feedback with recursive task decomposition, using models trained on smaller parts of the task to help humans give feedback on the broader task; GPT-3 is fine-tuned with behavioural cloning and reward modeling to summarise small sections and then recursively summarise those summaries. The authors report labelers could supervise and evaluate quickly without reading whole books, and that the resulting summaries are sensible and match human-written quality in a few cases (about 5% of books).
