links.why: Irving et al. ask whether self-play stably converges to honest debate equilibria and know of no theory guaranteeing it. Arnesen et al. report that self-play DPO training of their debaters is associated with 4 percentage points higher judge accuracy for the fully DPO-trained model than for the SFT model (p < 10^-6); this is empirical evidence comparing the fully DPO-trained and SFT debaters with a judge never trained on their transcripts, not a convergence result.

Irving et al. note no theory says self-play stably converges to optimal play. Brown-Cohen et al. state that prover-estimator debaters can be trained with standard methods that converge to Stackelberg equilibria, and Theorem 6.2 gives correct answers with probability at least 1 - 5 eps at A-leading Stackelberg equilibria under rho-stability and A-provability; this characterises equilibria rather than proving that gradient training converges.

Irving et al. leave open a natural debate protocol for stochastic simulation: with noise, a misaligned Alice could choose it so that each single step is plausible but the final result has extremely low probability, and fixing the random seed preserves PSPACE equivalence but gives a protocol likely unlearnable by practically realizable agents. Theorem 6.2 of Brown-Cohen et al. gives a protocol for K-Lipschitz probabilistic oracle machines in which A proposes the probability of each next bit and the provers sample it by coin-flipping through cross-examination, with O(K^2) oracle queries, completeness 3/5 and soundness 2/5; the guarantee needs the Lipschitz condition and cross-examination.

Irving et al. worry that a false opening the human already believes may win because of belief bias. Rahman et al. compare judges with mainstream or skeptical prior beliefs and report debate raising accuracy from 63.2% to 70.1% versus consultancy 61.4% to 60.0%, with a 15.2% advantage for mainstream-prior judges but only a non-significant 4.7% (p = 0.2) for skeptical-prior judges.

Irving et al. state debate had only an MNIST demonstration and that significant research is needed to know whether it works with human judges. Michael et al. report human-debater debates judged by non-expert humans reach 84% accuracy versus 74% for consultancy on hard reading comprehension questions where the judge has not read the source passage; the paper also compares human with AI debaters.

Irving et al. note their theory models judges as error-free and agents as unbounded and call for richer models. Brown-Cohen et al.'s Theorem 6.2 gives a debate protocol with cross-examination for any language decidable by a K-Lipschitz probabilistic oracle Turing machine, with completeness 3/5 and soundness 2/5, in which the verifier V samples from the oracle O to check A's proposed distribution. The authors say human judgement is fallible and reward models approximate it from limited samples, so in practical settings the verifier's oracle O is likely to be flawed, and that Theorem 6.2 partially addresses this by making each response of O stochastic and allowing verification of any computation that outputs the correct answer with a constant advantage over random guessing. The cited passages do not say how the provers' running time is bounded, so the link does not cover Irving et al.'s unbounded agents.

Christiano et al. state their experiments use a hand-coded decomposer on algorithmic tasks and shed no light on whether humans can decompose real-world tasks. Reppert et al. report human developers iteratively decomposing real science Q&A tasks, raising held-out accuracy (placebo description 25% to 65%, adherence 53% to 70%, Qasper 38% to 69%); the decompositions are hand-designed LM programs, not trained by amplification and distillation.

Christiano et al. note that in their experiments X is trained by supervised learning from Amplify_H(X), whereas in many important applications they suspect they would learn a reward function from Amplify_H(X) and train X to maximize it. Wu et al. report that their 175B RL policies significantly outperform their 175B BC baseline, though the improvement is smaller for the 6B models.

Christiano et al. leave open whether Iterated Amplification can be usefully applied to complex real-world tasks for which no other training strategy is available. Wu et al. combine human feedback with recursive task decomposition to summarise whole books, report labelers could supervise without reading whole books, and find summaries match human quality in about 5% of books; at inference time the model summarises small sections and then recursively summarises those summaries. Wu et al. say their task decomposition approach can be thought of as a specific instantiation of iterated amplification, except that they assume a fixed decomposition and start training from the leaf tasks rather than using the entire tree, and that their contribution is showing the approach can be realistically applied to a difficult, large-scale task. The passages do not show whether the task is beyond what humans could evaluate directly or whether no other training strategy is available for it.

Leike et al. call reward gaming possibly the greatest weakness of reward modeling and ask whether it can be overcome in practice. Bai et al. report RL-CAI policies can be over-trained into Goodharting behaviour, such as overly harsh replies or boilerplate like 'you are valid, valued, and cared for'; the reward model is trained on AI-generated labels, not user feedback.

Leike et al. ask whether reward gaming can be overcome in practice. Wen et al. report RLHF raises human approval by +6.0% to +14.3% across three setups while barely raising correctness, which the authors read as RLHF making the model appear more convincing to humans without improving performance on the intended task; the three setups are QA under a general training reward, QA under a task-specific training reward, and programming.

Both records concern debate's central assumption that it is easier for the agent to tell the truth than to lie. Leike et al. ask whether it holds outside domains of easily fact-checkable statements. Khan et al. report debaters get higher Elo when assigned the correct answer and that this advantage grows with aggregate Elo, suggesting that, for debates in QuALITY, telling the truth is easier than lying. In each of Khan et al.'s protocols, expert models present quotes from the text through a tool that marks a quote as verified when it directly matches a portion of the text, and the judge is instructed to trust only verified quotes; the cited passages do not show that this setting lies outside easily fact-checkable domains, so the two records ask the same question in different settings.

Leike et al. ask whether debate's central assumption holds outside domains of easily fact-checkable statements and whether humans can accurately judge a debate when the debaters have superior persuasion and deception ability. On closed tasks (MMLU, GSM8KQA, PrOntoQA, TruthfulQA, GPQA) without information asymmetry, Kenton et al. report debate beats consultancy but versus direct QA only GPT-3.5 benefits (p = 0.037), for Pro 1.0 the difference is not statistically significant (p = 0.1), and Gemma7B and Pro 1.5 do worse; judges are LLMs, not humans.

Leike et al. ask whether mistakes compound across levels of recursive reward modeling: whether the mistakes of the narrower agent A(k-1) lead to larger mistakes in training A(k), or can be dampened. Engels et al.'s NSO model plays a series of n games between Guards and Houdinis whose general Elos are spaced Delta_general/n apart, and picks n to maximise the product of the stepwise Guard win probabilities. With it they report that multiple steps of nested oversight can move Guard log odds from -3 to 3 in some regions, with the optimal number of steps growing with the general capability gap (Delta_general) at a fixed Delta_domain; in Houdini-favoured games (Delta_general < Delta_domain), one step of oversight appears optimal. Because each game is set by its Guard's and Houdini's general Elos and overall success is the product of stepwise win probabilities, the model does not show whether mistakes at one level lead to larger mistakes at the next, so neither record bears on the other's claim.

Leike et al. pose whether mistakes of narrower agents lead to larger mistakes higher up. Wu et al. report that policy errors at lower levels compound at each composition task, leading to large top-level errors, and that training on the full tree did not improve performance; their hierarchy is a fixed summarisation tree, not a chain of assistant agents training stronger agents.

Leike et al. ask whether errors accumulate or are dampened across recursive levels. Wen et al.'s Table 3 compares performance across recursive critique stages and reports values of 43.75 (response), 53.12 (critique), 56.25 (C2) and 54.69 (C3) for GAOKAO Math with Qwen2.5-7B, so the C3 value falls below the C2 value; these are values for a chain of critique stages, and the passage does not show recursive reward model training. Both records concern how results change across successive recursive levels, but neither bears on the other's claim or question: the cited Wen et al. lines pose no question about error accumulation, and Leike et al.'s passage reports no results, so the link is navigation only.

Amodei et al. ask how to ensure an agent respects aspects of an objective too expensive to evaluate often during training. Christiano et al. propose Iterated Amplification, which builds a training signal for problems too complicated for a human to evaluate by combining solutions to easier subproblems, and present results in algorithmic environments. There, amplification needed tens of thousands of examples to learn the decompositions, while supervised learning needed tens of millions, which they say would be a prohibitive cost if an external expert provided the examples.

Amodei et al. ask how an agent can respect objectives too expensive to evaluate frequently. Leike et al. propose recursive reward modeling, in which agent A(k-1) helps the user evaluate outcomes when training A(k), e.g. by summarising data or solving carved-off sub-problems; the cited passage presents it as a procedure to imagine ('Imagine repeating the following procedure') and reports no results.

Amodei et al. propose actively requested reward samples as a step for semi-supervised RL. Lightman et al. estimate that active learning on convincing wrong-answer solutions is about 2.6x more data efficient than uniform labelling when training process reward models; the supervision is synthetic (from a large PRM), the learner is a reward model, and no RL agent is trained.

Amodei et al. note human checking of risky actions runs into scalable oversight because the agent may need too many exploratory actions or may need to make them too fast for humans to judge. Bai et al. use the term 'Scaling Supervision' for techniques that leverage AI to help humans more efficiently supervise AI, making it possible to train systems to behave in desirable ways (for example, to be helpful and honest); the setting is training systems, not checking an RL agent's exploratory actions.

Anil et al. note that frozen-verifier stress tests cannot rule out incorrect proofs that are hard to find. Kirchner et al. attack verifiers with separately trained sneaky-only provers and report that steps-to-exploit rise over rounds and that 10^-2-size verifiers were not exploited beyond round 0 within 8k RL steps, while 10^-3 verifiers stayed exploitable until round 4; an attack with a fixed 8k-step budget still cannot prove no hard-to-find proof exists.

Anil et al. call for scaling PVGs to harder problems and studying behaviour at approximate equilibria. Kirchner et al. propose a training algorithm inspired by Anil et al.'s Prover-Verifier Game that trains small verifiers and helpful and sneaky provers on grade-school math, and report that helpful-prover accuracy and verifier robustness increase over training and that legibility training transfers to time-constrained humans; the passages do not show whether this training reaches or studies approximate equilibria.

Anil et al. call for scaling Prover-Verifier Games to more challenging problems. Hammond and Adam-Day report that every protocol they test modestly beats a verifier trained alone in final test accuracy, with nip and mnip gaining about 11% and mnip best on worst-case performance.

Wu et al. ask whether decomposition beyond a fixed algorithmic tree is feasible for hard real-world tasks. Reppert et al. report a human-in-the-loop workflow that iteratively refines decompositions of science Q&A tasks, raising held-out accuracy (e.g. Qasper 38% to 69%); the decompositions are designed by developers, not learned by a model, so the 'learned' part of Wu et al.'s question stays open.

Parrish et al. (single-turn) ask whether a multi-turn setting with counterarguments is needed. The two-turn follow-up adds a second round of counter-arguments and reports that humans perform similarly regardless of whether they have access to arguments.

Parrish et al. ask whether a multi-turn setting with explicit counterarguments is needed for debate to help. Michael et al. contrast their setting with the one- and two-turn debates of Parrish et al., in which debate did not significantly improve judge accuracy: their debates are unbounded in length, and debaters are expected to defend their position against criticism by their opponent for as long as the judge is not convinced of the answer. They report 84% judge accuracy for debate versus 74% for consultancy on hard reading comprehension questions; their judges have not read the source passage and see only expert arguments and short quotes selectively revealed by the debaters, and debaters are expert humans, so several factors differ.

Parrish et al. suggest debate's strength may rely on counterarguments that reference the other side. Arnesen et al. report debate 77% versus double consultancy 75% (both sides shown, no refutation) and that one-turn debates are judged as accurately as two-turn ones, concluding either debaters fail to refute meaningfully or the judge does not benefit; the judge is an LLM, not a human.

Parrish et al. say their study is limited in scope and is not strong evidence against the broad potential usefulness of a debate-style set-up. Khan et al. report that, for the most persuasive models, non-expert human judges reach 88% with debate versus 60% naive and 78% consultancy.

Parrish et al. note their time limit makes the task more artificial than they would like and that 120 seconds might still be too short. The two-turn follow-up keeps the top 16 of 32 pilot judges and sets 5 minutes per judgment; judge selection and counter-arguments also changed, so time is not isolated.

Saunders et al. state their summarisation task has no objective way to validate answers or critiques and that labelers may misevaluate answers by trusting the model summaries too much. McAleese et al. have contractors insert subtle bugs into model-written code, asking them to verify that an LLM critic misses each bug in at least one of three samples (not strictly enforced). They note that contractors may struggle to validate the correctness of free-form critiques and to spot important issues that critiques miss, and say the tampering approach provides high-quality, difficult reference bugs which ground the ranking task by allowing contractors to more easily discriminate between critiques catching and missing the problem.

Saunders et al. warn that positive critique results on an easy-to-evaluate task might not reproduce on harder tasks. McAleese et al. report broadly negative results on paired passing and failing solutions to hard competition-style problems: LLM critiques struggled to help contractors pick the correct solution within 20 minutes, which the authors suspect reflects critic compute not being scaled; this is an appendix result without code execution.

Saunders et al. note their base task is not very hard for humans to evaluate, leaving little headroom for assistance; humans take up to about ten minutes, so little speed-up is observed, and positive results on an easier task might not be reproducible on harder tasks. McAleese et al. report that LLM critics (prompted ChatGPT and CriticGPT) catch many more inserted bugs than the human annotators, a cohort representative of the contractors used for ChatGPT; the bugs are inserted, not naturally occurring. The McAleese et al. result compares LLM-written with human-written critiques rather than human evaluation assisted by critiques, and the cited passages do not show that the inserted-bug task is harder for humans to evaluate, so it does not bear on Saunders et al.'s concern, and Saunders et al.'s limitation of their own task does not bear on McAleese et al.'s comparison.

Saunders et al. propose training assistants that help train assistants, e.g. critiquers of critiquers. Wen et al. test whether critiquing a critique is easier than producing it and whether this holds recursively, using Human-Human, Human-AI and AI-AI experiments.

Bowman et al. call for empirical trials of debate under sandwiching. Michael et al. have non-expert judges who cannot read the passage judge debates between experts who can, reporting 84% for debate versus 74% for consultancy; the 'model' is often a human expert and there is no fine-tuning loop, so it is a relaxed sandwiching test.

Bowman et al. ask whether debate can be validated empirically under sandwiching. Khan et al. report that, for the most persuasive models, non-expert human judges reach 88% with LLM debate versus 60% naive and 78% consultancy, in an information-asymmetric setup.

Bowman et al. ask for empirical trials of debate and market-making. Lang, Huang and Li report that debate used in their approach performs better than all other variants, including market-making and consultancy, in test accuracy and PGR across all four tasks, at least in their settings; the 'weak supervisor' is a model, not a human.

Bowman et al. report participants sometimes give confidently wrong judgements and accept confident false model claims in human-model chat. Khan et al. report that in static debate, rejecting human judgements below 75% confidence keeps 65% of questions at 94% accuracy, that debate beats consultancy at all rejection thresholds, and that judges are better calibrated with debate; the protocol and task differ (LLM debate on QuALITY HARD vs chat on MMLU and QuALITY).

Bowman et al. report participants sometimes give highly confident wrong judgements. Rahman et al. report judges are overconfident under both debate and consultancy, with overconfidence most pronounced at confidence levels above 80%, but debate gives better calibration (Brier 0.231 vs 0.335); the setting is AI debate and consultancy on controversial claims.

Bai et al. leave open whether helpfulness and instruction-following can be achieved without human feedback. Wen et al. label 5,000 'more helpful, harmless, and honest' pairs with ICM, train a reward model and run RL for 250,000 episodes, reporting the assistant matches its human-label counterpart on average (higher chat and safety, lower math and code); scoring used a production-grade Claude 4 Opus reward model.

Bai et al. warn that scaling supervision may automate and obscure decision making and rely on chain-of-thought for legibility. Kirchner et al. report that optimising only for answer correctness can make solutions less legible, propose a training algorithm inspired by the Prover-Verifier Game to mitigate the loss, and show that legibility training transfers to time-constrained humans, whose accuracy rises over training when checking the helpful prover's solutions; the concern is solution legibility in math, not the legibility of an AI supervisor's decisions.

Bai et al. state that reducing the need for human feedback makes it easier to train and deploy AI systems not thoroughly tested and observed by humans, which could lead developers to deploy models with unforeseen failure modes. Goel et al. say their results indicate that as model blind-spots get harder to detect and humans defer more to AI oversight, models also make more similar mistakes, posing safety risks from correlated failures; they give this among potential implications if this trend continues.

Parrish et al. conclude debate may help in other set-ups, such as highly technical tasks, though not for multiple-choice reading comprehension. Rahman et al. report that on COVID-19 and climate-change factuality claims, debate between two AI systems improves human judges' accuracy and calibration and beats consultancy by 4-10%; the comparison is with consultancy, and the claims are possibly not highly technical (see obligation 2).

Reppert et al. expect that, without scalable infrastructure to support it, outcome-based training will eventually outcompete process supervision performance-wise. Lightman et al. state that their results show process supervision incurs a negative alignment tax.

Cohen et al. propose using several LM instances in factuality detection instead of one examiner. Du et al. report multi-agent debate improves factual accuracy (biographies 66.0 to 73.8, MMLU 63.9 to 71.1 versus single agent); this improves answer generation, not detection of another model's false claims, so the two share the question in different settings.

Du et al. report debates can converge confidently on an incorrect answer. Choi, Zhu and Li prove that under their condition (1) an agent's belief sequence is a martingale: its expected belief at the next round equals its current belief. They state that this neutral expectation means that, without additional bias towards correct signals, debate alone does not guarantee convergence to the truth.

Du et al. report debates can converge on a wrong answer and that models confidently affirm an incorrect answer as correct and consistent with all other agents' responses. Smit et al. report prompted agreement intensity significantly affects Multi-Persona accuracy, with MedQA and PubMedQA benefiting from high agreement while CIAR follows a reverse pattern; this bears on premature wrong consensus but measures accuracy, not convergence.

Du et al. note multi-agent debate is more computationally expensive than other prompting techniques. Smit et al. benchmark cost, time and accuracy and report MAD systems do not reliably beat self-consistency or ensembling, though with hyperparameter tuning several MAD systems, such as Multi-Persona, perform better; the cited passages do not show whether the benchmark includes Du et al.'s procedure or tasks.

Liang et al. state an LLM judge may prefer its own outputs and, to mitigate this, recommend that all roles, including the judge and debaters, use the same LLM, or alternatively another arrangement for the judge and debaters that the cited passage breaks off before stating. Goel et al. report an average Pearson r = 0.84 between judge scores and judge-model similarity for all judges, extending beyond self- or family-preference; their judges grade free-text answers for correctness, not debate sides.

Both records concern using more agents. Liang et al. list scheduling more agents in the debate in an appropriate manner as future work. Choi, Zhu and Li prove that for N agents that respond independently without interaction, with homogeneous initial beliefs alpha in which the correct answer has the largest belief, majority voting picks the correct answer with probability at least 1 - exp(-N (Delta/sqrt(K) - 1/sqrt(N))^2) when N > K/Delta^2, where Delta is the margin theta-bar_1 - theta-bar_2 of the mean of Dirichlet(alpha). This is a result about independent voters in a Dirichlet belief model, not about measured LLM behaviour or agents in a debate, and it says nothing about how to schedule agents in a debate, while Liang et al.'s item makes no claim about voting, so neither bears on the other's claim.

Liang et al. list AI feedback for model alignment as future work. Lang, Huang and Li use debate arguments from a large strong model as context when training a small weak model, whose labels then train the strong model, reporting better alignment on the OpenAI weak-to-strong NLP benchmarks; the cited passage does not say what 'alignment' measures on these benchmarks.

Lightman et al. evaluate reward models only by best-of-N and call RL on the generator a natural next step. Sun et al. compare PPO, DPO and ReST and report that models trained with PRM rewards, with human supervision on the easy tasks, reach a top performance of 34.0, outperforming the previous state of the art trained across all task levels (33.0), and that PRM rewards are more beneficial than final-answer rewards for hard tasks.

Michael et al. warn that strong dishonest strategies may exist that their human debaters did not find, and that testing needs more optimisation pressure, likely with AI debaters. Khan et al. optimise LLM debaters against win rate (judge preference) and report judge accuracy rises with debater aggregate rating; optimisation is inference-time.

Michael et al. say addressing whether debate works in the limit needs more optimisation pressure on debaters. Arnesen et al. train debaters with self-play DPO and report +4 points judge accuracy versus the SFT model.

Michael et al. hope eliciting judge uncertainty lets debate fail gracefully but find calibration hard at high confidence. Khan et al. report that in static debate rejecting judgements below 75% confidence retains 65% of questions at 94% accuracy, and that judges are better calibrated with debate than consultancy; this does not test the case of arguments too complex for the judge.

Michael et al. find calibration difficult in the high-confidence regime. Rahman et al. report judges are overconfident under both debate and consultancy, most above 80% confidence, while debate improves Brier score (0.231 vs 0.335); this supports the difficulty and shows debate only partly helps.

Michael et al. say debate is untested on political or ideologically charged issues and with judges holding strong priors. Rahman et al. test COVID-19 and climate claims with human judges holding either mainstream or skeptical beliefs and report debate beats consultancy by 4-10%; the debaters are AI systems.

Michael et al. say generalisation to reasoning or knowledge gaps beyond source-text access is unclear. Kenton et al. report that on closed tasks without information asymmetry debate beats consultancy but shows small or no benefit over direct QA for GPT-3.5 and Pro 1.0 judges; the judges are LLMs rather than humans.

Michael et al. call for evaluating debate where judges have strong inaccurate priors. Rahman et al. report that under consultancy mainstream-prior judges were less accurate than skeptical ones (OR 0.70, p = 0.11), while under debate accuracy was nearly identical across prior groups (OR 1.10, p = 0.66); neither odds ratio is significant.

Michael et al. note inductive or tacit knowledge may not admit short justifications and that alternative extraction methods may be needed. Wen et al. report ICM elicits a pretrained model's author-gender prediction at 80% (matching golden labels) while human labels reach only 60%; this is unsupervised label elicitation, not debate, and correctness is checked with golden labels. No cited passage shows author-gender prediction to be knowledge that lacks short justifications, so Wen et al.'s result does not bear on Michael et al.'s question, and Michael et al.'s question does not bear on Wen et al.'s result.

Michael et al. do not observe obfuscated arguments to be a significant problem in their free-text debates with evidence quoting and judge interaction, contrast these with debates scaffolded with explicit recursive structure, and say future work running debates on harder questions can monitor whether obfuscated arguments become an obstacle in practice. Brown-Cohen et al. state that existing recursive debate protocols run into the obfuscated arguments problem and propose prover-estimator debate, which under stability assumptions lets an honest debater win with computational efficiency comparable to its opponent, mitigating obfuscation; the result is theoretical and gives no empirical evidence on whether obfuscation arises in practice.

Brown-Cohen, Irving and Piliouras ask whether an intermediate model exists where the honest prover always has an efficient strategy but the computation need not have a polynomial-length human-verifiable transcript, noting unbounded-prover debate runs into obfuscated arguments. Prover-estimator debate is proposed as a recursive protocol that, under certain stability assumptions, lets an honest debater win with a strategy requiring computational efficiency comparable to its opponent, mitigating the obfuscated arguments problem.

Brown-Cohen et al. ask whether debate results extend to oracles that err on some queries. Buhl et al. argue random judge errors should wash out over training, so the concern is systematic error, and require bounded systematic error of simulated human input with respect to reality and of the simulation with respect to humans; this is a stated requirement in a safety-case sketch, not a theorem.

Chen et al. limit their experiments to zero-sum games and call the empirical study of general-sum language games an interesting future direction. Hammond and Adam-Day define nip with the prover's loss as worst-case positive-instance loss minus worst-case negative-instance loss and the verifier's loss as their sum, so the game is not zero-sum. The cited nip passage gives only a definition, with no experiment and no mention of language, so it does not answer Chen et al.'s call, and Chen et al.'s limitation does not bear on the definition; neither bears on the other's claim.

Chen et al. propose games with very large action spaces as a model for language games and AI debate, and ask for notions of equilibrium better suited to these games. Hammond and Adam-Day prove that, for a probabilistic decision problem that has a valid proof system, a profile is a valid interactive proof system iff it is an approximate verifier-leading Stackelberg equilibrium of a nip game, while noting worst-case losses and Stackelberg equilibria are hard to learn. The cited passages do not show that nip games are language games or AI debate games with very large action spaces, so Theorem 8 is not shown to answer Chen et al.'s call, and Chen et al.'s call does not bear on Theorem 8; neither bears on the other's claim.

Burns et al. state none of their methods work consistently and the reward modeling gap is far from recovered. Lang, Huang and Li report their debate-ensemble method raises PGR over finetuning with auxiliary confidence loss on all four tasks, e.g. CosmosQA 17.4% to 56.5% and AnthropicHH 35.0% to 70.0%; models are Qwen-7B and Qwen-14B, a small compute gap.

Burns et al. ask how important errors in the weak supervision are and how different kinds of weak label biases affect generalisation. Lang, Sontag and Vijayaraghavan give error bounds based on expansion of the data distribution and student hypothesis class that capture pseudolabel correction and coverage expansion; they show the expansion properties can be checked from finite data and give empirical evidence that they hold in practice.

Burns et al. ask how different kinds of weak label errors affect generalisation. Goel et al. report that, controlling for the accuracy gap, weak-strong similarity is inversely correlated with weak-to-strong gain (r = -0.35, p < 0.01), so tasks where supervisor and student make less correlated errors tend to yield greater improvements.

Burns et al. ask what makes a concept easy or hard to elicit and how to define salience. Wen et al. report ICM performs at chance on a 'poems mentioning sun are better' task with Llama 70B and attribute this to the concept not being salient; ICM is unsupervised elicitation, not weak-to-strong finetuning, and salience is not formally defined.

Hase et al. state their easy-to-hard results are limited to tasks humans label reliably and may not hold where humans cannot produce accurate labels. Wen et al. report a task where 5 human annotators are consistent but only 60% accurate while ICM matches golden labels at 80%; evaluation still uses golden labels, so the test setting itself has ground truth.

Khan et al. note their expertise gap is only access to information, whereas future models may differ in reasoning. Kenton et al. test closed tasks without information asymmetry and report debate beats consultancy but versus direct QA is mixed: GPT-3.5 benefits (p = 0.037), Pro 1.0 shows no statistically significant difference (p = 0.1) and Gemma7B and Pro 1.5 do worse. The Pro 1.5 judge is the same model as the debaters, so that case has no weak-strong asymmetry and, the authors say, does not inform much about scalable oversight; they read GPT-3.5 and Pro 1.0 as probably the most indicative of scalable oversight, showing small or no benefit of debate over QA without article. The cited Kenton et al. passage does not address Khan et al.'s concern that debate may not suit deceptive models.

Both records concern debate in which debaters cannot quote verified evidence from a source text. Khan et al. state their results are limited to setups where debaters can provide verified evidence to the judge, here via the quote tool; without it, a debater arguing for the incorrect answer could create an alternative narrative that a judge without access to the underlying story would have no means to discover. Kenton et al.'s closed tasks (MMLU, GSM8KQA, PrOntoQA, TruthfulQA, GPQA) have no article to use as a source and hence no information asymmetry; there debate beats consultancy but shows small or no benefit over QA without article for the judges the authors read as probably the most indicative (GPT-3.5 p = 0.037, Pro 1.0 no significant difference). Since the closed tasks have no underlying story hidden from the judge, Kenton et al.'s result does not test the invented-narrative case, and Khan et al.'s limitation, which concerns a judge without access to the underlying story, does not bear on Kenton et al.'s closed-task result; task type and evidence access change together.

Khan et al. warn that without the quote tool a debater arguing the wrong answer could invent a narrative. Wen et al. report RLHF-trained models defend incorrect answers on question answering by cherry-picking or fabricating supporting evidence and making consistent but untruthful arguments that mislead their human subjects; this is single-model QA under RLHF, not debate.

Yang et al. state they mainly experiment with two offline preference optimisation methods, SimPO and DPO, and leave online frameworks such as PPO to future work. Wen et al. study a standard RLHF pipeline and report models become better at convincing time-limited humans without becoming more correct, raising false positive rates by 24.1% (QuALITY) and 18.3% (APPS); the overseer is a human evaluator, not a weak model. Both ask whether training can lead models to mislead or deceive their overseer, in different settings, so SAME_QUESTION_DIFFERENT_SETTING; the cited Wen et al. passage names neither online training nor PPO.

McAleese et al. note human-inserted bugs differ from natural LLM errors and suggest training models to insert subtle in-distribution problems. Kirchner et al. report sneaky-prover solutions become harder for time-limited humans to label correctly over rounds and suggest the sneaky prover could serve as a tampering model for training critique models; this comes from a pilot study with design flaws, on math rather than code.

McAleese et al. suggest a single critique step may be weaker than multi-step procedures such as consultancy or debate. Hammond and Adam-Day compare protocols on APPS code validation and report stabilised expert iteration improves every protocol's worst-case performance with debate performing particularly well; verifiers are GPT-4o-mini models, not human contractors, and code snippets are APPS solutions. The cited passages include no single-critique protocol, so Hammond and Adam-Day's result does not bear on McAleese et al.'s claim, and McAleese et al.'s limitation does not bear on Hammond and Adam-Day's result.

McAleese et al. call critique only the first step of recursive reward modeling and ask whether critique can be used effectively for further steps. Wen et al. hypothesise and test that critiquing a critique is easier than critiquing, recursively, across Human-Human, Human-AI and AI-AI experiments; the passage does not show that they train a policy through RRM steps.

Kenton et al. name training debaters and consultants on the judge's signal as the most immediate future work. Arnesen et al. train with self-play and report judge accuracy rises with debate training but not with consultancy training; the judges are language-model based evaluators.

Kenton et al. say inference-only prompting gives little evidence about equilibria reached by training. Arnesen et al. train debaters with DPO and report the fully trained debater is associated with 4 percentage points higher judge accuracy than the SFT model (p < 10^-6), while consultant skill shows no apparent relationship with judge accuracy.

Kenton et al. name showing debate improves over direct QA baselines as a key challenge. Sudhir et al. report Debate outperforms all other tested protocols on inducing alignment (Figure 1) and on Expected Judge Score; the tested protocols include NaiveJudge, in which the judge does not give feedback based on the agent's response but reports its probability independently, as well as Propaganda and Consultancy. The alignment measure is not shown to be judge accuracy, and the results are on 100 GSM8K questions with one judge.

Kenton et al. state their study is limited by using LLM judges instead of humans. Rahman et al. compare both and report default GPT-4o (69.8%) and Qwen2.5-7B (70.7%) debate judges are comparable to human judges (70.1%), while persona-based GPT-4o judges are higher (up to 78.5%); this is one domain with GPT-4o debaters.

Kirchner et al. call for studying what assistance best helps humans judge large-model solutions. Wen et al. report that when humans judge Qwen2.5 recursive self-critiques, their accuracy at later stages exceeds the AI's previous-stage accuracy (e.g. 53.12% at critique, 7.03 points above the AI's 46.09%); tasks are multiple-choice and the questions were filtered by model accuracy.

Wen et al. ask whether scalable oversight methods such as debate work against misleading errors. Arnesen et al. report trained debaters add 96% more quoted words and their win rates transfer between judges (correlation 0.98), while trained consultants' transfer only at 0.51, which the authors read as consultants learning features idiosyncratically convincing to their judge; the judges are LLMs (a trained GPT-4-Turbo judge and an untrained GPT-4o judge).

Arnesen et al. say they focus only on reading comprehension with an information-access expertise gap. Rahman et al. report debate beats consultancy by 4-10% for human judges on COVID-19 and climate claims; the debaters are two AI systems and the Study I judges are humans. Rahman et al.'s Study I judges were recruited with either mainstream or skeptical beliefs on claims where people hold strong prior beliefs, and the improvement was most significant for mainstream-belief judges, so the study concerns whether debate can guide biased judges, while Arnesen et al.'s expertise gap relies on asymmetric access to textual information; Study II uses AI judges.

Arnesen et al. do not rule out that stronger models find judge-perplexing strategies such as obfuscated arguments. Brown-Cohen et al. propose prover-estimator debate, in which, under stability assumptions, an honest debater can win with a strategy requiring computational efficiency comparable to its opponent; it is a theoretical recursive protocol, not the QuALITY debate Arnesen et al. train.

Hammond and Adam-Day list not evaluating simultaneous versus sequential debate as a limitation of their own protocols, which they evaluate on only two domains, with a graph isomorphism task and a code-validation task. Sudhir et al. report no significant effect from switching between simultaneous and sequential debate or changing turn count, with a gpt-4o-mini judge on GSM8K, so the gap and the result concern different tasks; Hammond and Adam-Day train their agents, while the passage does not say whether Sudhir et al.'s debaters are trained.

Hammond and Adam-Day call for results on how computational abilities affect weaker agents' ability to verify stronger ones. Engels et al. fit scaling laws in which oversight-specific Elo is a double-ReLU function of general intelligence for Guards and Houdinis across four games and analyse nested oversight; these are empirical Elo fits, not learning-theoretic results.

Lang, Huang and Li, whose method is used to create a better weak supervisor to elicit the capabilities of strong models, ask which other combinations of scalable oversight and weak-to-strong generalisation work. Wen et al. report that when supervised models are larger than a fixed 7B critic, higher-order critiques generally give better PR scores than lower-order critiques, which they read as support for recursive self-critiquing as a scalable oversight approach where a weaker overseer supervises a stronger model. The passages do not show whether Wen et al.'s method is itself such a combination, so Wen et al.'s result does not answer Lang et al.'s question and neither bears on the other's claim; the link is navigation only until Wen et al.'s method is shown to combine scalable oversight with weak-to-strong generalisation.

Buhl et al. list as open whether prover-estimator debate avoids obfuscation and whether its debaters can be built in polynomial time. Theorem 6.1 (soundness) gives, for every prover, an estimator among circuits of size O(q 2^(3q) n d^2 / eta^2) with oracle access to the prover that caps a dishonest prover's payoff, and stresses that stability is needed only for completeness; the size bound is exponential in width q.

Buhl et al. ask for protocols that do not require stability, since it may not hold for relevant queries. Brown-Cohen et al. state rho-stability is required only for usefulness (completeness), not for safety: without it an honest estimator can still beat any incorrect argument by a dishonest prover; it does not address the gerrymandering concern across subclaims.

Buhl et al. note most debate experiments use QuALITY with simple low-depth protocols and ask whether debate measurably improves performance and what systematic errors humans make. Rahman et al. report debate improves human accuracy and calibration over consultancy on COVID-19 and climate claims, with smaller gains for skeptical-prior judges; the debaters are two AI advisors arguing opposing sides.

Parrish et al. conclude that, for reading comprehension, debate is not a helpful format, since judges perform similarly with or without two-turn arguments. Michael et al. report 84% judge accuracy for interactive human debate versus 74% for consultancy on QuALITY-hard; settings differ sharply: Michael et al.'s judges never see the passage, debates are interactive and unbounded, and the baseline is consultancy rather than no arguments.

Parrish et al. report human-written single-turn arguments did not improve time-limited judges' accuracy. Khan et al. report that, for the most persuasive models, non-expert human judges reach 88% with debate versus 60% naive on QuALITY HARD. Khan et al.'s setting is information-asymmetric with LLM debaters, while Parrish et al.'s judges have 90 s of passage access and read human-written single-turn arguments (snippets are a separate baseline), so the null and positive results come from different settings.

Khan et al. report that the Elo advantage of being assigned the correct answer increases for models with higher aggregate Elo in QuALITY debates, and that this holds across different judges. Kenton et al. find a positive correct-answer Elo advantage for every debater but not as clear a trend of it growing with aggregate Elo (slightly easier for honest debaters on extractive tasks, less clear on closed tasks), with a Gemini Pro 1.5 judge across extractive and closed tasks.

Du et al.'s results table has the rows Single Agent, Single Agent (Reflection), Multi-Agent (Majority) and Multi-Agent (Debate) and the columns Arithmetic (%), Grade School Math (%) and Chess (∆PS), and the cited lines then list eight scores from 67.0 ± 4.7 to 85.0 ± 3.5, so Du et al. compare multi-agent debate with multi-agent majority voting. Choi, Zhu and Li report that majority voting performs on par with MAD in most cases and say these findings suggest that MAD's effectiveness is largely driven by model ensembling rather than the iterative debate process itself.

Du et al. conclude from qualitative cases where all agents start wrong but end right that debate does not only amplify an initially present correct answer. Choi, Zhu and Li prove that under their condition (1) an agent's belief sequence is a martingale: its expected belief at the next round equals its current belief; individual cases can still go wrong-to-right under a martingale.

Du et al. report multi-agent debate improves reasoning and factuality, and present it as a complementary approach. Smit et al. report no protocol dominates on all datasets, Medprompt seems to perform best overall, and the debating protocols do not outperform the other protocols on the reasoning datasets. Both discuss whether multi-agent debate helps LLM reasoning, but the cited Du et al. passage compares debate with no other prompting protocol, and the cited Smit et al. lines compare the debating protocols with the other protocols as a group without showing a debating protocol failing to improve over a single agent, so neither bears on the other's claim and the link is navigation only.

Liang et al. report that on Counter-Intuitive AR (Table 3), Self-Reflect only marginally improves over the GPT-3.5-Turbo baseline, CoT and Self-Consistency bring more improvements, and their MAD framework, though not as good as GPT-4, outperforms all the other compared methods based on GPT-3.5-Turbo. Smit et al. list CIAR among their reasoning datasets (CosmosQA, CIAR and GPQA, alongside three standard medical datasets) and report that no protocol dominates on all datasets, that Medprompt seems to perform best overall, and that the debating protocols do not outperform the other protocols on the reasoning datasets. Smit et al.'s statement covers the reasoning datasets together rather than CIAR alone, and the compared methods differ (Smit et al. name Medprompt and Ensemble Refinement, Liang et al. name CoT, Self-Consistency and Self-Reflect), so the cited lines do not show a direct contradiction on CIAR. Both papers ask whether debate outperforms other prompting methods, in these different settings.

Burns et al. report strong students consistently outperform weak supervisors and present this as a route to eliciting strong capabilities. Yang et al. report weak-to-strong deception in all their settings, where strong models misbehave in cases the weak model does not know, intensifying as the capability gap grows; Yang et al. study multi-objective harmlessness alignment with conflicting targets, not Burns et al.'s single-objective tasks.

Hase et al. suggest from strong easy-to-hard generalization that scalable oversight may be easier than previously thought. Burns et al. report naive weak-to-strong generalization on ChatGPT reward modeling recovers only about 10% of the gap (almost never above 20%) and say their results suggest that naively using weak, human-level supervision will be insufficient to align strong, superhuman models; the two vary different axes (label difficulty versus supervisor strength).

Burns et al. define PGR as the fraction of the performance gap between the weak and strong ceiling models that is recovered with weak supervision. Goel et al. say PGR normalises the gain over the weak supervisor by an 'upper-bound' obtained by training the strong student on ground-truth labels, and that leveraging complementary knowledge effectively might actually allow Sw2s > Sgt, questioning that upper bound. They report a ceiling estimate of +14.1 for their Elicitation ∪ Complementary estimate versus +11.2 for the previous ground-truth elicitation estimate; the cited passages do not show whether this higher estimate is achievable.

Hase et al. define Supervision Gap Recovered with hard-data finetuning as the 100% reference. Sun et al. decline to define an SGR or PGR analogue because models trained only on easier tasks, particularly with RL, sometimes outperform those trained on all levels, which would push such metrics above 100%; Sun et al. report generator performance on the MATH500 test set, with generators optionally optimised by the evaluator, while Hase et al. compare finetuning on easy, hard or no data (zero-shot).

Anil et al. prove verifier-leading Stackelberg equilibria are necessary and sufficient for complete and sound protocols under their assumptions (realizable complete and sound verifier, instance revealed after the verifier commits). Hammond and Adam-Day say Anil et al.'s adp correspondence holds when prover strategies are deterministic functions from inputs to messages and verifier strategies are convex combinations of deterministic decision functions, and that relaxing these restrictions means the correspondence no longer holds. Their Proposition 7 gives a probabilistic decision problem and adp game where, although a valid proof with completeness error 0 exists, being a verifier-leading Stackelberg equilibrium is neither necessary nor sufficient for validity.

Saunders et al. report critique assistance helps labelers find about 50% more critiques of model- or human-written answers. McAleese et al. report broadly negative results when measuring human judge accuracy directly on hard competition-code problems: LLM critiques struggled to help contractors identify the correct solution within 20 minutes; the outcome measure (choosing the correct solution versus counting flaws found) and domain differ.

Michael et al. report that 52% of consultancy mistakes involve judges not getting key evidence from a dishonest consultant, and attribute consultancy's omitted key evidence to there being no opponent to call out misrepresentation of the evidence or to provide contradictory evidence. Arnesen et al. report double consultancy, where both sides' speeches are shown but never see each other, reaches 75% versus debate 77% (single consultancy 68%), suggesting most of the gain comes from seeing both sides rather than refutation. Because double consultancy shows the judge both sides without letting either side see the other's arguments, the result bears only on the call-out (refutation) part of Michael et al.'s explanation, not on the provision of contradictory evidence; judges are a fine-tuned GPT-4-Turbo, not humans.

Khan et al. report that best-of-N and critique-and-refinement make consultants relatively more persuasive for the incorrect answer, lowering judge accuracy. Arnesen et al. find no apparent relationship between trained consultant skill and judge accuracy; Arnesen et al. train Llama3-8B with DPO and use a fine-tuned GPT-4-Turbo judge, while Khan et al. apply best-of-N and critique-and-refinement to consultant models fine-tuned using RLHF, which tend to already perform well when advocating correct answers, and they give this as the reason optimisation might disproportionately improve advocacy for incorrect answers.

Khan et al. report that across all protocols humans have higher judge accuracy than LLM judges. Rahman et al. report default GPT-4o and Qwen2.5-7B debate judges are comparable to humans (69.8% and 70.7% vs 70.1%) and persona-based GPT-4o judges exceed them (up to 78.5%) on COVID-19 claims; the cited Khan et al. passage does not name its task or its LLM judges, and only it describes its debates as information-asymmetric.

Khan et al. report, for the most persuasive models, non-expert judge accuracy of 88% (humans) and 76% (LLMs) with debate versus 78% and 54% with consultancy. Sudhir et al. argue that judge accuracy relative to consultancy is the wrong alignment metric and that ASD, the score difference between arguing the true and false answer, is equivalent to judge accuracy for simultaneous debate but not for consultancy, so the baseline comparison in previous debate experiments is incorrect; if Khan et al.'s debates are simultaneous, only the consultancy side of the comparison would be affected.

Choi, Zhu and Li prove majority voting succeeds with probability approaching 1 as N grows, assuming homogeneous independent agents whose top belief is on the correct answer. Goel et al. say that as model blind-spots get harder to detect, models also make more similar mistakes, and that if this trend continues it could undermine benefits from using LM juries by compromising independence; Goel et al.'s passage concerns similar mistakes across models, while Choi et al.'s agents share homogeneous initial beliefs, so the challenge is to the independence assumption in practice.

Irving et al.'s Theorem 1 shows polynomial-step debate with a polynomial-time judge decides PSPACE under optimal play. Brown-Cohen et al.'s Theorem 5.1 gives a bisection protocol (A states a middle configuration, B picks a half) deciding any time-T, space-S oracle computation as an (O(T log T), O(S log T), O(1))-debate protocol, which the authors compare with doubly-efficient interactive proofs.

Brown-Cohen, Irving and Piliouras introduce doubly-efficient debate, in which two polynomial-time provers compete so that, under appropriate assumptions, any polynomial-time computation can be verified with a constant number of human-judgement queries. Brown-Cohen et al. (2025) propose a new recursive debate protocol that, under stability assumptions, keeps the honest debater's required efficiency comparable to its opponent's while addressing the obfuscated arguments problem that affects existing recursive protocols. Both ask whether debate can work with efficient debaters, in different settings.

Michael et al. state that their approach builds on Irving et al.'s AI Safety via Debate proposal, with notable differences: they assign debaters answer choices instead of letting them choose their own, and they allow the judge to interact with the debaters between each turn. Irving et al. define a debate game where two agents state answers, alternate statements and a judge picks the winner. Michael et al. define a debate where the judge states prior credences, interjects between turns, ends the debate when ready, and debaters can include certified verbatim quotes from the story up to l_q characters per turn; these additions change the game from fixed alternation to judge-controlled interaction.

Michael et al. define consultancy with a single expert assigned the correct or incorrect answer with 50% probability and judge-ended sessions. Khan et al. use the consultancy baseline established by Michael et al. for comparison with debate, with an LLM consultant for a pre-determined number of rounds matching debate.

Michael et al. define interactive information-asymmetric debate where debaters read the story and the judge sees only arguments and certified quotes. Arnesen et al. follow Michael et al. on information access but use a two-turn simultaneous structure similar to Khan et al. (opening claims without seeing each other, then follow-ups).

Anil et al. introduce prover-verifier games with one untrusted prover and one trusted verifier on decision problems. Hammond and Adam-Day define a generalised PVG as a messaging game among n_p provers and n_v verifiers on probabilistic decision problems, starting from a common input and ending with a deciding verifier's 0/1 output, so the single-prover, single-verifier game is a special case.

Anil et al. prove verifier-leading Stackelberg equilibria are necessary and sufficient for complete and sound protocols in verifier-leading sequential PVG formulations where the problem instance is revealed after the verifier picks its strategy. Hammond and Adam-Day prove that for a probabilistic decision problem with a valid proof system a profile is a valid interactive proof iff it is an approximate verifier-leading Stackelberg equilibrium of a nip game, and note the challenge of learning to minimise worst-case rather than expected loss. The cited passages show two parallel results, not one building on the other.

Anil et al. prove verifier-leading Stackelberg equilibria are necessary and sufficient for complete and sound protocols in verifier-leading sequential PVG formulations where the problem instance is revealed after the verifier picks its strategy. Kirchner et al.'s Theorem 1 proves the same equivalence for a PVG with verifier utility RV and prover utility RP, assuming H is the set of all deterministic mappings from X to Z.

Anil et al. define the desired protocol by perfect recall (completeness) and perfect precision (soundness). Kirchner et al. relax these to a high helpful-prover pass rate with high verifier recall, and a low false-positive rate on adversarial inputs from limited optimisation, calling the helpful prover legible to the verifier when both hold.

Christiano et al. define Amplify_H(X), a human plus copies of the current agent, as the system the agent learns from in the same way it would learn from H alone. Leike et al. define recursive reward modeling, where A(k-1) assists the user in evaluating outcomes when training A(k). Neither cited passage refers to the other scheme, so the passages show two schemes for the same problem in different settings rather than one building on the other.

Christiano et al. instantiate amplification by delegation: H names subquestions, X answers them and H composes an answer. Wu et al. describe task decomposition: a human splits a parent task into simpler subtasks whose responses help a human provide a training signal, and the resulting dataset is used to train a model to perform two fundamental operations, the first being Decompose. The cited Wu et al. passage does not mention Christiano et al. or amplification, so the link records two parallel decomposition schemes for the same question rather than one building on the other.

Saunders et al. fine-tune models with behavioural cloning to write critiques that help humans find flaws in summaries. McAleese et al. train critic models with RLHF to write critiques of model-written code, and report critiques preferred over human critiques in 63% of cases on natural errors.

Saunders et al. define a critique task (point out a flaw in an answer) plus critiqueability and helpfulness discrimination tasks. Wen et al. define a hierarchy from response to first-order critique to critique of critique (C2) and higher orders, using pairwise comparisons at each critique level; the cited Wen et al. passage cites standard RLHF practice (Ouyang et al., 2022) and does not refer to Saunders et al., so it does not show that Wen et al. build on Saunders et al.'s tasks.

Lightman et al. define ORMs trained on final results and PRMs trained on per-step feedback. Sun et al. train ORMs and PRMs as easy-to-hard evaluators on a training set often made of labelled easy tasks paired with unlabelled hard tasks given only as questions, and use their generalisation to supervise the generator on hard tasks.

Burns et al. define the weak-to-strong setup: a small model finetuned on ground truth produces weak labels on held-out data, and a strong pretrained model finetuned on them is the strong student. Lang, Huang and Li keep this pipeline but finetune the weak model with debate arguments from the large model appended as context, and use an ensemble of such weak models to label data for the strong student.

Liang et al. propose MAD with two debaters in a 'tit for tat' state and a managing judge. Smit et al. attribute Multi-Persona to Liang et al., describing it as a MAD strategy in which an affirmative agent (angel) and a negative agent (devil) each provide an answer to a judge agent who manages the process and obtains a final solution. Smit et al. add an agreement-intensity prompt ('agree with the other agents X% of the time') applied to Multi-Persona and to other MAD systems.

Leike et al. define recursive reward modeling, where A(k-1) helps the user evaluate A(k). Engels et al. group recursive reward modeling, iterated amplification and weak-to-strong generalization as sharing the goal of weaker systems overseeing stronger ones and define Nested Scalable Oversight as the iterated process in which weaker systems oversee stronger ones, which then oversee even stronger models in the next stage.

Khan et al. introduce persuasiveness, measured by judge approval without ground-truth labels, to study debate scaling. Sudhir et al. state they generalise the debater Elo used in earlier debate experiments, which they equate with persuasiveness in Khan et al., to other scalable oversight protocols with Expected Agent Score, EAS = (log p_true, log p_false) dotted with q, as a pure capability measure; only Khan et al.'s persuasiveness is stated to be label-free.

Buhl et al. require a debate protocol that avoids obfuscated arguments and rely on a forthcoming protocol that needs a stability assumption: the computation is not sensitive to small variations in input probabilities. Brown-Cohen et al. formalise rho-stability (argument validity cannot hinge on arbitrarily small changes in subclaim probabilities) for prover-estimator debate and require it only for usefulness, not safety.

Buhl et al.'s key claim 2 is that in approximate global equilibria the system errs on at most an eps'-fraction of cases. They require a debate protocol in whose global equilibrium both debaters are honest, and say they wrote the sketch with prover-estimator debate (forthcoming) in mind, though the argument structure should apply to other protocols. Brown-Cohen et al. state that debaters can be trained in prover-estimator debate via standard methods that converge to Stackelberg equilibria in zero-sum games, and that, given rho-stability and A-provability, Theorem 6.2 implies A will produce the correct answer with probability at least 1 - 5 eps, which is the kind of result claim 2 needs.

Irving et al. define debate as a zero-sum game in which each agent maximises its probability of winning. Brown-Cohen et al. define a debate, citing Irving et al., as a triple (A, B, V) of oracle Turing machines with an oracle O and a common input, in which provers A and B exchange messages over k rounds and the verifier V then outputs zero or one. Their training mapping has pretrained debaters trained by self-play to win the zero-sum game given by the debate protocol, with human labels only for verifier queries, and trusts A's output at inference unless B aborts or points out a flaw; this relies on the debate they credit to Irving et al., in their own formalisation.

Irving et al. state debate's usefulness rests on the empirical claim that it is harder to lie than to refute a lie. Lang, Huang and Li state that in their illustrative SciQ debate the incorrect debater's misleading arguments are convincingly refuted, that this conforms to Irving et al.'s claim, and that debate arguments can therefore inform weak models; the evidence offered is one example debate.

Burns et al. define PGR as the fraction of the performance gap between the weak and strong ceiling models that is recovered with weak supervision, that is (weak-to-strong minus weak) divided by (strong ceiling minus weak). Lang, Huang and Li define PGR with the same formula, so their PGR values are on Burns et al.'s scale.

Irving et al. show n-round debate with a polynomial-time judge corresponds to formulas with alternating quantifiers (Sigma_n P for fixed n, PSPACE with polynomially many rounds). Leike et al. credit this analogy to Irving et al. and argue reward modeling resembles NP while recursive reward modeling at depth k targets problems with k alternating quantifiers; no theorem is proved.

Amodei et al. describe scalable oversight as the case where the correct objective is known or can be evaluated, e.g. by a human, but too expensively to do often. Bowman et al. define scalable oversight as providing reliable supervision (labels, rewards, critiques) that stays effective past human-level performance, citing Amodei et al.; the emphasis shifts from evaluation cost to capability beyond the supervisor.

Bowman et al. define scalable oversight as reliable supervision that remains effective past broadly human-level performance. Sudhir et al. cite Bowman et al. and describe it as a feedback mechanism that scales to superhuman intelligence, framing it either as a training method making honesty the best policy or as an inference-time mechanism-design problem.

Irving et al. define debate as a zero-sum game where each agent maximises its probability of winning. Chen et al. state AI Safety via Debate is predominantly captured by zero-sum games, where coarse correlated and correlated equilibria are Nash equilibria, so the game can be played efficiently by minimising external regret.

Leike et al.'s Assumption 2 is that for many tasks evaluating outcomes is easier than producing correct behaviour. Sun et al. state their method is motivated by evaluation being easier than generation and train a verifier on easy tasks to supervise a generator on hard tasks; they hypothesise that an evaluator may offer a degree of easy-to-hard generalisation useful for improving a generator, which is consistent with the assumption but does not test it.

Leike et al.'s Assumption 2 is that for many tasks evaluating outcomes is easier than producing the correct behaviour. Wen et al. hypothesise that critique of critique can be easier than critique itself, extending the widely-accepted observation that verification is easier than generation to the critique domain, and that this relation holds recursively; the passage builds on the same idea but does not attribute it to Leike et al.

Kenton et al. define debate where a judge LLM answers after viewing two debater LLMs argue opposite answers. Engels et al. say they model their debate setup on Kenton et al. (2024), with the debaters as Houdinis and the judge as the Guard, and report judge (Guard) performance scaling with general intelligence rating while debater (Houdini) performance stays constant on TruthfulQA, with similar behaviour on QuALITY and PrOntoQA, and call this consistent with prior work including Kenton et al.

Du et al. define multiagent debate: each agent answers, then repeatedly reads others' answers via a consensus prompt and updates. Smit et al. describe Society of Minds, which they attribute to Du et al. ('Society of Minds (SoM) Du et al. (2023) propose a MAD approach'), as agents giving answers to each other over rounds, optionally summarised, so their SoM description relies on Du et al.'s procedure.

Irving et al. state debate rests on the empirical claim that lying is harder than refuting a lie. Khan et al. report debaters earn higher Elo when assigned the correct answer and that the advantage grows with aggregate Elo, which they read as truth-telling being easier than lying in QuALITY debates; the evidence is specific to that setting.

Khan et al. report that, for the most persuasive models, non-expert LLM judges reach 76% with debate versus 54% with consultancy on QuALITY HARD. Kenton et al. report that on extractive tasks (QuALITY, BoolQ, GPQA-extractive) where only debaters see the article, judges are more accurate under debate than under consultancy and QA without article, except that the weakest judge Gemma7B does no better with debate than with QA without article; both use LLM debaters with privileged article access.

Khan et al., who use GPT-4-Turbo to judge their debates, report a strong correlation between judge accuracy and debater aggregate rating: as debaters are optimised against win rate (judge preference), judge accuracy improves. Arnesen et al. report that the fully DPO-trained debate model is associated with 4 percentage points higher judge accuracy than the SFT model (p < 10^-6), although the judge is never trained on transcripts from these debaters.

Michael et al. report dishonest human consultants deceive judges 40% of the time on QuALITY-hard. Khan et al. report that in consultancy incorrect experts cause low judge accuracy, suggesting it is easier to be misled in consultancy. Michael et al. also found judges reach 87% accuracy with dishonest AI consultants, which they explain at least in part by their AIs being much worse at arguing convincingly for the wrong answer, so the support comes from Michael et al.'s human consultants rather than their AI consultants.

Michael et al. report 46% of incorrectly judged human debates involve the correct debater missing an important argument or piece of evidence (and 33% the judge ending early). Khan et al. report the most common human-judge error in LLM debate is weak arguments from the correct debater, usually poor choice of quotes, and take their LLM debaters to be the bottleneck.

Michael et al. report judge accuracy of 84% for human debate versus 74% for human consultancy, with AI debate at 78% and AI consultancy at 80%. Khan et al. report that, for their most persuasive models, non-expert human judges reach 88% with debate versus 78% with consultancy, so a debate-over-consultancy gap appears with model debaters, unlike Michael et al.'s AI debate and consultancy. The two papers ask the same question with different debaters, so Khan et al.'s result is not evidence for the gap Michael et al. found with human debaters.

Burns et al. report bootstrapping through intermediate model sizes improves PGR on chess puzzles, with only small gains on NLP tasks and none in the reward modeling setting in preliminary experiments. Yang et al. report that when the weak model supervises an intermediate model that then supervises Mistral-7B, generalization performance can improve and deception scores are consistently lower. Both ask whether supervising through an intermediate model helps, but in different settings: Yang et al. study weak-to-strong deception with Mistral-7B as the strong model, while Burns et al.'s positive result is on chess and they saw no improvement in the reward modeling setting.

Lightman et al. report process supervision significantly outperforms outcome supervision for training models to solve problems from the MATH dataset. Sun et al. report that with RL, PRM rewards are more beneficial than final-answer rewards for hard tasks, with models trained on PRM rewards reaching 34.0; Sun et al.'s PRM rewards use human supervision on the easy tasks.

Kenton et al. report that changes to the setup (number of turns, best-of-N sampling, few-shot, chain-of-thought) seem to have little effect on results. Sudhir et al. report no significant effect of changing the number of turns or switching between simultaneous and sequential debate; the passages do not show whether the two papers share agents, judges, tasks or metric.

Saunders et al. state critique-based assistance does not address problems a model cannot put into words and that the CD gap may stay large. Michael et al. ask whether debate can extract inductive or tacit knowledge lacking short citeable justifications, noting that in their human debates debaters needed to reveal only about 3.5% of the story on average; one concerns critique-based assistance, the other debate grounded in textual evidence from a story.

Sudhir et al. propose looking at worst-case rather than average-case ASD as an important direction, because superhuman oversight must prevent rare catastrophic actions. Brown-Cohen et al. state prover-estimator debate's guarantees are average-case only and the judge's payoff imperfectly tracks correctness, but say they believe such an average-case analysis is necessary and call formalising this an open question; one is an empirical benchmark metric, the other a complexity-theoretic guarantee.

Michael et al. report 84% for human debate versus 74% for human consultancy on QuALITY-hard with hidden passages. Rahman et al. report 70.1% for GPT-4o debate versus 60.0% for consultancy on COVID-19 claims for judges with strong priors; the domains (fiction QA versus contested health claims), debaters and information conditions differ, so effect sizes should not be pooled.

Hase et al. report LMs finetuned or prompted with easy data often do nearly as well on hard data as with hard data. Sun et al. report reward models trained on easy problems (e.g. levels 1-3) can supervise generators on hard problems via re-ranking or RL; Hase et al. study generators directly via ICL, probes and QLoRA, Sun et al. study evaluators, so results should not be transferred between them.

Burns et al. report strong models naively finetuned on weak-model labels outperform their supervisors but, with naive finetuning alone, fall far short of full capability, and that simple methods such as an auxiliary confidence loss can often significantly improve weak-to-strong generalization. Wen et al. report ICM, using no external labels, matches golden-label training and outperforms crowdsourced human supervision on GSM8K-verification, TruthfulQA and Alpaca reward modeling; one uses labels from a weak model, the other self-generated labels, and model families differ.

Burns et al. report larger strong students agree less with the weak supervisor's errors despite being trained to imitate it. Lang, Sontag and Vijayaraghavan prove a pseudolabel-correction bound (Theorem 4.1): when M'(S_i^good, F) satisfies (c, q)-expansion on (S_i^bad, S_i^good), a classifier f that disagrees with the weak labels or is not robust on S_i with small enough probability has true error on S_i bounded by its error against the weak labels plus terms in alpha_i and the expansion parameter c; this is a formal bound, not a measurement on trained students like Burns et al.'s.

Kenton et al. report stronger debaters (higher Elo) yield higher judge accuracy on extractive tasks with a Gemini Pro 1.5 judge, but are less differentiated on closed tasks. Engels et al. report that on TruthfulQA debater (Houdini) performance stays constant while the judge's (Guard's) performance scales with general intelligence rating, with similar scaling on QuALITY and PrOntoQA and mostly flat performance for both roles on BoolQ; they relate performance to general intelligence rating, whereas Kenton et al. relate judge accuracy to debaters' aggregate Elo.

Burns et al. report bootstrapping through two intermediate sizes improves PGR on chess, especially for larger students, but in preliminary experiments helps little on NLP and not on reward modeling. Engels et al.'s numerical NSO model finds multiple oversight steps can raise Guard log odds from -3 to 3, with more steps optimal as the general capability gap grows, but one step appears optimal in Houdini-favoured games; one is a training experiment, the other an Elo model of adversarial oversight games.

Kirchner et al. report that RL on answer correctness alone makes GSM solutions less legible, with human accuracy and speed deteriorating under a 45-second limit.
