chat models. Unsupervised labeling via the ICM algorithm achieves at least 81% accuracy across
all models—surpassing both zero-shot and many-shot chat baselines and matching or exceeding the
performance of human fine-tuned counterparts. Furthermore, fine-tuning pretrained models on their
own ICM-generated labels (FT-Unsupervised) yields modest but consistent improvements over the
raw ICM predictions.

questions.question: Do scalable oversight methods (critique, debate, decomposition) work on misleading errors?
questions.asked_by: Wen et al., Language Models Learn to Mislead Humans via RLHF
questions.remaining_question: Do task decomposition, critique and debate assistance raise human evaluators' detection of unintended, RLHF-induced misleading errors (U-SOPHISTRY) on tasks like QuALITY and APPS above unassisted evaluation, and does any gain hold when the policy is trained against the assisted evaluator?

links.reason: An answer would show whether debate, critique or decomposition assistance lets human evaluators catch misleading outputs that fool unassisted evaluators, evidence on whether misleading work escapes the reward signal as D4.2 worries, but for RLHF-induced errors on tasks like QuALITY and APPS rather than subtly misleading research papers.
The answer would be human-trial evidence on a systematic error of assisted human evaluators (being misled by plausible wrong outputs), the kind of evidence E6.1 says is needed, in QuALITY and APPS.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2608.17776v1: Debate Training Reduces Reward Hacking in RLAIF
findings.claim: RL fine-tuning against a frozen, weaker LLM judge, the single-player RLAIF baseline quickly learned to exploit the judge (e.g. meta-commentary impersonating the judge, authoritative language, declaring problems flawed, highly rewarded despite incorrect answers), whereas debate with a critic maintained judge performance and reached higher peak validation accuracy (45% of the performance gap recovered). The authors caution that math with verifiable answers may behave differently from tasks with ambiguous or hard-to-evaluate correctness.
findings.setting: Empirical, RL training. Gemini 2.5 Flash-class policy and critic, frozen Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite judge; mathematics tasks with verifiable final answers; LLM judge, no human evaluators.
findings.bears_on: Debate against misleading, judge-exploiting outputs that RL learns against an AI evaluator (an analogue of RLHF-induced misleading); not human evaluators and not U-SOPHISTRY on QuALITY or APPS.

passages.text:
We demonstrate that RL finetuning an LLM using debate, a two-player adversarial game between a
generator and a critic adjudicated by a weaker LLM judge, reduces reward hacking compared to a
reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) baseline. Reward hacking is a central obstacle in
RLAIF: as training progresses, the policy learns to exploit systematic errors in its AI judge, degrading task
performance, a problem that worsens precisely when the judge is weaker than the policy, the setting most
relevant to overseeing increasingly capable AI systems. We study mathematics tasks, where final-answer
correctness is verifiable, allowing us to measure reward hacking dynamics. We train a Gemini 2.5
Flash-class policy with a frozen, weaker Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite judge, comparing a single-player RLAIF
baseline against debate. While the baseline quickly hacks the judge, debate maintains judge performance
throughout training, leading to a higher peak validation accuracy (45% performance gap recovered)
that persists through many RL steps. Additional experiments show that: 1) further weakening the judge

Qualitative observations. In the baseline ( 𝐴), Alice develops explicit reward hacking behaviours
such as inserting meta-commentary impersonating the judge or Bob; using authoritative language;
relies heavily on mathematical shortcuts; and declaring a problem flawed. These behaviours are
associated with high reward despite incorrect answers. The impersonation behaviour hits an occurrence rate of about 90% when Alice is 30% of the way through training and almost 100% by the
time training reaches 60%. Other findings include: judge replicating all of Alice’s steps, accepting
unjustified claims and assumptions. The length of the judge’s visible response steadily decreases from
3,000 to 500 words, and its evaluation becomes more superficial.

Task domain and evaluation scope. We evaluate on mathematical reasoning with automatically
verifiable correctness. The tasks most relevant to scalable oversight, involving value judgments,
ambiguous correctness, or outputs difficult for humans to evaluate, may behave differently. In
non-verifiable or subjective domains, the lack of an objective truth anchor means that persuasive,
sycophantic, or plausible-sounding arguments may be substantially harder for an LLM judge to
distinguish from sound reasoning compared to crisp mathematical deductions.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2608.06422v1: Sharding Prevents LLM Oversight Failures and Adversarial Exploitation
findings.claim: On legal-work grading, a one-sided persuasion memo (underlying work fixed) raised the strongest judge's over-acceptance of genuinely unmet criteria from 0.33 to 0.51; sharding the criteria lowered it to 0.40 and adding an opposing advocate to 0.16. Under five rounds of adaptive rewriting, cumulative acceptance of unmet criteria was 0.55 against sharding versus 0.39 with opposition (false-reject cost 0.24-0.31); the authors note this contrast was tested on one dataset and depends on judge capability, and that within-criterion decomposition gave no general accuracy benefit.
findings.setting: Empirical. LLM judges (the strongest judge tested, and a Sonnet tier) facing an attacker that writes one-sided compliance memos and, in a second experiment, adapts them over five rounds; JudgmentBench legal tasks scored against lawyer labels; within-criterion decomposition also compared on other datasets, including clinical ones. Differs from the question's setting: no human evaluators, and the misleading content is an attacker's persuasion, not errors learned through RLHF.
findings.bears_on: Debate-style opposition and a decomposition-like intervention (splitting requirements into shards) against deliberately misleading presentations of failing work: opposition helps against per-criterion persuasion, sharding against overload attacks.

passages.text:
The two failures call for different interventions. Sharding first ensures that every criterion receives scrutiny.
An opposing advocate then ensures that the scrutiny is not one-sided: for each claimed success, a skeptical
challenger states the case that the criterion is unmet, and an adjudicator compares the claim with its rebuttal
and the underlying evidence. On JudgmentBench with the strongest judge tested, the one-sided compliance
memo raises over-acceptance from 0.33 to 0.51. Sharding reduces it to 0.40; an evidence directive and three
same-side skeptics reach 0.37, while adding the opposing advocate reduces it to 0.16, below the unattacked
sharded baseline of 0.26 (Figure 4(a); Table S22). More attention is therefore sufficient when the attack
exploits omitted examination, but balanced evidence is required when the attack persuades a decision that is
already being examined.

We next let the attacker adapt. After each round, it learns which criteria the deployed defense still rejects
and rewrites the memo to target them. Against sharding alone, each newly targeted criterion still arrives as a
one-sided case; across five rounds the attacker obtains acceptance on 0.55 of the genuinely unmet criteria
against the strongest judge tested, while opposition generates a fresh counterargument for each target and
limits the cumulative rate to 0.39, at a false-reject cost of 0.24 to 0.31 (Figure 4(b); Table S21). The separation
is larger at the Sonnet tier: the attacker reaches 0.96 against sharding alone and 0.56 against opposition,
which retains kappa 0.40 against the lawyer labels at the final round, compared with 0.12 for the single judge
and 0.07 for sharding alone, at a 0.20 false-reject rate on genuinely met criteria (Table S12). Sharding is
effective against load-based attacks but not universal: it removes decisions settled without examination, while
opposition addresses misleading arguments considered during examination.

tasks, the persuasion attack increases over-acceptance less for the strongest judge tested (0.330 to 0.505)

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2512.02157v1: Factor(T,U): Factored Cognition Strengthens Monitoring of Untrusted AI
findings.claim: In the APPS control setting, red-teamed against backdoor attempts from an adversarial GPT-4.1 Nano, adding factored cognition to a trusted monitoring protocol can boost safety from 41% to 63%; the authors find safety improves because monitor performance improves, as attacks on Factor(D,U) child tasks are more suspicious than on the root tasks. The protocols show low usefulness in APPS, and the authors say the powerful decomposer allowance, needed given the weakness of T, may result in overestimating their safety.
findings.setting: Empirical AI-control evaluation. APPS coding tasks; an adversarial GPT-4.1 Nano attempts backdoors; trusted monitoring, with a weak trusted model T and a powerful decomposer allowance; monitor suspiciousness compared for child and root tasks. Differs from the question's setting: no human evaluators, and the errors are deliberately inserted backdoors, not errors learned through RLHF.
findings.bears_on: Task decomposition as an oversight aid against deliberately inserted, hidden errors (backdoors): positive for monitor detection in this setting.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2512.14745v1: Factor(U,T): Controlling Untrusted AI by Monitoring their Plans
findings.claim: When an untrusted (stronger but potentially malicious) model decomposes and trusted models implement the child tasks, monitors distinguishing malicious from honest decompositions performed poorly (AUROC 0.52) compared with monitors evaluating complete Python solutions (AUROC 0.96); Factor(D,U), which uses a trusted decomposer and monitors concrete child solutions, reached AUROC 0.96 and 1.2% ASR. The authors note untrusted decomposers can create misleading child tasks that appear benign, and suggest improving decomposition-only monitor elicitation alone may be insufficient to close the safety gap.
findings.setting: Empirical AI-control evaluation. BigCodeBench Python coding tasks, with backdoors as the attack; an untrusted (stronger) decomposer and trusted (weaker) implementers; monitors of decompositions compared with monitors of complete or child solutions. Differs from the question's setting: no human evaluators, and the misleading content is a deliberately malicious decomposition, not errors learned through RLHF.
findings.bears_on: Limits of decomposition-based oversight when the decomposition itself is adversarial: plan-only monitoring fails on misleading child tasks, implementation-level monitoring works.

This approach works when decomposition is simple.
However, for many tasks, decomposition itself may be the
hardest step, requiring the most capable models available—
which may be untrusted (Shlegeris 2023). While using
stronger, untrusted decomposers enables more useful protocols, it also introduces new threats: untrusted decomposers

First, decomposition capabilities may require validation before deployment. While Factor(U ,T ) enables use of
stronger models for decomposition, the severe monitoring
degradation suggests that untrusted decomposition introduces security challenges that current monitoring techniques
cannot reliably address.
Second, we can assume that protocols relying on trusted

The architectural nature of the discrimination loss suggests that improving decomposition-only monitor elicitation

questions.question: How can model similarity be measured on free-text answers and reasoning, to study its role in debate and process supervision?
questions.asked_by: Goel et al., Great Models Think Alike and this Undermines AI Oversight
questions.remaining_question: Does a free-text similarity measure between models (for example residualised compression distance on outputs, the judge's likelihood of a response, or a CAPA-style agreement computed on answer-matched free-form answers) predict how often a weaker judge sides with a similar debater in judged debate with ground-truth labels, and how often a process reward model misses step errors made by a similar policy?

links.reason: An answer would show whether a model judge's similarity to a debater predicts it siding with that debater, a possible systematic error of a model judge relevant to C5.2's bound on the simulated judge, though C5.2's named failure mode is scheming and the question's judges are LLMs, not simulations of human judgement.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2609.03422v1: Inferred Generative-Process Diversity Predicts Correlated Failure Across Language Models
findings.claim: Across 38 language models, a model-pair distance computed on raw free-text responses to open-ended prompts (Normalised Compression Distance residualised against a permutation control) is reported to predict cross-task variation in chance-corrected correlated wrong answers on ten disjoint closed-form benchmark families beyond semantic similarity and capability (cross-benchmark partial rank association -0.216, 95% interval [-0.309, -0.122]). The authors call the evidence pairwise and observational and leave ensemble or multi-agent benefits to future work.
findings.setting: Empirical, observational. 38 LMs; the distance is estimated from repeated responses to 100 open-ended Infinity-Chat prompts (model input-output behaviour only, no agent scaffolding); the outcome is chance-corrected correlated wrong-answer agreement on ten closed-form benchmark families; controls for semantic distance and pair capability. No debate, judge, or process-supervision experiment.
findings.bears_on: The 'how can similarity be measured on free-text answers' half: a free-text, black-box model-pair similarity validated against correlated failure. It does not measure reasoning traces and does not study a role in debate or process supervision.

passages.text:
Drawing from Algorithmic Information Theory, we use Normalised Compression
Distance between raw model outputs, residualised against a permutation control,
as a measure of inferred generative-process diversity. Across 38 language models,
this measure identifies population structure missed by semantic similarity and
predicts cross-task variation in chance-corrected correlated failure among model
pairs across ten disjoint benchmark families, beyond semantic similarity and modelpair capability. The cross-benchmark partial rank association is −0.216 with a 95%
interval of [−0.309, −0.122], and the estimate is negative on all ten benchmarks.
These results indicate that increased generative-process diversity is associated
with reduced correlated failure in model pairs that is not attributable to semantic
similarity or capability. Inferred generative-process diversity offers a novel and
practical approach for investigating diversity of multi-model systems in safetyrelevant contexts.

answers among pairs in the same model population on ten disjoint closed-form benchmark families,
controlling for semantic similarity and capability. The design tests whether process-level variation
inferred from observable model behaviour identifies model pairs whose failures are more independent

findings.claim: In a fully crossed pairwise LLM-as-judge design with 9,312 judgments, the authors report that a common per-family statistic is strongly confounded with candidate quality (r = 0.95 with Bradley-Terry ability); under a corrected estimator that holds the candidate family fixed and compares judges, all four families show a positive same-family lift (3.4-8.4 percentage points; global FPS 0.067). findings.later_paper: arXiv 2603.05293v1: Knowledge Divergence and the Value of Debate for Scalable Oversight
findings.claim: Under the paper's assumptions, the debate advantage has an exact closed form governed by principal angles between the debating models' representation subspaces: with identical training corpora debate reduces to an RLAIF-like setting where a single-agent method recovers the same optimum, and same-weight self-play debate is the degenerate zero-angle case with no advantage. The author offers this as a theoretical explanation of Goel et al.'s finding and states that the knowledge-divergent regime where debate has practical bite is not studied empirically.
findings.setting: Theory: proofs parameterizing debate's value by principal angles between the debating models' representation subspaces (closed form, regimes, existence and negative results); the passages report no experiments. Similarity here is the principal-angle spectrum between representation subspaces, not a metric computed on free text.
findings.bears_on: The role of similarity in debate (prediction: debate's value vanishes as models converge); offers no practical free-text similarity metric and no test of the prediction.

passages.text:
AI safety via debate and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) are both proposed methods for scalable oversight of advanced AI systems, yet no formal framework
relates them or characterizes when debate offers an advantage. We analyze this by parameterizing debate’s value through the geometry of knowledge divergence between debating
models. Using principal angles between models’ representation subspaces, we prove that
the debate advantage admits an exact closed
form. When models share identical training
corpora, debate reduces to RLAIF-like where
a single-agent method recovers the same optimum. When models possess divergent knowledge, debate advantage scales with a phase
transition from quadratic regime (debate offers
negligible benefit) to linear regime (debate is
essential). We classify three regimes of knowledge divergence (shared, one-sided, and compositional) and provide existence results showing that debate can achieve outcomes inaccessible to either model alone, alongside a negative
result showing that sufficiently strong adversarial incentives cause coordination failure in
the compositional regime, with a sharp threshold separating effective from ineffective debate.

Irving et al. (2018) notes that “symmetry between the agents’ capabilities is easy to achieve,
since we can use the same weights for both agents
via self play.” Our work reveals this as a feature
that eliminates debate’s advantage because sameweight debate corresponds to θi = 0 whcih is the
degenerate case. The complexity-theoretic results
on debate (Brown-Cohen et al., 2024, 2025, 2026)
establish what debate can solve in principle, but
our framework shows these results have practical
bite only in the knowledge-divergent regime that
no current work studies empirically.

Goel et al. (2025) empirically demonstrate that
as frontier models become more capable, their errors become more correlated, and that diversity
between models improves oversight quality. Our
framework provides a theoretical explanation as
models converge on the same training data and
representations, principal angles shrink and the debate advantage vanishes. The empirical benefits of
model diversity in oversight are consistent with the
tan(θ/2) scaling.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2606.20632v2: Post-Training Recipe, More Than Model Family, Shapes Multi-Agent LLM Conversational Behavior
findings.claim: The authors compute mean pairwise Jensen-Shannon divergence over the distribution of scored conversational moves (challenge, repair, hedging) in multi-LLM conversations and report 0.034 for a family-diverse three-model panel versus 0.251 for a recipe-diverse same-base Llama panel. findings.later_paper: arXiv 2604.03809v1: Representational Collapse in Multi-Agent LLM Committees: Measurement and Diversity-Aware Consensus

No judged debate, no oversight, no process supervision; similarity within one model, not across models.
findings.bears_on: One way to measure similarity of free-text reasoning traces and its sensitivity to the embedding proxy; within one model, not across models, and not tied to oversight.

Multi-agent LLM committees replicate the same model under different role prompts and
aggregate outputs by majority vote, implicitly assuming that agents contribute complementary
evidence. We embed each agent’s chain-of-thought rationale and measure pairwise similarity:
across 100 GSM8K questions with three Qwen2.5-14B agents, mean cosine similarity is 0.888
and effective rank is 2.17 out of 3.0, a failure mode we term representational collapse. DALC,
a training-free consensus protocol that computes diversity weights from embedding geometry,
reaches 87% on GSM8K versus 84% for self-consistency at 26% lower token cost. Ablation
experiments reveal 1–3 point per-protocol run-to-run variance, confirm that hint sharing contributes more than diversity weighting alone, and show that encoder choice strongly modulates
collapse severity (cosine 0.908 with mxbai versus 0.888 with nomic) and downstream accuracy.
The more robust finding is that collapse is measurable, worsens on harder tasks, and that the
choice of embedding proxy is a first-order design decision for any latent communication protocol.

questions.question: Can a debate protocol avoid needing stability, for example by targeting honesty instead of correctness?
questions.asked_by: Buhl et al., An alignment safety case sketch based on debate
questions.remaining_question: Can a recursive debate protocol that rewards honest reporting of the debaters' beliefs (rather than deciding L(x)), or that uses non-black-box access to human judgment or the debaters' bounded computation, achieve completeness on decompositions whose fractional block sensitivity rho makes rho^d superpolynomial, while keeping prover-estimator debate's soundness without stability (an average-case guarantee)?

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2506.13609v2: Avoiding Obfuscation with Prover-Estimator Debate
findings.claim: The authors introduce rho-stability (the validity of arguments cannot hinge on arbitrarily small changes in subclaim probabilities) for prover-estimator debate and state that they require it only for usefulness, not safety: even if stability does not hold, an honest estimator can still win against any incorrect argument by a dishonest prover. They note that a rho-stable decomposition is required only in the completeness case, so the protocol must ensure B can still win when a dishonest debater A produces an unstable decomposition. Their results hold in an average-case rather than a worst-case sense: they do not prove that the judge can always tell which debater is correct on every question.
findings.setting: Theory. Prover-estimator debate: the prover (Alice) decomposes a problem into subclaims, the estimator (Bob) assigns probabilities to them, and the prover uses these to choose which subclaim to debate further; stability is required only in the completeness case; results hold in an average-case, not a worst-case, sense.
findings.bears_on: Whether a protocol can avoid needing stability: for this protocol, yes for safety (soundness, in an average-case sense), no for usefulness (completeness); does not address an honesty-targeting variant.

the prover (Alice) decomposes a problem into subclaims. The estimator (Bob) has the sole task of assigning
probabilities to the prover’s subclaims. The prover uses these probabilities to decide which subclaim to
recursively debate further. This departs from previous debate protocols, where the opponent selects which
subclaim to challenge. We show that Bob can always produce probabilities that are indistinguishable from
the truth by Alice, while expending computational effort not too much greater than Alice. Alice cannot
therefore (on average) select a subproblem where Bob is non-trivially wrong. However, prover-estimator
debate has limitations. Alice’s task becomes harder because Bob can defeat an argument by assigning low
probabilities to many subclaims. This rules out certain delicate, yet correct arguments that are highly
sensitive to the probabilities assigned to subproblems. We formalize this condition by introducing a stability
requirement, ρ-stability, which demands that the validity of arguments cannot hinge on arbitrarily small
changes in subclaim probabilities1 . We require stability only for usefulness, not safety: even if stability does
not hold, an honest estimator can still win against any incorrect argument by a dishonest prover.

Notice that we only require that L admits an A-provable, ρ-stable decomposition in the completeness case.
This means that a dishonest debater A may produce an incorrect decomposition into queries y k for some input
x such that MD (x, y k , z k ) is not ρ-stable, with answers to queries that cannot be answered by any function
in A. Therefore, our protocol must account for situations where A produces an unstable decomposition into
hard-to-answer queries, and ensure B is still able to win.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2610.02557v1: How to Have a Sensitive Debate: An Instance-Optimal Protocol for AI Debate
findings.claim: The authors show that any protocol with only black-box access to human judgments must make at least Omega(rho^d) queries to find a flawed sub-claim with constant probability, matching the cost of their FBS debate protocol; the bound holds instance-wise: if the best decomposition of an original claim x into a tree of sub-claims has fractional block sensitivity rho in each step, then rho^d queries are required on that instance. In their lower-bound model an honest Bob and the judge form one adaptive checker that receives the full visible tree and outputs a bit intended to equal L(x), with pairwise-distinct leaf queries. They say the black-box assumption is critical for the lower bound and view the result as showing it must be relaxed to make further progress, and they leave open whether a protocol can go beyond this barrier by using Bob's ability to solve the same problems as Alice or some other relaxation of the black-box oracle assumption.
findings.setting: Theory. Debate over a recursive decomposition of a claim into a tree of sub-claims of depth d; human judgment modelled as a black box accessible only via queries; instance-wise lower bound on the queries needed to find a flawed sub-claim, in a model where an honest Bob and the judge form one adaptive checker that receives the full visible tree, makes adaptive queries to the oracle O and outputs a bit intended to equal L(x); leaf queries assumed pairwise distinct.
findings.bears_on: Narrows how a stability-free protocol could work: with black-box judgment, a checker that must output L(x) needs Omega(rho^d) queries when the best decomposition has fractional block sensitivity rho in each step, leaving non-black-box judgment or exploiting the debaters' computation as routes. The bound concerns deciding L(x); it does not address a protocol that targets honesty instead of correctness.

Instance-wise optimality. Finally, we show in Section 5 that any protocol with only black-box
access to human judgments must make at least Ω(ρd ) queries to find a flawed sub-claim with constant
probability, matching the cost of our FBS debate protocol. This lower bound holds instance-wise: if
the best decomposition of an original claim x into a tree of sub-claims has fractional block sensitivity
ρ in each step, then ρd queries are required on that particular instance x. The assumption of
black-box access to human judgments is critical for the lower bound to hold. One can view this
instance-wise optimality as demonstrating that the black-box judgment assumption, which is common
to all prior theoretical work on debate, must be relaxed in order to make further progress on debate
protocols.

Given this discussion, the question remains: is it possible to design a protocol that goes beyond
the fractional block sensitivity barrier we identify? One might hope that utilizing Bob’s ability
to solve the same problems as Alice could help with this issue, perhaps by allowing Bob to take
advantage of Alice’s computational limitations in some way. Alternatively, our lower bounds only
apply when human judgment is modeled as a black box, accessible only via queries. Classical
results in interactive proofs like IP = PSPACE show that opening up the black box yields much
stronger protocols. It seems implausible that these methods can be adapted to the case of human
judgment—one would need to essentially be able to “read the code” that implements the human
judgment. However, it is still possible that some other relaxation of the black-box oracle assumption
could lead to better debate protocols.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2610.02557v1: How to Have a Sensitive Debate: An Instance-Optimal Protocol for AI Debate
findings.claim: The authors state that their new debate protocol provides worst-case guarantees for the original, stronger dominant-strategy equilibrium concept and handles exactly the same class of sufficiently stable problems as prover-estimator debate. In FBS debate, an honest Alice can always win (completeness, Theorem 4.1) if there exists a decomposition tree for x in which Alice can calculate the children of any non-leaf node in time T_D, can solve L at any node in time T and Q queries to O, and every non-leaf node has fractional block sensitivity at most rho at the correct answers to its sub-problems. Honestly and correctly following the protocol is a dominant strategy for each debater, in contrast to prover-estimator debate, which only guarantees soundness under a Stackelberg equilibrium condition.
findings.setting: Theory. FBS debate over a decomposition tree T of a claim x, with queries to an oracle O; completeness and soundness hold whatever strategy the opponent uses (soundness with overwhelming probability); for completeness Alice must compute each non-leaf node's children in time T_D, solve each node (Solvability) in time T with Q queries to O, and meet the fractional block sensitivity bound at every non-leaf node. That the protocol handles the same class of sufficiently stable problems as prover-estimator debate is the authors' statement; the quoted lines do not prove it.
findings.bears_on: By the authors' account, a later protocol handles exactly the same class of sufficiently stable problems as prover-estimator debate, and its completeness theorem assumes a decomposition with bounded fractional block sensitivity; it changes the guarantees (worst-case, with honesty and correctness as dominant strategies) rather than dropping the stability restriction, so it does not show a protocol that avoids needing stability.

passages.text:
In this paper we design a new debate protocol that provides worst-case guarantees for the original,
stronger dominant-strategy equilibrium concept. The protocol handles exactly the same class of
sufficiently stable problems as prover-estimator debate, while also being simpler to execute and
analyze. We further prove that this protocol is instance optimal unless further structural assumptions
are made on the human judgments used to verify debates.

Theorem 4.1 (Completeness). Let T, TD , Q be three
parameters. An honest Alice can always win

in the FBS debate on input x in O d · (TD + q · T ) time and O(d · q · Q) queries to O if there exists
a decomposition tree T for x such that
• Alice can calculate the children of any non-leaf node in T in time TD .
• Alice can solve L(x̂u ) at any node u in T in time T and Q queries to O;

(Solvability)

• For every non-leaf node u in T , if y are the sub-problems in the child nodes of u and z are the
correct answers to y, then fbsz (MD (x̂u , y, ·)) ≤ ρ.

Honesty and correctness are dominant strategies. Our protocol for fractional block sensitivity
(FBS) debate satisfies the key properties of completeness and soundness. Completeness requires that
if the original claim x is correct, then no matter what strategy Bob employs, Alice can always win
by honestly and correctly decomposing every claim. Similarly, soundness requires that if the original
claim x is incorrect, then no matter what strategy Alice employs, Bob can win with overwhelming
probability by honestly following the prescribed protocol. In other words, honestly and correctly
following the prescribed protocol is a dominant strategy for each player in the debate game. This is
in contrast to the prior prover-estimator debate protocol, which only guarantees soundness under the
following Stackelberg equilibrium condition: for any dishonest strategy selected by Alice, there exists
a winning strategy by Bob, which in general depends on Alice’s strategy in a potentially complicated
way. This is a technically much weaker condition, and in practice training for dominant strategy
equilibria is much more stable and tractable than Stackelberg equilibria.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2607.03561v1: How to Avoid Debate: Scalable AI Safety via Doubly-Efficient Interactive Proofs
findings.claim: In work that presents single-prover interactive proofs as a way to avoid debate, the authors suggest that many natural tasks may be able to be made robust (output unchanged when a small fraction of answers to oracle queries are modified) using redundancy, e.g. rephrasing the question or asking multiple people and taking the majority answer, and pose formalising this intuition as a theoretical model as an open question.
findings.setting: Theory: doubly-efficient single-prover interactive proofs and arguments for oracle-aided computations (the oracle may be human judgment) that are robust, i.e. the output does not change if at most a small fraction of oracle answers are incorrect; not a debate protocol. The suggestion about redundancy is informal.
findings.bears_on: The 'transform an unstable computation into a stable one' route: raised as an open direction in a neighbouring model, not achieved.

passages.text:
Robust computation. We say that a computation is robust if the output does not change even if
a small fraction of answers to oracle queries are modified. Intuitively, robustness allows a verifier to
“spot-check” oracle calls instead of having to evaluate all of them. It seems natural to assume that the
computation is robust, especially in the setting where the oracle is taken to represent human judgment:
human judgment is already error-prone, so as a safeguard, the output of the computation should not
change if a small number of the human answers change, otherwise the output is not very meaningful.
More broadly, many natural tasks may be able to be made robust using redundancy, e.g., in the case of
human judgment, we might rephrase the question or ask multiple people and take the majority answer.

• Scope of robust computation. As mentioned previously, many natural tasks may be able to
be made robust using redundancy. Can we formalize this intuition as some theoretical model (and
then apply our protocol for robust computation)?

In this work, we show how to avoid debate: we initiate the study of single-prover interactive proofs
for AI safety. Prior results in single-prover interactive proofs do not immediately carry over to the AI
safety setting: for example, they do not work when the computation has access to an oracle, such as
to human judgment or an external database such as the web. We present doubly-efficient single-prover
interactive proofs and arguments for oracle-aided computations (also known as relativizing proofs),
in the settings where (1) the computation is robust, in the sense that the output does not change if
at most a small fraction of the answers to oracle queries are incorrect, or (2) the oracle is a low-degree
polynomial. These results suggest that interactive verification is possible even without debate, under
structured or noise-tolerant oracle access.

(2) Adaptive provers: our necessity results fix the prover's tree; whether a prover that changes decomposition in response to B's estimates can beat the barrier min(r^(d+1), 1/fbs_alpha(F_T)) of its realised tree is not settled here. (3) Beyond black-box judges and unbounded opponents: 2610.02557v1 settles the query lower bound for black-box judges (fixed revealed tree, distinct leaves); protocols with structured or partly transparent judgments, and opponents that cannot find sensitive blocks, remain open, as that paper also states (p14 L47-56). And which natural problem classes (beyond weighted thresholds, Lipschitz aggregators, AND-like proofs) have small global fbs for some A-provable decomposition? (5) Q47: a protocol that provably elicits coherent, leaf-calibrated reports with an fbs-independent incentive gap, and a useful notion of honesty whose conversion to correctness costs less than fbs_alpha(F_T), are open; the unstable-to-stable transformation route (M to M*) is not addressed here. (6) General-q proofs of the phi-uniform closed form and of the unstable-cut statement (both only derived and checked for q = 2, 3).

questions.asked_by: Brown-Cohen et al., Avoiding Obfuscation with Prover-Estimator Debate
questions.remaining_question: Is there a debate protocol, trained end to end, whose guarantees survive (a) human judges with bounded but systematic, correlated errors and (b) debaters free to choose among winning decompositions or subclaims to leak or steer information, and does it keep its reward-hacking benefits in domains without verifiable ground truth?

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2608.17776v1: Debate Training Reduces Reward Hacking in RLAIF
findings.claim: On mathematics tasks with verifiable final-answer correctness, the authors train a Gemini 2.5 Flash-class policy with a frozen, weaker Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite judge: the single-player RLAIF baseline quickly hacks the judge, while debate maintains judge performance and reaches a higher peak validation accuracy (45% performance gap recovered). findings.setting: Experiment, RL training: a Gemini 2.5 Flash-class policy trained with debate (adversarial self-play) or a single-player RLAIF baseline, with a frozen, weaker Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite judge; mathematics tasks with verifiable final-answer correctness; critique word limits used to balance the game. Our results suggest a positive update on the promise of debate as a practical training protocol for
scalable oversight. Prior empirical work found debate’s benefits limited to toy settings, informationasymmetric tasks, or inference-only evaluation; and concurrent work struggles with saturation and
reward hacking. In contrast, we find that the key benefit of debate emerges through RL training itself:
the adversarial self-play keeps rewards in check, maintains judge performance leading to higher peak
accuracy that persists through many RL steps, and prevents the accuracy collapse seen under the
RLAIF baseline.
This has practical implications. In domains without ground-truth labels, practitioners cannot
identify when reward hacking begins or select an optimal checkpoint. A training protocol that sustains
peak performance by default, rather than requiring careful early stopping, is therefore of direct value.
Debate appears to provide this property, at least in our setting.
Several important questions remain open, we discuss some in the Limitations below (Section 5.2).
The most critical is whether debate’s benefits transfer to domains without verifiable ground truth.

relevant to overseeing increasingly capable AI systems. We study mathematics tasks, where final-answer
correctness is verifiable, allowing us to measure reward hacking dynamics. We train a Gemini 2.5
Flash-class policy with a frozen, weaker Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite judge, comparing a single-player RLAIF
baseline against debate. While the baseline quickly hacks the judge, debate maintains judge performance
throughout training, leading to a higher peak validation accuracy (45% performance gap recovered)
that persists through many RL steps. Additional experiments show that: 1) further weakening the judge
leads to faster hacking, but this can be compensated by adding an additional debate round; 2) debate
incentives override prompted misalignment; 3) RL using an LLM judge has a smaller train/validation
reward gap than RL from verifiable rewards; 4) learning to critique to convince the judge using ground
truth labels is possible but slow. Taken together, our results are a positive update on the feasibility of
debate, while highlighting that balancing multi-agent training is critical: without player constraints,

adversarial training risks defaulting to critic judge-hacking. We show that critique word limits (effective
up to 150 words) successfully balance the game and avoid judge hacking, though this introduces a
trade-off by restricting critic expressive clarity.

We test whether debate can improve RLHF-style reward labels. In visible-information code and logic
settings, proposer–critic debate helps only when the critic is a better correctness classifier than the
judge evaluating the answer alone. At test time, most of the gain comes from the critic’s opening

reward labels in verifiable domains, not a complete safety mechanism or evidence that the result
transfers to fuzzier domains without further validation.

Despite theoretical promise, debate as a scalable oversight protocol has produced
mixed empirical results: gains in some settings, and null effects in others, especially
when the judge does not have information hidden from it. We study proposer-critic
debate in a stronger-debater/weaker-judge setting on programmatically verifiable
code and logic tasks. Debate helps the judge over a consultancy baseline when the
critic provides a usable advantage: the critic’s classification ability must exceed
the judge’s, and the judge must treat critic speeches as claims to verify rather than
testimony to summarize.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2609.29189v1: When Honesty is Not Enough in AI Debate
findings.claim: The authors formalise task-admissible latent optimisation: because a correct verdict does not fix which arguments support it, debaters can encode information about a hidden variable while still winning; in debate with cross-examination the disclosed information can grow linearly with the number of rounds, and a sliding-window consistency check narrows the persistent perturbations compatible with task success, which the authors say limits the studied disclosure strategy rather than establishing transcript confidentiality.
findings.setting: Theoretical framework (strategic interactive oversight) instantiated as a proof-of-concept in debate with cross-examination; the latent objective is disclosing information about a hidden variable; the mitigation studied is a sliding-window consistency check. Differs from the question's ask: debate with cross-examination, not prover-estimator debate's subclaims.
findings.bears_on: The authors' ask about 'the potential for debaters to hide information in the subclaims': formalises a closely related channel (free choice among winning strategies) and gives a partial mitigation in a different protocol.

passages.text:
on incentivizing honest arguments that lead to correct verdicts. Yet a correct verdict need not uniquely
determine the arguments used to support it. Agents may retain discretion over which correct claims
to present, how to frame them, and in what order to disclose them. This residual freedom can allow
agents to shape what the verifier learns beyond the task-relevant conclusion, pursuing latent objectives
without compromising verdict correctness.
To study this phenomenon, we introduce the framework strategic interactive oversight (SIO), which
treats oversight jointly as a verification mechanism and a strategic communication channel. Within this
framework, we formalise the notion of task-admissible latent optimisation, which entails the pursuit of
latent objectives while maintaining a prescribed task performance. As proof-of-concept, we instantiate
SIO in the establish protocol debate with cross-examination and quantify a tradeoff between task success
and information disclosure about a hidden variable. The trade-off identifies a strategic window in
which substantial disclosure remains compatible with task admissibility. Towards mitigation, we reduce

required for the task. In standard debate, the task objective is to win. However, there are generally
many strategies by which it can do so. This non-uniqueness allows the debater to select, among
task-successful strategies, those that additionally encode information about the latent variable. We
show that, even when the disclosure in each round is small, the total information revealed can grow
linearly with the number of cross-examination rounds. Local report-accuracy conditions and a correct
terminal verdict therefore do not prevent the oversight interaction from becoming a channel for latent
information.

Third, as a step towards mitigation, we augment cross-examination with a sliding-window consistency
check that tests for persistent discrepancies across rounds. This narrows the range of persistent
perturbations compatible with task success, at the cost of additional verifier work, while leaving the
debaters’ per-round sampling work unchanged. The resulting guarantee limits the disclosure strategy
studied here rather than establishing transcript confidentiality.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2610.05461v1: AI Safety via Debate is Compromised by Cognitive Biases
findings.claim: In a study with 369 participants judging 68 LLM-generated dialogues about detective mysteries, four bias interventions applied to either side, pooled across bias types, significantly shifted judgments toward the manipulated side; the authors conclude that cognitive biases can shift adjudications toward the side deploying a bias-inducing intervention, potentially weakening the connection between winning a debate and correctness, and suggest asking judges to assess evidentiary support, logical validity and responses to counterarguments before adjudicating, interventions they say warrant further evaluation.
findings.setting: Human-subject experiment: 369 participants adjudicate 68 LLM-generated dialogues (inspired by competitive debate) about detective mysteries with known culprits; one of four interventions (anchoring, fallacy oversight, pro-jargon, verbosity) is applied to the side advocating for the true culprit or for an innocent suspect. The proposed procedural mitigations were not tested.
findings.bears_on: The authors' ask for 'protocols which mitigate systematic errors in human input': confirms the vulnerability empirically and proposes, but does not test, mitigations.

passages.text:

cognitive biases or irrational models of decision-making may give a competitive advantage to strategies
that exploit those imperfections. Our results identify one such vulnerability: cognitive biases can shift
adjudications toward the side deploying a bias-inducing intervention, potentially weakening the connection
between winning a debate and correctness.

Adapting these approaches to AI debate could involve asking judges to assess evidentiary support, logical
validity, and responses to counterarguments before adjudicating; such interventions warrant further evaluation. These procedural changes should complement approaches that model systematic biases in human
judgment.

we investigate whether this advantage persists when debaters use rhetorical strategies that exploit biases
in human judgment. Inspired by competitive debate, we construct 68 LLM-generated dialogues about
detective mysteries with known culprits, spanning four interventions: anchoring, fallacy oversight, projargon, and verbosity. We apply each intervention to either the side advocating for the true culprit or
the side advocating for an innocent suspect, allowing us to distinguish influence on adjudication from
correctness. In a study with 369 participants, we find that, pooled across bias types, these interventions
significantly shift judgments toward the manipulated side. These findings expose a vulnerability in
debate-based supervision: human adjudication is sensitive to manipulative rhetorical strategies.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2607.03561v1: How to Avoid Debate: Scalable AI Safety via Doubly-Efficient Interactive Proofs
findings.claim: The authors give doubly-efficient single-prover interactive proofs and arguments for oracle-aided computations when the computation is robust to a small fraction of incorrect oracle (e.g. human-judgment) answers or the oracle is a low-degree polynomial, suggesting verification without debate under structured or noise-tolerant oracle access.
findings.setting: Theory (interactive proofs). Single prover, no opponent; oracle models human judgment or external databases; robustness to a small fraction of wrong oracle answers.
findings.bears_on: Systematic human error: an alternative to debate tolerating a bounded fraction of wrong human answers; not a debate variant and not targeted at systematic (correlated) errors.

passages.text:
convince a weak verifier, or a human, of the correctness of their claim. However, debate assumes that
the two AI models possess equal abilities and that one of them is truthful, which may not be realistic.
In this work, we show how to avoid debate: we initiate the study of single-prover interactive proofs
for AI safety. Prior results in single-prover interactive proofs do not immediately carry over to the AI
safety setting: for example, they do not work when the computation has access to an oracle, such as
to human judgment or an external database such as the web. We present doubly-efficient single-prover
interactive proofs and arguments for oracle-aided computations (also known as relativizing proofs),
in the settings where (1) the computation is robust, in the sense that the output does not change if
at most a small fraction of the answers to oracle queries are incorrect, or (2) the oracle is a low-degree
polynomial. These results suggest that interactive verification is possible even without debate, under
structured or noise-tolerant oracle access.

questions.question: Open: is stability necessary, and which problems admit stable decompositions?
questions.asked_by: Brown-Cohen et al., Avoiding Obfuscation with Prover-Estimator Debate
questions.remaining_question: Outside the black-box judgment model of 2610.02557 (e.g. exploiting the debaters' equal computational power or a relaxed judgment oracle), can a debate protocol efficiently decide problems all of whose decompositions have large fractional block sensitivity, and which natural problem classes (proof-like vs evidence-aggregating claims) admit decompositions with rho^d polynomial in the input size?

links.reason: An answer would show whether stability is necessary for debate to decide some problems and which problem classes admit stable decompositions, evidence on whether C4.6 can be supported or avoided, though the questions the case needs would still have to be placed in those classes.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2610.02557v1: How to Have a Sensitive Debate: An Instance-Optimal Protocol for AI Debate
findings.claim: The authors state that their protocol and matching lower bound show that fractional block sensitivity precisely characterizes the set of problems efficiently solvable by debate within the recursive-decomposition framework, that prover-estimator stability is equivalent to fractional block sensitivity, and that their new protocol handles the same class of sufficiently stable problems with worst-case correctness and dominant-strategy honesty, and is instance-wise optimal among protocols making only black-box queries to human judgments.
findings.setting: Theory, as above (recursive decomposition, black-box judgment oracle); the equivalence with prover-estimator stability is asserted in the text, not proved in the quoted lines.
findings.bears_on: Second part ('which problems admit stable decompositions'): restates the class as problems with low-FBS decompositions and shows it is the right class for black-box debate, but gives no structural classification of natural problems (e.g. proofs vs noisy empirical evidence).

passages.text:
Our protocol and matching lower bound show that fractional block sensitivity precisely characterizes
the set of problems that can be efficiently solved by debate within this recursive-decomposition
framework. Notably, the protocol does not require Bob to determine whether or not Alice’s answers
to subproblems are correct, but only to understand the structure of the argument well enough to
sample subproblems to which the outcome is sufficiently sensitive. This stands in contrast to the

but solves a more limited class of problems. Most closely related to our work is that of Brown-Cohen
et al. [2025], which introduced the prover-estimator debate protocol to handle a broader class of
recursively decomposable problems for computationally bounded debaters. Prover-estimator debate
introduced the notion of stability (equivalent to fractional block sensitivity) that we study in this
paper.

to complex problems with limited supervision. Specifically, the current best protocol has been
shown to work for all problems that have sufficiently stable decompositions into subproblems.
In this paper, we design a new protocol for this same class of problems that improves on the
prior work in several ways. First, correctness holds in a worst-case rather than an average-case
sense. Second, being honest and correct is a dominant-strategy equilibrium for both debaters,
rather than a Stackelberg equilibrium. Finally, we prove black-box lower bounds, showing that
our new protocol is instance-wise optimal. That is, no protocol for this class of problems can
outperform ours while making only black-box queries to human judgments. We obtain these
results by relating the notion of stable problem decompositions to the concept of fractional block
sensitivity from query complexity.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2607.03561v1: How to Avoid Debate: Scalable AI Safety via Doubly-Efficient Interactive Proofs
findings.claim: The authors summarise Barbara, Chiesa and Guan (BCG25) as proving that no interactive proofs relativize for all computations, and explain it intuitively: if a computation makes many queries to a random oracle and its output is unstable, hinging on all oracle answers being correct, the verifier would need to check every oracle call.
findings.setting: Theory, single-prover relativizing interactive proofs; the cited impossibility is in the random oracle model; the 'intuitively' gloss is the authors'.
findings.bears_on: Necessity of a stability-like condition in a neighbouring model (single prover, no opposing debater), not in prover-estimator debate.

passages.text:
Unfortunately, Barbara, Chiesa, and Guan [BCG25] prove that there do not exist interactive proofs
that relativize for all computations. Intuitively, their observation is that if the computation uses many
oracle gates to a random oracle, and the output of the computation is unstable, in the sense that it
hinges on the answers of all the oracle queries being correct, then the verifier would need to check the
correctness of every oracle call, and thus would not be efficient.

maths.settled: Q51, depth 1: in the Figure 2 game with r = 1/rho (rho >= 1) on one instance, the honest bound (exists A, for all B, E[payoff] >= 1/rho^2) holds iff the root is rho-stable, i.e. iff fbs_z(f) <= rho; the exact value is 1/(rho max(rho, fbs)). Q51, any depth, Figure 2 with r = 1/rho: if the root node of the prover's tree is not rho-stable, every prover strategy is held below the Theorem 6.1 bound 1/rho^(d+1) by some estimator. So root stability is necessary for the conclusion of Theorem 6.1 on that tree. Q51, margin barrier: for every reward ratio r >= 0, every tree T and every prover using T, some valid estimator holds the expected payoff to <= min(r^(d+1), 1/W) for every fractional packing of sensitive blocks of the path-indexed composed function F_T with total weight W; at the LP optimum, <= min(r^(d+1), 1/fbs_alpha(F_T)). So no choice of the protocol parameter gives the honest prover more than 1/fbs_alpha(F_T), and the conclusion of Theorem 6.1 on T forces fbs_alpha(F_T) <= rho^(d+1). Q51(b), sufficient classes with constants: weighted-margin functions are (sum w)/m-stable; weighted-Lipschitz score thresholds with margin delta are (sum w)/delta-stable; [#true >= theta] is t/(t - theta + 1)-stable at t >= theta true inputs and (q - t)/(theta - t)-stable below (exact: equals fbs for q <= 5); every function is q-stable. Q51(b), lower bounds and one-level composition: k disjoint sensitive blocks rule out rho < k (AND of q bits: best constant exactly q); if inner functions are rho2-stable and the outer function is rho1-stable, the composition is rho1 rho2-stable (inner functions may share inputs).
maths.remains: (1) Exact characterization of completeness for Figure 2 on a fixed tree: an unstable sensitive cut is sufficient for failure (derived) and all-nodes-stable is sufficient for success (Theorem 6.1); the conjecture that 'no unstable sensitive cut' is also sufficient for success (exact for all q = 2, d = 2 trees computed) needs a proof and tests for q >= 3; a closed form for Val(x,T,1/rho) on non-uniform trees is open. (2) Adaptive provers: our necessity results fix the prover's tree; whether a prover that changes decomposition in response to B's estimates can beat the barrier min(r^(d+1), 1/fbs_alpha(F_T)) of its realised tree is not settled here. (3) Beyond black-box judges and unbounded opponents: 2610.02557v1 settles the query lower bound for black-box judges (fixed revealed tree, distinct leaves); protocols with structured or partly transparent judgments, and opponents that cannot find sensitive blocks, remain open, as that paper also states (p14 L47-56). (4) Q51(b) converse: does a decomposition with small global fbs_alpha(F_T) <= R imply one of depth O(d) with local fbs <= C R^(1/d)? And which natural problem classes (beyond weighted thresholds, Lipschitz aggregators, AND-like proofs) have small global fbs for some A-provable decomposition? (5) Q47: a protocol that provably elicits coherent, leaf-calibrated reports with an fbs-independent incentive gap, and a useful notion of honesty whose conversion to correctness costs less than fbs_alpha(F_T), are open; the unstable-to-stable transformation route (M to M*) is not addressed here. (6) General-q proofs of the phi-uniform closed form and of the unstable-cut statement (both only derived and checked for q = 2, 3).

questions.asked_by: Lang et al., Theoretical Analysis of Weak-to-Strong Generalization
questions.remaining_question: Does making the contrastive pretraining objective aware of the pseudolabeler ỹ (e.g. defining or weighting positive pairs with the weak labels) lower the strong student's error on the true labels compared with pseudolabeler-agnostic contrastive pretraining under the same weak labels, and if so, does the gain come with greater measured expansion between correctly and incorrectly pseudolabeled sets?

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2510.07884v3: Contrastive Weak-to-strong Generalization
findings.claim: ConG uses contrastive decoding between the pre- and post-alignment weak models to generate higher-quality training samples for the strong model, motivated by a structural equivalence between implicit rewards and contrastive decoding; the authors report consistent improvements across model families. 'Contrastive' here refers to decoding of the weak supervisor's outputs, not to the strong student's (pre)training objective.
findings.setting: LLM weak-to-strong alignment with samples generated by aligned weak models; empirical; no representation pretraining.
findings.bears_on: Near miss for the question's 'contrastive' ingredient: it changes how weak supervision is generated, not how the student is pretrained.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2412.03881v2: Weak-to-Strong Generalization Through the Data-Centric Lens
findings.claim: Building on Lang et al.'s framework, the authors identify overlap points and give an algorithm that estimates which of several data sources has the largest overlap density, recommending investment in data from sources likely to produce overlaps rather than in algorithms.
findings.setting: Theory building on Lang et al.'s framework plus an algorithm that estimates which of several data sources has the largest overlap density; intervention on data acquisition, not on pretraining.
findings.bears_on: An alternative, data-side way to exploit the expansion framework the question appeals to; does not test contrastive pretraining.

passages.text:
Equipped with this intuition, we characterize the notion of overlap and provide theoretical results
building on a recent theoretical framework for generalization (Lang et al., 2024). In practice, however,
overlap points are latent, and it can be difficult to distinguish between points with just an easy pattern
and those with overlaps. To address this challenge, we introduce an approach for identifying points
with overlaps and build on it to obtain an algorithm that can, when presented with multiple sources of
data, estimate which one contains the largest overlap density. This suggests a future course of action
for practitioners focused on maximizing weak-to-strong generalization: rather than focusing on
algorithms, invest in the data—and specifically into obtaining data from sources that are likely to
produce the most overlaps.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2605.05710v1: On the Blessing of Pre-training in Weak-to-Strong Generalization
findings.claim: In a high-dimensional single-index model with spiked Gaussian data, modeling pretraining as a spectral initialization step (PCA), the authors prove W2S is achievable when pretraining gives a geometric warm start into an effective region, with a generalization bound showing improvement then saturation set by the weak supervisor's bias; they note the PCA proxy may not capture nonlinear feature learning in large models.
findings.setting: Theory: single-index model, spiked Gaussian data, pretraining modelled as an unsupervised spectral initialization step (PCA) that does not see the pseudolabeler; a stylised theoretical model, not contrastive or pseudolabeler-aware pretraining.
findings.bears_on: Links a spectral (pseudolabeler-agnostic) pretraining step to W2S success; does not make pretraining aware of the weak labels.

The paradigm of Weak-to-Strong Generalization (W2SG) suggests that a pretrained strong model can surpass its weak supervisor, yet the decisive role of
pre-training remains theoretically and empirically under-explored. In this work,
we identify pre-training as the essential prerequisite for the emergence of W2SG.
Theoretically, we formalize the W2SG problem within a high-dimensional singleindex model framework using spiked Gaussian data, modeling pre-training as a
spectral initialization step. Building upon prior impossibility results regarding the

when pre-training provides a geometric warm start that places the model within an

questions.question: Why does direct supervision beat recursive critique when a stronger model supervises a weaker one, and would better critique abilities change that?
questions.asked_by: Wen et al., Scalable Oversight for Superhuman AI via Recursive Self-Critiquing
questions.remaining_question: In AI-AI recursive self-critiquing where the critic is stronger than the supervised model, does improving the supervised model's self-critique (for example by RL critique training) or making the critic verify rather than defer to that self-critique remove the advantage of direct critique over higher-order critique on the asking paper's tasks?

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2605.27483v1: Debate Helps Weak Judges Reward Stronger Models
findings.claim: In proposer-critic debate with a stronger debater and a weaker judge, debate raised macro-F1 over consultancy on three of five model pairings and had no effect on two; the authors report that the split follows whether the critic's classifier macro-F1 exceeds the judge's and whether the judge verifies rather than summarises the critic's claims, with verification rates dropping by tens of points once a critic entered on the non-responder pairings. They flag this as a hypothesis well supported within five pairings, not a law.
findings.setting: Empirical. Five stronger-debater/weaker-judge LLM pairings: Qwen3.5-122B/35B, gpt-oss-120B/20B and Qwen3.5-35B/Qwen3-4B on Code Contests, Gemini 3.1 Pro/3 Flash and Opus 4.6/4.5 on ARC-AGI-2; programmatically verifiable tasks; LLM judges; consultancy baseline. No recursive critique and no strong-critic/weak-supervised setting.
findings.bears_on: By analogy only, the 'would better critique abilities change it' part: a critique helps its reader only when the critic out-classifies the reader and the reader verifies it. Not tested for higher-order self-critique by a weaker supervised model read by a stronger critic.

passages.text:
ground truth—proposer–critic debate raises macro-F1 over consultancy on three of five model pairings
and shows no effect on the other two. The split is governed by a single condition: debate helps only
when the critic provides a usable advantage. That condition has two sub-parts, both of which must
hold. First, the critic’s classifier macro-F1 must exceed the opening-only consultancy judge’s—there
has to be a margin worth importing; raw judge capability and the critic’s generator–verifier gap
do not predict the split, but this critic–judge classifier gap does. Second, the judge must treat the
critic’s stance as a claim to verify rather than testimony to summarize. Behavior reviews of the
transcripts (§4.2, Appendix L) show the mechanism: on responder pairings both sub-parts hold and
judges import the critic’s signal; on the two non-responder pairings in our set, both sub-parts fail
together—the critic’s and judge’s binary-classification ability are within noise of each other, and
verification rates drop by tens of percentage points once a critic enters the transcript, with the critic’s
disagreement parsed as testimony rather than a claim to check.

We flag a small-N caveat: with five pairings, the gap diagnostic is a hypothesis well-supported
within our experimental set, not a law established at scale. We also note that with ARC-AGI-2
substantially harder than Code Contests, our pairings do not let us cleanly separate the critic–judge
gap from broader capability differences; the two conditions we identify (judge verification behavior
and critic–judge classifier gap) are themselves capability properties, just more specific ones than
raw solve rate. Whether the same mechanism transfers to fuzzier domains where programmatic
verification is unavailable is a hypothesis warranting further work, not a finding from our experiments.

Debate improves macro-F1 over consultancy on three of five pairings and has no effect on the other
two (Figure 2). It helps Qwen3.5-122B/35B on Code Contests (+14.0pp under our canonical prompt
and +7.3pp under a simpler one, both p < 0.001), and Gemini 3.1 Pro/3 Flash and Opus 4.6/4.5
on ARC-AGI-2 (+14.0pp and +15.7pp, both p < 0.01). It does not help gpt-oss-120B/20B or
Qwen3.5-35B/Qwen3-4B on Code Contests (+1.4pp, p = 0.23 and −0.2pp, p = 0.93). We call the
first group responder pairings and the second non-responder pairings.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2606.00424v2: Weak Critics Make Strong Learners: On-Policy Critique Distillation for Scalable Oversight
findings.claim: With a weak model critiquing a stronger model's answer before the strong model revises, the authors report that weak critiques improved the frozen strong model, but that misleading critiques can hurt performance even relative to no critique; reusing a critique from a chain where a correct answer was revised to an incorrect one ('worst critic') performed worst among the critique-quality baselines on GPQA Diamond, falling slightly below the strong model alone (S) only at pass@16.
findings.setting: Empirical, inference-time critique-and-refine (the paper's training method is not quoted here). A weak critic (W) critiques a frozen strong model's (S) initial answer, which the strong model then revises; Phi-4 results on GPQA Diamond, with IFEval also reported; pass@k. The best/worst-critic baselines are chosen post hoc from outcome labels. Not recursive critique read by a stronger critic.
findings.bears_on: Related evidence that critiques from a weaker model can mislead a stronger model and that critique quality matters, but in a weak-critic/strong-reviser setting, not recursive self-critique judged by a stronger critic.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2509.05396v2: Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Understanding Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate
findings.claim: In multi-agent debate among LLM agents of differing capability, the authors report that introducing a weaker agent into a debate with a stronger one can detrimentally affect the outcome, giving results worse than if the agents had not discussed, and that the weaker agent disrupts the stronger agent's performance. Separately, among agents that change their answers, more shift from correct to incorrect than the reverse, which the authors say indicates that debate can actively mislead agents who started with correct answers.
findings.setting: Empirical. Multi-round multi-agent debate among LLM agents, including debates that mix a weaker and a stronger agent; answer transitions between correct and incorrect tracked across rounds; not recursive critique by a stronger supervisor.
findings.bears_on: Corroborates, in a different protocol, the asking paper's explanation that a weaker model's reasoning can mislead a stronger one; says nothing about whether better critique ability would change the result.

questions.question: Proposed experiments: can RL learn nearly as fast with reward on 10% of episodes?
questions.asked_by: Amodei et al., Concrete Problems in AI Safety
questions.remaining_question: In simple continuous-control tasks (cartpole balance, pendulum swing-up) with deep RL, when the true reward is revealed on only a random 10% of episodes, does an agent that also learns from the unlabeled episodes (e.g. via a learned reward model) match the learning curve of an agent given reward on every episode, and how much does actively choosing the labeled episodes change this?

findings.later_paper: arXiv 1706.03741v4: Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences
findings.claim: The authors report solving Atari games and simulated robot locomotion without access to the reward function while providing feedback (human preferences between pairs of trajectory segments) on less than 1% of the agent's interactions. On the simulated robotics tasks (eight tasks implemented in MuJoCo; the authors also say they included a simple cartpole task, 'pendulum', for comparison) they are 'able to nearly match reinforcement learning' on the real reward with 700 labels; training with learned reward functions tends to be less stable and higher variance, while having a comparable mean performance.
findings.setting: Experiment: RL from preferences between pairs of trajectory segments, without access to the reward function; 700 queries to a human rater, or 350, 700 or 1400 synthetic queries; compared with RL learning from the real reward; eight simulated robotics tasks in MuJoCo (OpenAI Gym, slightly modified) and a simple cartpole task the authors say they included for comparison. Differs from Q02: the feedback is pairwise comparisons of segments, not the true reward revealed on a random 10% of episodes.
findings.bears_on: Q02's core question (can RL do nearly as well with feedback on a small fraction of experience), but with pairwise segment comparisons instead of reward on 10% of episodes, and the passages compare performance ('nearly match'), not explicitly learning speed.

passages.text:
In this work, we explore goals defined in terms of (non-expert) human preferences
between pairs of trajectory segments. We show that this approach can effectively
solve complex RL tasks without access to the reward function, including Atari
games and simulated robot locomotion, while providing feedback on less than
1% of our agent’s interactions with the environment. This reduces the cost of
human oversight far enough that it can be practically applied to state-of-the-art

The first tasks we consider are eight simulated robotics tasks, implemented in MuJoCo (Todorov
et al., 2012), and included in OpenAI Gym (Brockman et al., 2016). We made small modifications
to these tasks in order to avoid encoding information about the task in the environment itself (the
modifications are described in detail in Appendix A). The reward functions in these tasks are linear
functions of distances, positions and velocities, and all are a quadratic function of the features. We
included a simple cartpole task (“pendulum”) for comparison, since this is representative of the
complexity of tasks studied in prior work.
Figure 2 shows the results of training our agent with 700 queries to a human rater, compared to
learning from 350, 700, or 1400 synthetic queries, as well as to RL learning from the real reward.

With 700 labels we are able to nearly match reinforcement learning on all of these tasks. Training
with learned reward functions tends to be less stable and higher variance, while having a comparable
mean performance.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 1706.03741v4: Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences
findings.claim: On Atari games the preference-based method has more difficulty matching RL on the true reward: synthetic labels match or come close to RL on BeamRider and Pong, eventually reach near RL but learn more slowly on Seaquest and Qbert, and never match RL on SpaceInvaders and Breakout.
findings.setting: Experiment: RL from preferences between pairs of trajectory segments, without access to the reward function, on seven Atari games in the Arcade Learning Environment (results named for BeamRider, Pong, Seaquest, Qbert, SpaceInvaders, Breakout); 5,500 queries to a human rater or a limited number of synthetic queries; compared with RL learning from the real reward. Differs from Q02: pairwise comparisons, not reward revealed on 10% of episodes.
findings.bears_on: Same topic as Q02 (learning from sparse feedback compared with full reward, on Atari), but the feedback is segment comparisons rather than reward on a fraction of episodes, so it does not bear directly on whether RL with reward on 10% of episodes learns nearly as fast.

In this work, we explore goals defined in terms of (non-expert) human preferences
between pairs of trajectory segments. We show that this approach can effectively
solve complex RL tasks without access to the reward function, including Atari
games and simulated robot locomotion, while providing feedback on less than
1% of our agent’s interactions with the environment. This reduces the cost of
human oversight far enough that it can be practically applied to state-of-the-art

The second set of tasks we consider is a set of seven Atari games in the Arcade Learning Environment (Bellemare et al., 2013), the same games presented in Mnih et al., 2013.
Figure 3 shows the results of training our agent with 5,500 queries to a human rater, compared to
learning from 350, 700, or 1400 synthetic queries, as well as to RL learning from the real reward.
Our method has more difficulty matching RL in these challenging environments, but nevertheless it
displays substantial learning on most of them and matches or even exceeds RL on some. Specifically,
on BeamRider and Pong, synthetic labels match or come close to RL even with only 3,300 such
labels. On Seaquest and Qbert synthetic feedback eventually performs near the level of RL but learns
more slowly. On SpaceInvaders and Breakout synthetic feedback never matches RL, but nevertheless
the agent improves substantially, often passing the first level in SpaceInvaders and reaching a score of
20 on Breakout, or 50 with enough labels.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2406.13909v2: Beyond Optimism: Exploration With Partially Observable Rewards
findings.claim: In Mon-MDPs, baselines that learn relatively quickly when rewards are fully observable drop drastically in performance when rewards are partially observable; even random observability (positive and negative rewards unobservable with probability 50%, zero rewards always observable) is enough to make Optimism converge to suboptimal policies, and the Q-Counts, UCB, Intrinsic Reward and Naive baselines learn suboptimal policies in most seeds, especially in harder Mon-MDPs; the authors' exploration is reported to be only slightly affected.
findings.setting: Experiment: Q-Learning with six exploration policies (the authors'; greedy with optimistic initialization; naive, count-based intrinsic-reward, UCB-bonus and Q-Counts epsilon-greedy) on Mon-MDPs (e.g. River Swim); every algorithm learns a reward model to replace unobserved rewards. In the 'Random Monitor' version positive and negative environment rewards are unobservable with probability 50% at each step (r̂tE = ⊥), zero rewards always observable; compared with fully observable rewards. Differs from Q02: half of the non-zero rewards are hidden per step, rather than reward being given on only 10% of episodes.
findings.bears_on: The closest direct test of Q02's random case, though with non-zero rewards hidden on 50% of steps rather than reward given on 10% of episodes: whether learning with randomly withheld rewards is nearly as fast as with full reward. In this setting the answer depends on the exploration strategy (baselines degrade drastically under partial observability, and random hiding alone makes Optimism converge to suboptimal policies; the authors' method is only slightly affected).

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2510.00144v1: Which Rewards Matter? Reward Selection for Reinforcement Learning under Limited Feedback
findings.claim: When only a budgeted subset of states in an offline dataset gets reward labels, the authors find that effective selection of which rewards to label yields near-optimal policies with significantly fewer reward labels than full supervision; critical rewards are those guiding the agent along optimal trajectories and supporting recovery after deviations.
findings.setting: Experiment: offline RL from a dataset collected by a data-collecting policy that contains no reward; environment rewards are obtained only at a selected subset of states under a labeling budget; selection by heuristics (state visitation, partial value functions) or by strategies pre-trained using auxiliary evaluative feedback; six prototypical domains (Graph, Tree, TwoRooms, TwoRooms-Trap, FrozenLake, CliffWalk) and four MinAtar games (Breakout, Freeway, Seaquest, Asterix).
findings.bears_on: Q02's active case (choosing which samples get reward) and its Atari-like step: carefully chosen labels can approach full supervision, but offline, per state, and in final policy return rather than online learning speed with reward on random episodes.
