relying on human feedback. When reinforcement learning must proceed with limited feedback—only
a fraction of samples get rewards labeled—a fundamental question arises: which samples should
be labeled to maximize policy performance? We formalize this problem of reward selection for
reinforcement learning from limited feedback (RLLF), introducing a new problem formulation that
facilitates the study of strategies for selecting impactful rewards. Two types of selection strategies are
investigated: (i) heuristics that rely on reward-free information such as state visitation and partial
value functions, and (ii) strategies pre-trained using auxiliary evaluative feedback. We find that
critical subsets of rewards are those that (1) guide the agent along optimal trajectories, and (2)
support recovery toward near-optimal behavior after deviations. Effective selection methods yield
near-optimal policies with significantly fewer reward labels than full supervision, establishing reward
selection as a powerful paradigm for scaling reinforcement learning in feedback-limited settings.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2512.13106v1: TraPO: A Semi-Supervised Reinforcement Learning Framework for Boosting LLM Reasoning
findings.claim: In semi-supervised RLVR, where a small labeled set guides RL on unlabeled samples, the method with 4K labeled and 12K unlabeled samples is reported to outperform the fully supervised model trained on the full 45K labeled samples on all benchmarks, using only 10% of the labeled data.
findings.setting: Experiment: semi-supervised RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for LLM mathematical reasoning; six mathematical reasoning benchmarks (AIME24/25, AMC, MATH-500, Minerva, Olympiad) and three out-of-distribution tasks (ARC-c, GPQA-diamond, MMLU-pro); labels on a small subset of training samples; accuracy compared, not learning curves; the fully supervised model is trained on the full 45K labeled samples, the semi-supervised run on 4K labeled and 12K unlabeled samples. Differs from Q02: LLM reasoning, final accuracy, labeled samples rather than rewarded episodes.
findings.bears_on: An analogue of Q02's 'reward on 10% of episodes' question in LLM RLVR, about final performance rather than speed in control tasks.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2011.06709v2: Active Reinforcement Learning: Observing Rewards at a Cost
findings.claim: Formalises active RL, where the agent sees the reward only if it pays a query cost, and evaluates heuristic query strategies in multi-armed bandits and tabular MDPs with known dynamics; the authors say the results show the value of online, state-dependent querying but are not a rigorous evaluation, and leave large state spaces to future work.
findings.setting: Heuristic query strategies for active RL (the agent observes the reward only if it pays a query cost c > 0), evaluated in multi-armed bandits and tabular MDPs (e.g. a chain environment) with known dynamics; experiments the authors say should not be taken as a rigorous evaluation.
findings.bears_on: Q02's active-learning variant (agent requests reward where most useful); no comparison of learning speed with full-reward RL on control or Atari tasks.

passages.text:
Active reinforcement learning (ARL) is a variant on reinforcement learning where
the agent does not observe the reward unless it chooses to pay a query cost c > 0.
The central question of ARL is how to quantify the long-term value of reward
information. Even in multi-armed bandits, computing the value of this information
is intractable and we have to rely on heuristics. We propose and evaluate several
heuristic approaches for ARL in multi-armed bandits and (tabular) Markov decision
processes, and discuss and illustrate some challenging aspects of the ARL problem.

differentially querying different state-actions, but should not be taken as a rigorous evaluation of the
strength of the proposed algorithms.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2012.06899v1: Semi-supervised reward learning for offline reinforcement learning
findings.claim: In experiments with a simulated robotic arm, semi-supervised reward learning from limited annotations plus unlabelled data greatly improves upon behavioural cloning and closely approaches the performance achieved with ground-truth rewards; with episode-level annotations, semi-supervised reward learning techniques greatly reduce the gap to ground truth compared to behavioural cloning while using exactly the same annotations.
findings.setting: Experiment: offline RL (agents trained on a logged dataset; CRR policies) on a simulated robotic arm (tasks including box, insertion, slide); supervision is limited timestep annotations or demonstrations (and, in passage 2, episode-level annotations) plus unlabelled data; policy score compared with a CRR policy given ground-truth rewards and with behavioural cloning.
findings.bears_on: Q02's challenge of using unlabeled episodes to approach fully labeled performance, but offline and in final score, not learning speed, and the passages do not say what fraction of episodes is annotated.

In offline reinforcement learning (RL) agents are trained using a logged dataset.
It appears to be the most natural route to attack real-life applications because in
domains such as healthcare and robotics interactions with the environment are
either expensive or unethical. Training agents usually requires reward functions,
but unfortunately, rewards are seldom available in practice and their engineering
is challenging and laborious. To overcome this, we investigate reward learning
under the constraint of minimizing human reward annotations. We consider two
types of supervision: timestep annotations and demonstrations. We propose semisupervised learning algorithms that learn from limited annotations and incorporate
unlabelled data. In our experiments with a simulated robotic arm, we greatly
improve upon behavioural cloning and closely approach the performance achieved
with ground truth rewards. We further investigate the relationship between the
quality of the reward model and the final policies. We notice, for example, that the

In Fig. 3 we show the performance of the policies that use episode-level annotations for determining
rewards as described in Sec. 3.2 and Tab. 1. BC policy reaches only between 1/3 and 2/3 of the score
attained by a CRR policy with ground truth rewards (GT). SQIL with memorized reward values
works well in some cases (box), but its performance is worse than BC in other cases (insertion, slide).
Learning a reward function from flat reward assumption with regularisation as in ORIL improves
significantly over BC. Finally, TGR-i further improves the results making it to be among the best
performing strategies across all tasks. To sum up, semi-supervised reward learning techniques greatly
reduce the gap to GT compared to BC while using exactly the same annotations.

questions.question: Can Iterated Amplification be applied to complex real-world beyond-human-scale tasks?
questions.asked_by: Christiano et al., Supervising strong learners by amplifying weak experts
questions.remaining_question: Can a full amplify-and-distill loop, with humans (or a learned model of them) decomposing, be trained on a real-world task where neither demonstrations nor reliable evaluations of the final output are available, and how would success be verified there?

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2406.04604v4: Learning Task Decomposition to Assist Humans in Competitive Programming
findings.claim: In a 177-hour human study on competitive programming problems, decomposed solutions produced by critique, refine and rank steps that learn in context from collected human repair data let non-experts solve 33.3% more problems, sped them up by 3.3x, and let them match unassisted experts. The objective, assistive value, summarizes solution quality over the human repair process, with solution quality set to the passing rates on unit test cases. The authors read this as showing that even when LMs cannot solve the problem themselves, they can still learn to assist humans by learning from human repair experiences, and say the results highlight the potential of learning-based methods to assist humans with scalable oversight.
findings.setting: Human-subject experiment (177 hours of human study) on competitive programming problems: non-experts repair decomposed solutions whose critique, refine and rank steps learn in context from a collected dataset of human repair experiences; objective is assistive value (feasibility and speed of human repair), with solution quality measured as passing rates on unit test cases; assisted non-experts are compared with unassisted experts. One assistance step only; no amplify-and-distill loop. Differs from the question's setting: a task on which unassisted experts are the reference and unit tests give an automatic quality check, not a beyond-human-scale task lacking other training signals.
findings.bears_on: The amplification step of the question (a human aided by a model that decomposes) on a hard real task, not the full iterated loop and not a task lacking any other training signal.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2309.08589v2: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning is a Policy Improvement Operator
findings.claim: An amplify-then-distill loop (solve with chain-of-thought, then train the next model to answer directly) let language models teach themselves addition up to 29 digits without ground-truth examples beyond an initial supervised phase on numbers of 6 or fewer digits. The authors say this is far from showing models can self-learn in general and ask whether it extends to more complex tasks such as multiplication, general mathematics or programming.
findings.setting: Experiment: language models trained with the SECToR self-learning loop (solve with chain-of-thought, then train the next model to answer directly) on addition problems only; no human expert or decomposer. Differs from the question's setting: one arithmetic task, not a complex real-world or beyond-human-scale task.
findings.bears_on: Whether an iterated amplify-then-distill loop works beyond the training distribution without external labels; it does not address real-world tasks.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2512.24601v3: Recursive Language Models
findings.claim: Recursive Language Models let an LLM programmatically examine, decompose and recursively call itself over snippets of a long prompt; the authors report processing inputs over an order of magnitude beyond the context window and median gains over compaction and coding-agent baselines on four long-context tasks, and a small post-trained RLM-Qwen3-8B improving on Qwen3-8B. They state that evaluations on more difficult and natural long-context tasks remain highly underexplored.
findings.setting: Experiment: inference-time scaffold with frontier LLMs (e.g. GPT-5) as the recursive caller; small-scale post-training of Qwen3-8B; four long-context tasks; no human expert, no iterated amplify-and-distill training. Differs from the question's setting: a model recursively calling itself over long inputs, not Iterated Amplification with human decomposition and distillation.
findings.bears_on: Loosely parallels the 2018 paper's idea of decomposing questions over contexts too large to observe at once, applied to real long-input tasks by a model calling copies of itself; it is not Iterated Amplification as defined there.

passages.text:
We study allowing large language models (LLMs) to process arbitrarily long
prompts through the lens of inference-time scaling. We propose Recursive Language Models (RLMs), a general inference paradigm that treats long prompts
as part of an external environment and allows the LLM to programmatically examine, decompose, and recursively call itself over snippets of the prompt. We
find that RLMs can successfully process inputs more than an order of magnitude
beyond model context window limits and, even for shorter prompts, dramatically
outperform the quality of vanilla frontier LLMs and common long-context and
coding scaffolds (e.g., on GPT-5 by a median across the evaluated benchmarks of
26% against compaction, 130% against CodeAct with sub-calls, and 13% against
Claude Code) across four diverse long-context tasks while having comparable
cost. At a small scale, we post-train the first model around the RLM. Our model,
RLM-Qwen3-8B, outperforms the underlying Qwen3-8B model by a median of
28% and even approaches the quality of vanilla GPT-5 on three long-context tasks.

While RLMs show strong performance on tasks beyond the context window limitations of existing
LMs at reasonable inference costs, evaluations for more difficult and natural long-context processing
tasks and the best mechanisms for implementing guardrails for RLMs both remain highly underexplored. Broadly, RLMs add a layer of complexity on top of existing LMs that may lead to
unintentional side-effects like exploding sub-call costs, which we leave for future work to solve.

questions.question: What is needed to automate decomposition, error analysis and program repair?
questions.asked_by: Reppert et al., Iterated Decomposition: Improving Science Q&A by Supervising Reasoning Processes
questions.remaining_question: Can an LM revise the decomposition of a multi-step LM program, localize what causes a failure and repair it reliably enough to replace human iteration (e.g. a failed-to-success flip rate approaching a human developer's), both on tasks with automatic evaluation (where, on Who&When, the best of three attribution methods found the decisive failure step only 14.2% of the time and a trained tracer, AgenTracer-8B, only improved on frontier LLMs) and on tasks with subjective answers that have no ground-truth answers or automatic evaluation function?

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2408.08435v2: Automated Design of Agentic Systems
findings.claim: A meta agent that iteratively programs new agentic systems in code, conditioned on an archive of earlier designs and scored on validation data from the target domain, discovered agents that outperformed hand-designed agents, by 13.6 F1 on reading comprehension and 14.4% accuracy on math, with smaller gains on multi-task and science. The authors note the search uses only numerical evaluation results and propose, as future work, letting the meta agent analyse running logs for debugging; they add that many tasks involve subjective answer evaluations that do not have ground-truth answers and that it is also important to design novel evaluation functions in ADAS to address these tasks.
findings.setting: Experiment: Meta Agent Search, in which a meta agent iteratively programs new agents in code, conditioned on an archive of earlier designs; Reading Comprehension, Math, Multi-task and Science domains; agents scored by numerical performance results on validation data from the target domain, with no analysis of running logs.
findings.bears_on: Automatically adapting LM programs (Reppert's end state; the passages do not mention decomposition as such): a meta agent can program agents in code that outperform hand-designed agents when candidate agents can be scored numerically on validation data from the target domain; analysis of running logs for debugging (items 3-4) is not used and is named as a future direction, and the authors call it important to design novel evaluation functions for tasks without ground-truth answers. Shown only where such a numerical score exists, so it settles no part of what automation needs without one.

findings.claim: Trace jointly optimised the meta-prompt and two code functions (create_prompt and extract_answer) of a DSPy-based LLM agent on Big-Bench Hard beyond what DSPy's COPRO optimizer can, especially on algorithmic tasks; in another experiment, masking OptoPrime's execution trace led to a significant decline in performance and stability. The Big-Bench Hard result used automatic comparison to ground truth, unlike open-ended tasks without such a check.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2505.00212v3: Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? On Automated Failure Attribution of LLM Multi-Agent Systems
findings.claim: On the Who&When dataset of annotated failure logs, the best of three automated failure-attribution methods identified the failure-responsible agent 53.5% of the time but the decisive failure step only 14.2%, some methods were below random, and reasoning models such as OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek R1 did not reach practical usability.
findings.setting: Benchmark evaluation (experiment) on the Who&When dataset: failure logs from 127 LLM multi-agent systems with fine-grained annotations linking failures to specific agents and decisive error steps; three automated failure-attribution methods, with the primary experiments using GPT-4o, and other open-source and closed-source models and the reasoning models OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek R1 also evaluated.
findings.bears_on: Error analysis (Reppert item 3): the automated failure-attribution methods tested, including with reasoning models, could not reliably localize the step causing a failure in LLM multi-agent systems.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2509.03312v2: AgenTracer: Who Is Inducing Failure in the LLM Agentic Systems?
findings.claim: The authors report that state-of-the-art reasoning LLMs score generally below 10% on agentic failure attribution, and that AgenTracer-8B, trained with multi-granular RL on trajectories annotated automatically by counterfactual replay and programmed fault injection, outperforms Gemini-2.5-Pro and Claude-4-Sonnet on Who&When by up to 18.18% and gives feedback that improves MetaGPT and MaAS by 4.8-14.2%.
findings.setting: Experiment: AgenTracer-8B trained with multi-granular RL on TracerTraj, failed multi-agent trajectories annotated automatically by counterfactual replay and programmed fault injection; evaluated on Who&When against proprietary LLMs (Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-4-Sonnet); feedback given to the multi-agent systems MetaGPT and MaAS.
findings.bears_on: Reppert item 4 (diagnosis learned by LMs): a lightweight failure tracer trained on automatically annotated failed trajectories outperformed large proprietary LLMs on Who&When by up to 18.18%; the quoted lines do not establish that its absolute accuracy is high enough to replace human analysis.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2603.23994v2: Understanding the Challenges in Iterative Generative Optimization with LLMs
findings.claim: The authors state that generative optimization, which uses LLMs to iteratively improve artifacts such as code, workflows or prompts using execution feedback, remains brittle in practice (only 9% of surveyed agents used any automated optimization). They argue this brittleness arises because setting up a learning loop requires 'hidden' design choices, and through case studies find that three such factors (the starting artifact, the credit horizon for execution traces, and batching trials and errors into learning evidence) can determine whether generative optimization succeeds. They argue the lack of adoption is not a consequence of inadequate infrastructure support or insufficient software abstraction, and conclude that the lack of a simple, universal way to set up learning loops across domains is a major hurdle for productionization and adoption.
findings.setting: Case studies (experiments) with LLM-based generative optimization on MLAgentBench, Atari and BigBench Extra Hard (BBEH); plus a survey figure the authors give (only 9% of surveyed agents used any automated optimization) and their argument, pointing to the ecosystem of agent-building libraries, that low adoption is not due to inadequate infrastructure or software.
findings.bears_on: Reppert items 3-4: the authors argue that a major hurdle for automated LLM-based improvement of code, workflows or prompts is setting up the learning loop rather than missing infrastructure or software; this is an argument plus case studies on benchmarks, not a test of LM-program repair in Reppert et al.'s open-ended setting.

passages.text:
Generative optimization uses large language models (LLMs) to iteratively improve
artifacts (such as code, workflows or prompts) using execution feedback. It is
a promising approach to building self-improving agents, yet in practice remains
brittle: despite active research, only 9% of surveyed agents used any automated

optimization. We argue that this brittleness arises because, to set up a learning
loop, an engineer must make “hidden” design choices: What can the optimizer edit
and what is the “right” learning evidence to provide at each update? We investigate
three factors that affect most applications: the starting artifact, the credit horizon
for execution traces, and batching trials and errors into learning evidence. Through
case studies in MLAgentBench, Atari, and BigBench Extra Hard, we find that these
design decisions can determine whether generative optimization succeeds, yet they
are rarely made explicit in prior work. Different starting artifacts determine which
solutions are reachable in MLAgentBench, truncated traces can still improve Atari
agents, and larger minibatches do not monotonically improve generalization on
BBEH. We conclude that the lack of a simple, universal way to set up learning
loops across domains is a major hurdle for productionization and adoption. We

This lack of adoption is not a consequence of inadequate infrastructure support or insufficient software
abstraction. On the contrary, over the past two years, a rich ecosystem of powerful libraries for
building agentic systems has emerged (Khattab et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024; LangChain, 2024; Cheng
et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). Many of these libraries offer mechanisms for automatically optimizing
different targets, ranging from tuning prompts (Khattab et al., 2024; Yuksekgonul et al., 2025) to
program synthesis (Cheng et al., 2024). Most of them have received considerable attention from
agent engineers, suggesting that the low adoption rate cannot be attributed solely to limited awareness
or inadequate software.

questions.question: Can several examiner models, or a trained examiner, make cross-examination better at detecting factual errors?
questions.asked_by: Cohen et al., LM vs LM: Detecting Factual Errors via Cross Examination
questions.remaining_question: Does training the examiner's question generation (e.g. with RL rewarded on detection correctness), or pooling several diverse examiners, raise cross-examination F1 at detecting factual errors above a single prompted examiner with a majority-vote or trained (e.g. linear) decision rule, and do correlated mistakes across capable examiner LMs limit the gain from pooling?

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2501.01558v4: Predicting the Performance of Black-box LLMs through Follow-up Queries
findings.claim: The authors ask a black-box model follow-up questions, take the probabilities of its responses as representations, and train a linear model on them that, they report, reliably and accurately predicts model correctness on question-answering and reasoning benchmarks and can even outperform white-box linear predictors that operate over model internals or activations. Predictive performance increased as the number of elicitation prompts increased, with the rate of increase slowly diminishing. The questions are fixed prompts treated as abstract features; the authors note that further work could perform discrete optimization over the prompts.
findings.setting: Experiment: black-box LLMs as examined models; question-answering and reasoning benchmarks; fixed follow-up questions; trained linear predictors on response probabilities predicting answer correctness. Not an interactive cross-examination of a claim, and no examiner model is trained.
findings.bears_on: Both parts, partially: a trained decision rule over many follow-up questions detects incorrect answers and more questions help; training the question-generating examiner, and using several examiner models, are not tested.

findings.claim: A logistic-regression classifier on a model's yes/no answers to a predefined set of unrelated follow-up questions detected lies with high accuracy and, when trained only on GPT-3.5 prompted to lie about factual questions, generalised to other LLM architectures, LLMs fine-tuned to lie, sycophantic lies and lies emerging in real-life scenarios such as sales. findings.bears_on: Trained-examiner part, by analogy: training the decision rule of a follow-up-question detector works for lies; the questions themselves were not trained.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2311.01740v2: SAC3: Reliable Hallucination Detection in Black-Box Language Models via Semantic-aware Cross-check Consistency
findings.claim: In a scenario where the dataset only contains hallucinated samples (accuracy of detecting hallucinated samples at a preset threshold of 0.5), the model-level cross-check with verifier LMs performed well on the prime-number dataset but failed to accurately detect hallucination on the senator-search dataset, because both verifier LMs refused to answer a large portion of its questions for lack of sufficient information. The verifier LMs are asked the questions themselves; there is no examiner dialogue or cross-examination of the target LM.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2603.24579v1: MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination
findings.claim: MARCH has three agents: a Solver generates an initial RAG response, a Proposer decomposes it into claim-level verifiable atomic propositions, and a Checker validates these propositions against retrieved evidence in isolation, without the Solver's original output. For each question generated by the Proposer, the Checker generates multiple independent audit trajectories and a majority vote determines the consensus answer. The shared policy of the three agents is optimised with PPO (multi-agent RL). From Llama3.1-8B, the policy trained on General QA data improved the average accuracy from 29.7 to 51.6 (+21.9) and the policy trained on STEM data reached 52.3 (+22.6), with gains across all eight dimensions; the authors say these 8B policies reach or surpass the performance of many much larger judge models.
findings.setting: Experiment: retrieval-augmented generation; one shared policy for Solver, Proposer and Checker, starting from Llama3.1-8B and trained with multi-agent RL (PPO) on General QA or STEM data; evaluated on hallucination benchmarks and on average accuracy over eight dimensions, compared with judge models. The Checker verifies against retrieved evidence, not by cross-examining the examinee's other beliefs, and the questions come from the system's own Proposer.
findings.bears_on: Trained-examiner part, by analogy: training a question-proposing verification pipeline improved its factual-consistency judgments in a RAG setting.

questions.question: Open question: how do strong models perceive the knowledge boundaries of weak supervisors?
questions.asked_by: Yang et al., Super(ficial)-alignment: Strong Models May Deceive Weak Models in Weak-to-Strong Generalization
questions.remaining_question: In Yang et al.'s weak-to-strong preference-alignment setup with a conflicting target, given that correctness of weak preference orders alone lets the strong model perceive weak-unknown samples, does it do so by checking each weak order against its own knowledge (as F2's stronger model predicting the weaker model's correctness suggests) or by inferring per-domain weak competence from the portion and distribution of supervised samples across domains, as would be tested by ablations that equalize the per-domain distribution while holding the correctness of the orders and the strong model fixed?

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2604.25077v3: Evaluating Risks in Weak-to-Strong Alignment: A Bias-Variance Perspective
findings.claim: Across four weak-to-strong pipelines spanning SFT, RLHF and RLAIF on PKU-SafeRLHF and HH-RLHF, the authors find that, among the BVC quantities they study, strong-model variance is the one most strongly associated with 'blind-spot deception' (cases where the strong model is confidently wrong while the weak model is uncertain); covariance provides additional but weaker information, indicating that weak-strong dependence matters but does not by itself explain the observed failures. They treat a cross-dataset reversal as exploratory evidence for their claim that blind-spot deception also depends on how the weak model's training procedure shapes the regions where weak supervision is uncertain. They interpret the correlation results, based on only eight pipeline-dataset settings, as exploratory diagnostic evidence, and their experiments use only Llama-family models and harmlessness-style preference datasets.
findings.setting: Empirical; four weak-to-strong pipelines spanning SFT, RLHF and RLAIF on the harmlessness-style preference datasets PKU-SafeRLHF and HH-RLHF; only Llama-family models; correlations over eight pipeline-dataset settings. 'Deception' here is the blind-spot metric (strong model confidently wrong where the weak model is uncertain), not Yang et al.'s measure, so the result is not obtained in the question's own setup.
findings.bears_on: Whether strong-model errors in weak-unknown regions track weak-strong dependence (a perception channel) or the strong model's own confidence dispersion.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2509.24988v2: Generalized Correctness Models: Learning Calibrated and Model-Agnostic Correctness Predictors from Historical Patterns
findings.claim: The authors find that an LLM predicting the correctness of its own outputs generally does no better than an unrelated LLM, and hypothesise that exposure to a target model's historical predictions is key. When Qwen2.5-72B and Llama3-70B are finetuned on MMLU to predict each other's and their own correctness, Qwen2.5-72B predicts Llama3-70B's correctness, as well as its own, better than Llama3-70B does, which they attribute to Qwen2.5-72B being stronger with more knowledge of the true answers.
findings.setting: Correctness prediction trained with explicit correctness labels on MMLU; Qwen2.5-72B vs Llama3-70B (small capability gap); no weak-to-strong training and no conflicting objective.
findings.bears_on: Whether a stronger model can learn a weaker model's knowledge boundary from its track record and its own knowledge of the answers, one channel Yang et al. suggest.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2410.13787v1: Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection
findings.claim: For GPT-4o, GPT-4 and Llama 70B, self-prediction models consistently outperform their cross-prediction counterparts on a set of held-out tasks: e.g. Llama 70B predicts its own behavior more accurately (48.5%) than GPT-4o does (31.8%), despite GPT-4o's superior capabilities, and GPT-4o predicts itself better (49.4%) than Llama 70B does (36.6%); GPT-3.5 has a statistically significant but very small (+0.8%) self-prediction advantage. In a data-scaling analysis, GPT-4o's cross-prediction of Llama 70B does not meaningfully increase after 10,000 samples and plateaus at 35.2%, far below the 48.5% self-prediction accuracy.
findings.setting: Self- vs cross-prediction finetuning among GPT-4o, GPT-4, GPT-3.5 and Llama 70B on held-out behavior-property tasks; predicts behavior properties, not knowledge or correctness; no weak-to-strong training.
findings.bears_on: Limits on how well a more capable model can model another model from observed behavior; contrasts with 2509.24988's finding for correctness.

passages.text:
Self-prediction models consistently outperform their cross-prediction counterparts for GPT-4o,
GPT-4, and Llama 70B on a set of held-out tasks, as shown in Figure 5. For instance, Llama
70B predicts its own behavior more accurately (48.5%) than GPT-4o (31.8%), despite GPT-4o’s
superior capabilities (Chiang et al., 2024). The same pattern holds the other way around: GPT-4o
predicts itself better (49.4%) than Llama 70B does (36.6%). GPT-3.5 has a statistically significant
but very small (+0.8%) self-prediction advantage (p = 0.002). For models other than GPT-3.5, the
self-prediction advantage holds across most datasets and behavior properties (see Figure 14). This
provides evidence that these models use introspection. Further evidence is that the self-prediction
advantage also holds on the set of tasks used in self-/cross-training (A.2.2).

Another possibility is that cross-prediction training requires more training samples and would eventually improve over self-prediction. We conduct a data-scaling analysis on GPT-4o predicting Llama
70B (Section A.2.7). Cross-prediction accuracy does not meaningfully increase after 10,000 samples: it plateaus at 35.2%, far below the self-prediction accuracy of 48.5%.

questions.asked_by: Engels et al., Scaling Laws For Scalable Oversight
questions.remaining_question: What escape probability per deployment does the Elo-gap win probability of Eq. (5) predict, and what is observed, in realistic settings such as RLHF, supervised fine-tuning and AI-control environments (with prompted and trained attackers), across a controlled range of attacker-monitor capability gaps, audit budgets and horizons, and how does it extrapolate toward the ASI regime?

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2506.05296v3: Control Tax: The Price of Keeping AI in Check
findings.claim: In a setting where LM attackers insert backdoors and LM monitors are used under optimal sequential monitoring with a 5% fixed auditing budget, the authors compute achievable safety (the probability of detecting the first inserted backdoor given optimal attacker/monitor strategies) against monitor cost; e.g. moving from Gemini 2.0 Flash to o3-mini on the Pareto frontier requires a 45x increase in cost for an absolute improvement of 0.15 in safety (from about 0.70 to about 0.85) against a GPT-4o attacker. For an unknown (effectively infinite) deployment horizon they say one effective attacker strategy appears to be to insert backdoors as infrequently as possible, which reveals a fundamental weakness of pure monitoring in long-term deployments, 'as a patient attacker will eventually succeed'.
findings.setting: Backdoor insertion by LM attackers (GPT-4o, o3-mini) against LM monitors (including Gemini 2.0 Flash and o3-mini) under optimal sequential monitoring with a 5% fixed auditing budget; safety versus monitor cost. Current models, not ASI; not computed from the Elo-gap model.
findings.bears_on: Gives attacker-win / safety probabilities in one AI-control environment (a setting Engels et al. name) and shows they depend on monitor choice, audit budget and deployment horizon; not an estimate of p_c(ASI).

passages.text:
Figure 1: Control Tax. Achievable safety (probability of detecting the first inserted backdoor given
optimal attacker/monitor strategies) versus the average cost of different LM monitors (the ’control
tax’). The plots compare monitors against attackers GPT 4o (left) and o3-mini (right), under
optimal sequential monitoring with a 5% fixed auditing budget. Safety is shown with bootstrapped
95% confidence intervals.

The main takeaway of this work is that the most expensive, highest-performing monitor is not always
the best choice for maximizing safety. As our Control Tax analysis in Figure 1 demonstrates, a
practitioner with a limited budget might achieve higher overall safety by using a cheaper, albeit
weaker, monitor (e.g., Gemini 2.0 Flash) because the cost savings allow for a more robust, highervolume auditing strategy. Yet the Control Tax is non-linear: achieving marginal gains in safety can
require significant investments. For example, moving from Gemini 2.0 Flash to o3-mini on the Pareto
frontier requires a 45x increase in cost to achieve an absolute improvement of 0.15 in the safety score
(from ∼0.70 to ∼0.85) against a GPT-4o attacker.

(2) In infinite-horizon scenarios, be wary of patient attackers. When the deployment horizon is
unknown (effectively infinite), one effective strategy appears to be patient and insert backdoors as
infrequently as possible (pb → 0). This reveals a fundamental weakness of pure monitoring in
long-term deployments, as a patient attacker will eventually succeed.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2508.19461v1: Reliable Weak-to-Strong Monitoring of LLM Agents
findings.claim: Across 36 attacker-monitor pairs in SHADE-Arena, monitor reliability (AUC-ROC) correlates with the monitor's relative advantage in MMLU-Pro score over the agent's backbone LLM, but the strength of this association varies across monitor types (weakest for the hybrid monitor); even weaker models such as GPT-4o-mini and Claude 3.6 Haiku achieve a monitoring AUC above 0.85 against all agents. The authors conclude that while it is challenging for a single weak LLM to reliably monitor a stronger LLM, a well-designed ensemble of weaker monitors (e.g. the hybrid approach) can yield a significantly more reliable monitoring system.
findings.setting: Experiment; SHADE-Arena as dataset and environment; 'aware' agents (Claude 3.6 Sonnet, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro) using CoT obfuscation as their evasion strategy; 10 monitor LLMs, each used to build 4 types of monitoring system; capability gap measured by MMLU-Pro difference; detection AUC-ROC, not escape probability. Current models, not ASI.
findings.bears_on: Capability-gap dependence of oversight in an agent-monitoring (AI-control-like) environment, modulated by scaffolding; no escape-probability estimate or ASI extrapolation.

passages.text:
Setup. We use Claude 3.6 Sonnet, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Gemini 2.5 Pro as aware agents. Each
agent uses CoT obfuscation as their evasion strategy. For monitors, we employ Claude 3.6 Haiku, Claude 3.6
Sonnet, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, o3, and
o4-mini, resulting in a total of 36 attacker-monitor pairs. We use each monitor LLM to build the 4 types of
monitoring systems as mentioned in Section 3.5. We use SHADE-Arena as the dataset and environment.

In Figure 6, we plot the AUC-ROC scores for each agent-monitor pairs against the difference of their MMLU Pro
scores. For each monitor type, we fit a line to the corresponding data points.
Summary of Findings. First, we observe that the reliability of a monitor is correlated with its relative advantage
in MMLU-Pro score compared to the backbone LLM of the agent. However, the strength of this association varies
across monitor types—with the hybrid monitor exhibiting the weakest association with the capability gap.
Notably, even with weaker models such as GPT-4o-mini and Claude 3.6 Haiku, we achieve a monitoring AUC
exceeding 0.85 against all agents. Second, the reliability scores of the hybrid monitor consistently surpass those
of the baseline, hierarchical, and sequential monitors by a substantial margin, indicating that the sequential and
hierarchical approaches are complementary and can be effectively combined into a more powerful hybrid monitor.
Overall, our results show that while it is challenging for a single weak LLM to reliably monitor a stronger LLM,
a well-designed ensemble of weaker monitors (e.g., the hybrid approach) can yield a significantly more reliable
monitoring system.

findings.claim: Under GRPO training of 0.5B and 1.5B Qwen2.5 policies on GSM8K against frozen LLM judges, the depth of judge hacking tracks the judge (plateau correlates with judge AUC, Spearman -0.69 over 12 cells), and two pre-specified pairs contradict the capability-gap account for the pace; the author states that with 12 cells judge AUC and the gap cannot be formally separated.

findings.bears_on: Whether a capability-gap account predicts oversight failure in an RL-against-a-judge setting (close to the RLHF setting Engels et al. name); inconclusive and small-scale; no escape probability.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2606.11998v1: Bootstrapped Monitoring: Leveraging Transparent Reasoning to Oversee Stronger AI Agents
findings.claim: A three-tier monitoring protocol (a weaker trusted model auditing a stronger untrusted monitor's chain-of-thought) improves catch rates over trusted-only monitoring on BashArena even when the untrusted monitor colludes, given raw chain-of-thought; collusion is elicited by system prompt, BashArena covers a narrow attack surface, and scaling studies over the capability gap are left to future work.
findings.setting: Experiment; AI-control environment BashArena (multi-turn software engineering); several agent and monitor model families; prompted collusion; catch rates.
findings.bears_on: Applies a nested oversight chain in an AI-control environment but reports catch rates, not an escape probability, and does not vary the capability gap.

passages.text:
model (T ) oversees Um ’s reasoning to detect collusion. We evaluate bootstrapped
monitoring on multi-turn software engineering tasks (BashArena) across multiple
agents and monitors. Bootstrapped monitoring substantially improves catch rates
over trusted-only monitoring, even when the untrusted monitor actively colludes
with the agent, provided we have access to its raw chain-of-thought. Our results
suggest that bootstrapped monitoring can extend the useful lifetime of trusted
models in control as AI capabilities advance.

Limitations. Collusion in this work is elicited via system prompt. A model fine-tuned or trained
via reinforcement learning to produce deceptive reasoning might achieve more natural-sounding
collusion. However, fine-tuning frontier-scale models was beyond our resources. BashArena also
covers a narrow slice of the agentic attack surface, so results may differ with other attack vectors.
Future work. Agentic monitors that can execute commands in a sandbox rather than passively
reading actions may further improve catch rates. Adversarial training of Um against T would provide
a lower bound on the protocol’s robustness. Scaling studies that vary the capability gap between T
and Um would clarify how long a given trusted model remains useful as frontier capabilities advance.

The passages do not name the topologies tested.

Recent work [9] characterizes the belief evolution in MAD as a martingale. We restate this property
under our notation to motivate our proposed method.
Proposition 2.2 (Martingale Property of Standard MAD). In a closed debate system without external
oracle signals, if the belief update rule is linear (as in Eq.(1)) and symmetric, the sequence of the
average belief in the ground truth, denoted as µt = p̄(t) (y ∗ ), forms a martingale:
E[µt+1 | H (t) ] = µt .

The “Debate-as-Martingale” hypothesis [9] poses a fundamental challenge to the field: if MAD
cannot theoretically outperform majority voting in expectation, then the computational cost of iterative
interaction is unjustifiable. However, we contend that this theoretical characterization relies on strong
assumptions: specifically, that initial errors are independent and that the aggregation is purely linear.

1. Voting Stagnates in Correlated Noise. As detailed in Table 1, Majority Voting struggles to extract
correct answers in the challenging interval. Across all datasets, the voting baseline shows negligible
improvement, or even degradation, as the ensemble size increases. For instance, increasing N from
2 to 5 fails to break the performance ceiling on tasks like TruthfulQA and LogiQA. This empirical
plateau confirms that errors in these adversarial regimes are highly correlated; simply adding more
static agents merely reinforces the false consensus rather than diluting it.
2. Debate Consistently Outperforms Voting. Table 1 demonstrates that this limitation is structural
to voting, not the models. All MAD variants consistently outperform Majority Voting across
the tested benchmarks. In the most challenging reasoning tasks such as ARC-C and BBH, debate
mechanisms achieve substantial margins over the voting baseline. This indicates that the debate
process itself, regardless of the specific topology, acts as a necessary “denoising” filter that disrupts
the homogeneous error patterns of the crowd.

maths.label: Proved
maths.settled: Within the formal model described in formal_statement, Lean proves the following without sorry. (1) The one-step martingale identity for an agent is equivalent to the paper's condition (1) at that state. (2) From a homogeneous start, on any observation structure, agent i's belief is a martingale iff every agent i observes has the same observation set as i. On the paper's undirected graphs with self-observation, all agents' beliefs are martingales iff the graph is a disjoint union of cliques. With heterogeneous starts this holds iff, in addition, the agents in each clique start with equal alpha^(1) and total. So the paper's Proposition 1 (fully connected, isolated, isolated homogeneous cliques) is also necessary: no other debate topology satisfies condition (1) at all rounds. The line, the ring (Sparse MAD), stars and paths fail already after one round. Without self-observation only the edgeless graph works. (3) Weaker averaged versions hold more widely. On every d-regular undirected graph, e.g. the ring, with equal initial totals, the uniform average belief and the paper's collective belief q_t are exact martingales, although (1) fails for every agent. On K1+K2 the individual beliefs are martingales but q_t is not. On the line example the uniform average drifts. (4) From a homogeneous start, on every topology, each agent's unconditional expected belief stays at its initial value at every round. The paper's consequence 'expected belief unchanged' (stated for homogeneous, fully connected agents) therefore does not depend on the topology; the topology question concerns only the conditional (martingale) property.
maths.remains: (i) Necessity for averaged beliefs, still a conjecture: on undirected graphs with a homogeneous start, is the uniform average belief (or any fixed positive weighting) a martingale only when every connected component is regular, and the collective belief q_t only when the graph is regular? This is checked exhaustively only for n <= 6 and 2-3 rounds. (ii) A precise characterisation for averages on directed observation structures, where the simple regular-and-balanced rule is sufficient but not necessary. (iii) Formalising the passage from 'identity at every reachable state' to a measure-theoretic martingale for the paper's filtration. (iv) Variants of the update the paper mentions (weighted or soft counts, heterogeneous influence), correlated answers within a round, and whether any of this predicts LLM debate behaviour (the paper's near-martingale observation for Sparse MAD).

questions.question: Is learned task decomposition feasible for hard real-world tasks, and where does it fail?
questions.asked_by: Wu et al., Recursively Summarizing Books with Human Feedback
questions.remaining_question: Can a decomposition model trained from human feedback beat a fixed decomposition on a hard real-world task without verifiable answers (e.g. book-length summarization), measured by the quality of the human supervision it enables, and on which tasks do cross-part dependencies make it fail?

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2406.04604v4: Learning Task Decomposition to Assist Humans in Competitive Programming

findings.setting: Human study (177 hours) on competitive programming problems: non-experts repair decomposed solutions with the method's help and are compared with unassisted experts; the decomposition is improved by learning to critique, refine and rank decomposed solutions, with human repair data as in-context examples (in-context and supervised learning only; no RL fine-tuning of the decomposition model). Differs from the question's setting: a programming task, not book summarization (the asking paper's task), and what is decomposed is a solution that humans repair.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2512.24601v3: Recursive Language Models
findings.claim: Letting an LLM choose its own decomposition at run time (examining, decomposing and recursively calling itself over snippets of a long prompt) handled inputs more than an order of magnitude beyond the context window and outperformed compaction and coding scaffolds by median margins (on GPT-5: 26% against compaction, 130% against CodeAct with sub-calls, 13% against Claude Code) across four long-context tasks; a small post-trained Qwen3-8B, trained with only 1,000 samples from unrelated domains, improved by a median of 28.3% across the four evaluation tasks. The authors say evaluations for more difficult and natural long-context tasks remain highly underexplored.
findings.setting: Experiment: inference-time scaffold in which frontier LLMs (e.g. GPT-5) examine, decompose and recursively call themselves over snippets of long prompts; small-scale post-training of Qwen3-8B with 1,000 samples from unrelated domains; four long-context tasks. Differs from the question's setting: the decomposition is chosen by the model at run time (plus light post-training), on long-context benchmarks with no human feedback, not learned from human supervision on a hard real-world task.
findings.bears_on: First sub-question: feasibility of model-chosen (and, at small scale, trained) decomposition instead of fixed chunking on long-input tasks of the kind book summarization involves.

passages.text:
We study allowing large language models (LLMs) to process arbitrarily long
prompts through the lens of inference-time scaling. We propose Recursive Language Models (RLMs), a general inference paradigm that treats long prompts
as part of an external environment and allows the LLM to programmatically examine, decompose, and recursively call itself over snippets of the prompt. We
find that RLMs can successfully process inputs more than an order of magnitude
beyond model context window limits and, even for shorter prompts, dramatically
outperform the quality of vanilla frontier LLMs and common long-context and
coding scaffolds (e.g., on GPT-5 by a median across the evaluated benchmarks of
26% against compaction, 130% against CodeAct with sub-calls, and 13% against
Claude Code) across four diverse long-context tasks while having comparable
cost. At a small scale, we post-train the first model around the RLM. Our model,
RLM-Qwen3-8B, outperforms the underlying Qwen3-8B model by a median of
28% and even approaches the quality of vanilla GPT-5 on three long-context tasks.

Finally, at a small scale, we post-train the first natively recursive language model, demonstrating
that RLMs can be improved quickly with little additional training. While a small open model
(Qwen3-8B; Yang et al. 2025) struggles to solve long context tasks even in an RLM scaffold, our
simple general-purpose training recipe uses only 1,000 samples from unrelated domains to improve
its performance by a median of 28.3% across the four evaluation tasks.

While RLMs show strong performance on tasks beyond the context window limitations of existing
LMs at reasonable inference costs, evaluations for more difficult and natural long-context processing
tasks and the best mechanisms for implementing guardrails for RLMs both remain highly underexplored. Broadly, RLMs add a layer of complexity on top of existing LMs that may lead to
unintentional side-effects like exploding sub-call costs, which we leave for future work to solve.

findings.claim: Breaking reasoning tasks into a problem decomposition phase and a problem solving phase, the authors hypothesize that decomposition should be easier to distill into a smaller model than problem solving, and find that they can distill the problem decomposition phase while achieving good generalization across tasks, datasets and models, whereas the problem solving capability is harder to distill without losing performance and the resulting distilled model struggles with generalization.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2509.18632v1: A Good Plan is Hard to Find: Aligning Models with Preferences is Misaligned with What Helps Users
findings.claim: In a study where 126 users answered 300 multi-step questions with LLM plans, user/model preferences and agent success did not accurately predict which plans helped users, so common alignment feedback can misalign with helpfulness; the gap was not due to user-specific preferences, as users were similarly successful when using plans they preferred or dispreferred. The authors argue that aligning helpful LLMs needs feedback from real user interactions, not just preferences of what looks helpful.
findings.setting: Human-subject experiment (Planorama interface): 126 users solve 300 multi-step math and trivia questions with calculator and web search tools, using 600 LLM-created plans; 4388 plan executions and 5584 comparisons; agents and reward models recreate the setup to see whether they simulate or prefer what helps users. Differs from the question's setting: no decomposition model is learned here; it tests whether preference feedback on model-given decompositions (plans) tracks whether they help.
findings.bears_on: Where learned decomposition can fail (and the asking paper's further sub-question on how else ML models can assist humans, not in the question as worded): preference feedback on decompositions (plans) can diverge from whether they actually help, which bears on learning or selecting decompositions from preferences.

findings.claim: In the authors' market-making implementation, a trader model generates an argument intended to maximally shift the market maker M's prediction value, and M produces new judgments that consider the trader's previous arguments; the impact is measured by comparing the accuracy of M's final judgment with the accuracy of its initial judgment (the baseline without trader influence). findings.setting: Experiment with prompted models: a market-maker model M and a trader, filled by identical models in every trial. The trader argues to shift M's prediction value; the cycle stops after at most N = 10 judgments or when the range of the last three prediction values is at most T = 0.2. The accuracy of M's final judgment is compared with that of its initial judgment, per model family, on several datasets including ETHICS Justice. Both roles are models, and the judgment whose accuracy is measured is M's own, not a separate weaker overseer's.
findings.bears_on: The market-making part: the only later empirical market-making implementation found besides Lang et al.'s weak-to-strong variant. It is outside the sandwiching setting.

passages.text:
Given M’s judgment, the trader model then generates an argument intended to maximally shift M’s
prediction value. This is analogous to a trader introducing new information to change the market
price.
Each subsequent iteration proceeds with M producing a new judgment while also considering the
trader’s previous arguments. Exact prompting details are provided in Appendix B. The cycle repeats
until the market maker has provided at most N judgments or has reached an equilibrium; we consider
an equilibrium to have been reached when the range of the last three prediction values satisfies
max{pt−2 , pt−1 , pt } − min{pt−2 , pt−1 , pt } ≤ T,
where T is a threshold constant. In our experiments, we set N = 10 and T = 0.2.
Finally, we measure the impact of market making by comparing the accuracy of M’s final judgment
before termination against the accuracy of its initial judgment (i.e., the baseline without trader
influence) across all dataset samples.

We find a net increase in the percentage of accurate answers provided by the models. This can be seen
in Figure 2 where each model family has an overall improvement in accuracy over their baselines in
the majority of the datasets excluding ETHICS Justice.

Our experiments exclusively employed identical models for both market maker and trader roles
within each trial. This configuration may not capture the dynamics that emerge when models with
different capabilities, training objectives, or architectures interact.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2602.04210v2: Steering LLMs via Scalable Interactive Oversight
findings.claim: The authors validate their interactive oversight method, which they describe as a recursive interaction that iteratively decodes vague user intent into expert-level specifications before execution, using what they call the "sandwich" protocol (Bowman et al., 2022): a non-expert user attempts to guide a strong model to achieve tasks that only an expert can verify. On full-stack website development, where non-experts produce Product Requirement Documents (PRDs), they report that the method significantly outperforms standard vibe coding baselines (e.g. Claude Code, Gemini CLI) and vanilla interaction methods, improving alignment scores by up to 54%. To scale the experiments, non-expert behaviour is emulated by a user simulator implemented with deepseek-R1, and large-scale evaluation uses an LLM judge based on Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct. In 10 cases, one hired non-expert collaborated with GPT-5, and alignment scores increased as interaction rounds progressed.
findings.setting: Mostly simulated sandwich-protocol evaluation of an interactive steering method: a non-expert, emulated by a deepseek-R1 user simulator when experiments are scaled, guides a strong model to produce PRDs for full-stack website development; large-scale evaluation is by an LLM judge based on Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct rather than by human experts; plus a 10-case study in which one hired non-expert collaborates with GPT-5. The method steers the model through interaction before execution; it is not debate, market making or recursive reward modeling.
findings.bears_on: The RRM part, loosely: the closest recursive protocol found (the authors call it a recursive interaction) that is tested in a self-described sandwich set-up, mostly with a simulated non-expert and an LLM judge. It is not recursive reward modeling.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2406.04604v4: Learning Task Decomposition to Assist Humans in Competitive Programming
findings.claim: In a human study on competitive programming, assistance from the authors' decomposition model let non-expert programmers repair model-generated programs about as well and as efficiently as unassisted experts. Strict accuracy of repaired programs rose from 30.0% to 63.3% for non-experts and from 56.7% to 90% for experts (paired t-tests, p < 0.01). The authors note that their non-experts are still more skilled than novice programmers.
findings.setting: Human-subject experiment: expert and non-expert programmers repair model-generated programs with or without the authors' decomposition model; strict accuracy of repaired programs and labeling efficiency are measured. The non-experts could solve 30% of the problems and are still more skilled than novice programmers. Decomposition assistance, not debate, market making or recursive reward modeling.
findings.bears_on: The RRM part only by analogy: a sandwiching-like expert/non-expert comparison for one level of AI decomposition assistance. It is not recursive reward modeling.

passages.text:
Decomposition enables non-experts to be comparable with experts Remarkably, when assisted
with our decomposition model, non-experts achieve
performance comparable to non-assisted experts in
labeling efficiency and quality. This aligns with the
overarching goal of scalable oversight, empowering human labelers to oversee models in superhuman tasks.

Humans provide higher-quality labels with decomposition Beyond efficiency, we evaluate how
decomposition impacts the final quality of human
labels. As shown in Figure 3, our decomposition model enables humans to repair more modelgenerated programs. For instance, decomposition
improves the strict accuracy of repaired programs
from 56.7% to 90% for experts and from 30.0%
to 63.3% for non-experts. Paired t-tests confirm
the significance (p < 0.01) of these improvements.

One limitation of our work is that our non-expert
participants, who could solve 30% of the problems while spending 74 minutes, are still more
skilled than novice programmers (e.g., programmers who can only solve Leetcode easy-level
problems) or non-programmers. Nonetheless, we
demonstrate the effectiveness of our decomposition model, which successfully enables assisted
non-experts to be comparable with non-assisted experts. We leave the investigation of leveraging decomposition to assist novice programmers or even
non-programmers as future work.

questions.question: Open question: does process supervision's advantage generalize beyond math?
questions.asked_by: Lightman et al., Let's Verify Step by Step
questions.remaining_question: With step labels of comparable quality to PRM800K's human labels, does process supervision beat outcome supervision outside math (e.g. law, medicine, open-ended writing), and which task properties (how definable steps are, chain-of-thought length, label noise) decide the sign of the effect?

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2501.01290v1: ToolComp: A Multi-Tool Reasoning & Process Supervision Benchmark
findings.claim: In what the authors call a preliminary analysis on multi-step tool use, their best PRM beat an ORM at picking the best of 30 trajectories (rank@1 42.65% vs 23.89% on base-model generations; the PRM reached 60.25% on fine-tuned-model generations) and outperformed the ORM at every training-data scale tested.
findings.setting: Experiment (preliminary): PRM and ORM trained on additionally generated synthetic data for multi-step tool use, a non-math domain; rank@1 selection over base-model and SFT-model generations, compared with the generator's pass@30; training-data scale varied.
findings.bears_on: Whether the PRM-over-ORM advantage in best-of-N reranking appears outside math, here in multi-step tool use.

passages.text:
Recent works have demonstrated the power of process supervision signals in domains such as mathematical reasoning (Lightman et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024a). Despite this, the application of
process-supervised signals towards tool-augmented LLMs remains under-explored. By focusing on
the process rather than just the outcome, process-supervised models could provide more granular
feedback during multi-step tool-use, leading to faster convergence, especially in complex applications where each step is associated with dynamic feedback from the environment. In this section,
we provide a preliminary analysis to assess the value of process supervision for multi-step tool-use
by training PRM and ORM models using additionally generated synthetic data.

PRM outperforms ORM in selecting the best trajectory In Figure 3, we observe that for both
the base model generations and the SFT model generations, our best PRM model (see Table 4)
outperforms the ORM in rank@1 accuracy. On the base model generations, the PRM achieves an
accuracy of 42.65% compared to the ORM accuracy of 23.89%. Moreover, towards enhancing an
already fine-tuned model, we see that the PRM is able to push rank@1 accuracy to 60.25%, nearly
matching the generator’s pass@30 performance. Overall, these results suggest that PRMs are able
to efficiently translate these per tool call step-level signals to provide superior performance than
utilizing just outcome-level signals. In Appendix B, we also find the PRM scales better than the
ORM on increasing prompt complexity.

PRM scales better than ORM with increasing data Part of the design of our experiment is to
measure the scaling performance of PRMs versus ORMs as we incorporate more training data. In
Figure 3, we find that the PRM rank@1 performance consistently outperforms the ORM at all training data scales in ranking both the base model completions as well as the SFT model completions.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2412.12583v3: Process-Supervised Reward Models for Verifying Clinical Note Generation: A Scalable Approach Guided by Domain Expertise
findings.claim: For verifying clinical notes, the authors' PRM outperformed all baselines across all tasks, including a vanilla ORM, Gemini Pro 1.5 and SOTA reasoning models. Scoring the same checkpoint as a PRM or as an ORM gave comparable results on verification tasks, while the PRM was better on the preference-based A-Prefer evaluation (56.2% vs 51.2%). Scored as an ORM, the model also significantly outperformed the vanilla ORM, which predicts only overall correctness without learning step-level reward signals; the authors say this suggests that learning to predict step-level correctness during training is essential for strong performance.
findings.setting: Experiment: a reward model usable as a PRM or an ORM (step-wise vs note-level aggregation) for verifying generated clinical notes; two in-distribution verification tasks (Dialogue-G, A-Validate) and two OOD tasks (A-Verify, preference-based A-Prefer); baselines are a vanilla ORM, Gemini Pro 1.5 and SOTA reasoning models.
findings.bears_on: Process vs outcome supervision outside math, in clinical note generation, for verification and best-of-N style selection.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2510.00492v3: Rethinking Reward Models for Multi-Domain Test-Time Scaling
findings.claim: Across 14 MMLU-Pro domains, discriminative ORMs performed on par with discriminative PRMs, generative PRMs were not competitive (which the authors note is contrary to Lightman et al. and to their own math-domain results) and generative ORMs were most robust in best-of-N; they attribute the generative PRM's weaker performance to label noise from LLM-based automatic step labelling and to stepwise aggregation compounding errors as reasoning length grows.
findings.setting: Experiment plus a theoretical analysis of stepwise aggregation: R1-Distill-Qwen-14B reward-model backbone in the quoted results; training chains of thought from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with process labels auto-annotated by Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct (no human step labels); best-of-N with five generator LLMs; MMLU-Pro is multiple choice.
findings.bears_on: Directly tests whether the PRM advantage over ORM holds outside math under one protocol; in this setting it did not.

passages.text:
answer, and process reward models (PRMs), which score intermediate reasoning steps. Although PRMs are often viewed as advantageous due to their finer-grained supervision, much
of the supporting evidence comes from math-adjacent settings, and their relative benefits
across broader domains remain unclear. We present the first unified evaluation of four reward model variants, discriminative ORM and PRM (dORM, dPRM) and generative ORM
and PRM (gORM, gPRM), across 14 diverse domains. Contrary to conventional wisdom,
we find that (i) dORM performs on par with dPRM, (ii) gPRM is not competitive, and
(iii) overall, gORM is the most robust, yielding significant and consistent gains across every
tested domain. We attribute the worse performance of gPRM to the stepwise scoring process, which inherits label noise from LLM-based automatic labeling, leading to difficulties
in evaluating long reasoning trajectories, including those involving self-correcting reasoning.
Both our theoretical analysis and empirical observations indicate that stepwise aggregation
compounds errors as reasoning length increases. These findings challenge the common assumption that fine-grained supervision is always better and support generative outcome
verification for multi-domain deployment. Our code is publicly available to facilitate future
research in multi-domain settings.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2410.17621v2: Process Supervision-Guided Policy Optimization for Code Generation
findings.claim: In RL for code generation, a line-level PRM, whose labels were produced automatically (a code prefix is labelled correct if some completion of it passes all unit tests), used both as a dense reward and for value initialisation improved pass@1 over an RL baseline trained on unit-test rewards alone (e.g. Qwen2.5-7B-RL: MBPP 62.4% to 65.4%, LiveCodeBench 27.5% to 30.1%).
findings.setting: Experiment: RL fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-7B and Doubao-Lite with unit-test rewards; PRM labels from automated completion and testing of code prefixes, not human labels; evaluation pass@1 on HumanEval, MBPP and LiveCodeBench.
findings.bears_on: Process supervision outside math and in RL training, a setting the asking paper did not test (it used best-of-N only).

passages.text:
Reinforcement learning (RL) with unit test
feedback has enhanced large language models’
(LLMs) code generation, but relies on sparse rewards provided only after complete code evaluation, limiting learning efficiency and incremental improvements. When generated code fails
all unit tests, no learning signal is received, hindering progress on complex tasks. To address
this, we propose a Process Reward Model (PRM)
that delivers dense, line-level feedback on code
correctness during generation, mimicking human
code refinement and providing immediate guidance. We explore various strategies for training
PRMs and integrating them into the RL framework, finding that using PRMs both as dense rewards and for value function initialization significantly boosts performance. Our experimental
results also highlight the effectiveness of PRMs in
enhancing RL-driven code generation, especially
for long-horizon scenarios.

costly and not scalable. Instead, we employ an automated
approach inspired by techniques used in recent works (Wang
et al., 2024a;b; Luo et al., 2024). Our method leverages the
model’s own capabilities to generate completions for partial code prefixes and uses automated testing to assess their
correctness. The key idea is to determine whether a partial
code prefix can be extended—by any means—into a complete program that passes all unit tests. If so, we consider
the prefix as potentially correct; otherwise, it is labeled as
incorrect.

Combining PRM for both dense rewards and value initialization yields significant performance improvements.
In Qwen2.5-7B-RL, Pass@1 increases from 62.4% to
65.4% on MBPP and from 27.5% to 30.1% on LiveCodeBench. Similarly, in Doubao-Lite-RL, Pass@1
improves from 65.1% to 70.9% on HumanEval, 61.9% to
63.8% on MBPP, and 28.2% to 29.8% on LiveCodeBench.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2502.06737v2: VersaPRM: Multi-Domain Process Reward Model via Synthetic Reasoning Data
findings.claim: The authors report that existing PRMs trained on math data perform poorly in other domains, and that a multi-domain PRM trained on synthetic reasoning data gives consistent gains across domains, e.g. 7.9% over majority voting in MMLU-Pro Law via weighted majority voting versus 1.3% for Qwen2.5-Math-PRM.
findings.setting: Experiment: diverse domains including MMLU-Pro Law; PRM trained on synthetic chain-of-thought data whose step labels come from Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct evaluating each chain step by step to locate the earliest erroneous step (LLM labels, not human labels); PRMs used for weighted majority voting and compared with majority voting; the quoted lines include no ORM comparison.
findings.bears_on: Whether math-trained process supervision transfers to other domains (it largely did not) and whether domain-matched process labels help.

passages.text:
Process Reward Models (PRMs) have proven
effective at enhancing mathematical reasoning
for Large Language Models (LLMs) by leveraging increased inference-time computation. However, they are predominantly trained on mathematical data and their generalizability to nonmathematical domains has not been rigorously
studied. In response, this work first shows that
current PRMs have poor performance in other
domains. To address this limitation, we introduce VersaPRM, a multi-domain PRM trained
on synthetic reasoning data generated using our
novel data generation and annotation method. VersaPRM achieves consistent performance gains
across diverse domains. For instance, in the
MMLU-Pro category of Law, VersaPRM via
weighted majority voting, achieves a 7.9% performance gain over the majority voting baseline—
surpassing Qwen2.5-Math-PRM’s gain of 1.3%.

5.2. Auto-Labeling
To annotate our synthetic CoT data, we adopt an approach
inspired by the critic models in the work of Zheng et al.
(2024). Specifically, we utilize Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct as a
strong LLM to evaluate each CoT using step-by-step reasoning, locating the earliest erroneous step, if any. To enhance
accuracy and consistency, we identified two key additional
components.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2306.01693v2: Fine-Grained Human Feedback Gives Better Rewards for Language Model Training
findings.claim: On long-form question answering, RL with dense per-segment rewards learned from fine-grained human error labels produced fewer factual, irrelevance, repetition and incoherence errors than RL with a holistic preference reward; in overall comparisons annotators preferred it in 30.5% of examples, preferred preference-RLHF in 24.5%, and judged 45% ties.
findings.setting: Experiment: policy trained with RL; human annotators mark erroneous sentences or sub-sentences by error type; tasks are long-form QA and detoxification; the dense units are output segments, not reasoning steps, and the comparison also changes the feedback type (error labels vs preference feedback).
findings.bears_on: Whether finer-grained, step-like human supervision beats outcome-level feedback outside math, in RL training.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2501.12948v2: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
findings.claim: Reporting it as an unsuccessful attempt, the DeepSeek-R1 authors say a PRM faces three practical limits (defining fine-grained steps in general reasoning, judging step correctness without scalable annotation, and reward hacking) and that, while PRMs rerank top-N responses well, their advantages were limited relative to the added compute during large-scale RL in their experiments; they add that this does not imply such approaches cannot work.
findings.setting: Experience report from training large reasoning models with large-scale RL; no controlled PRM vs ORM numbers in these lines; domains are not separated in the quoted text.
findings.bears_on: Whether process supervision pays off in large-scale RL for general reasoning, beyond best-of-N reranking.

passages.text:
In the early stages of developing DeepSeek-R1, we also encountered failures and setbacks along
the way. We share our failure experiences here to provide insights, but this does not imply that
these approaches are incapable of developing effective reasoning models.

Process Reward Model (PRM) PRM is a reasonable method to guide the model toward better
approaches for solving reasoning tasks (Lightman et al., 2024; Uesato et al., 2022; Wang et al.,
2023a). However, in practice, PRM has three main limitations that may hinder its ultimate
success. First, it is challenging to explicitly define a fine-grain step in general reasoning. Second,
determining whether the current intermediate step is correct is a challenging task. Automated
annotation using models may not yield satisfactory results, while manual annotation is not conducive to scaling up. Third, once a model-based PRM is introduced, it inevitably leads to reward
hacking (Gao et al., 2022), and retraining the reward model needs additional training resources
and it complicates the whole training pipeline. In conclusion, while PRM demonstrates a good
ability to rerank the top-N responses generated by the model or assist in guided search (Snell
et al., 2024), its advantages are limited compared to the additional computational overhead it
introduces during the large-scale reinforcement learning process in our experiments.

questions.question: What makes a concept easy or hard for a strong model to learn from weak labels, and can weak-to-strong generalization error be estimated without labels?
questions.asked_by: Burns et al., Weak-to-Strong Generalization: Eliciting Strong Capabilities With Weak Supervision
questions.remaining_question: Can the absolute test error of a weak-to-strong model (not only its trend across weak supervisors) be estimated with no ground-truth labels, including for hyperparameter selection, for fully finetuned models, for reward modeling and when realizability fails? And which property of a concept (expansion, overlap density, linear decodability, salience) causally determines whether it is easy or hard to learn from weak labels when manipulated directly rather than only correlated?

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2502.00620v4: Representations Shape Weak-to-Strong Generalization: Theoretical Insights and Empirical Predictions
findings.claim: The authors report that a representation-based metric derived from their theory, computed without the finetuning task's labels, predicts trends in weak-to-strong performance, with strong correlation across 8 datasets, 150 small transformers and 52 LLMs, including a replication of Burns et al.'s SciQ, Amazon Polarity and Cosmos QA setup with Qwen-7B fully finetuned and 28 smaller LLMs as weak models. In that full-finetuning experiment the metric's hyperparameters were tuned per dataset and the best result reported, so labels entered hyperparameter choice, and the metric is validated as a trend (correlation) predictor, not as an estimate of the error value.
findings.setting: Experiments across 8 datasets with 150 small transformers and 52 LLMs, including Exp. III: a replication of Burns et al.'s setup on SciQ, Amazon Polarity and Cosmos QA with Qwen-7B as the strong model (entire model finetuned, unembedding layer replaced by a linear head, CE loss) and 28 smaller LLMs as weak models; W2S error measured as classification error; the metric is evaluated by its correlation with W2SG performance; in Exp. III hyperparameters were tuned per dataset, reporting the best result.
findings.bears_on: Second half of the question: estimating weak-to-strong generalization error without labels.

passages.text:

performance in practice without having the finetuning task
labels. This metric, which measures the overlap between the

with W2SG performance across various settings. The
extensive experiments across 8 datasets, involving 150 small
transformers and 52 LLMs, not only validate our theoretical
insights but also suggest their potential applications in managing W2SG, providing a deeper understanding of LLM
behavior through their internal representation structures.

Exp. III: NLP tasks with end-to-end finetuned LLMs.
We replicate a setup from (Burns et al., 2023) on three
datasets: (1) SciQ (Welbl et al., 2017), containing crowdsourced science exam questions; (2) Amazon Polarity
(Zhang et al., 2015), consisting of Amazon reviews;
and (3) Cosmos QA (Huang et al., 2019), involving
commonsense-based reading comprehension. Both data
preprocessing and finetuning strictly follow (Burns et al.,
2023). The entire model is finetuned with the unembedding
layer replaced with a linear head, using CE loss. We use
Qwen/Qwen-7B (Bai et al., 2023) as the strong model
and 28 smaller LLMs as weak models (details in Appx.
D.1). Errw2s is measured in terms of classification error.

In Exp. I, we set αw = αs = 0.1 and βw = βs = 0.1 for all datasets. In Exp. II, we set αw = 0.001, αs = 0.05,
λw = 0.0001, and λs = 0.01 for both datasets. In Exp. III, we tune the hyperparameters for each dataset, reporting the best
result. Specifically, we set αw = αs and vary them within the range {0.02, 0.05}, and vary βw and βs independently within
