findings.later_paper: arXiv 2405.15116v2: Quantifying the Gain in Weak-to-Strong Generalization
findings.claim: Theorem 1 (weak-to-strong generalization under realizability) states that, for a convex set Fs of functions on the strong representation, if the strong model's function fsw minimises the distance dP to the weak model's function over Fs and there exists fs in Fs with fs∘hs = f⋆∘h⋆ (realizability), then the error of the weakly supervised strong model on the true data is at most the true error of the weak model minus the misfit (the strong model's error on data labeled by the weak model), i.e. it improves over the weak model by at least the misfit. The authors say this lets one predict the amount by which the strong model will improve over the weak model, and choose among weak models, based on the misfit; the bound still contains the weak model's true error.
findings.setting: Theory: ground-truth representation h⋆ and real-valued finetuning task f⋆; strong and weak representation maps hs and hw; the strong model's function chosen from a convex set Fs to minimise the distance dP to the weak model's function; realizability assumed (Theorem 1). The abstract mentions empirical assessments that the passages do not describe.
findings.bears_on: Label-free estimation: under these assumptions the W2S gain is bounded below by the misfit, which is measured against the weak model's labels rather than ground truth; also why gains vary with the weak model chosen.

In this work, we present a theoretical framework for understanding weak-tostrong generalization. Specifically, we show that the improvement in performance
achieved by strong models over their weaker counterparts is quantified by the misfit
error incurred by the strong model on labels generated by the weaker model. Our
theory reveals several curious algorithmic insights. For instance, we can predict
the amount by which the strong model will improve over the weak model, and also
choose among different weak models to train the strong model, based on its misfit
error. We validate our theoretical findings through various empirical assessments.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2501.19105v2: Relating Misfit to Gain in Weak-to-Strong Generalization Beyond the Squared Loss
findings.claim: The authors extend the misfit-based characterization of the gain to losses that are Bregman divergences when the strong class is convex, which covers classification because the cross-entropy loss can be expressed as a Bregman divergence, and, for classification, to convex combinations of k strong models, up to an additional error term that vanishes as k gets large. In their plots (Figures 2, 3a, 3b) the gain is directly proportional to the misfit, but the theory's suggestion that the gain should be at least the misfit 'does not quite hold': the misfit is consistently larger than the difference between the weak and strong model loss; one significant reason, they say, is that their result assumes realizability, which they verified does not hold in their experiments.
findings.setting: Theory with Bregman-divergence losses, a convex strong class and assumed realizability; convex combinations of k strong models for classification; experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets (the passages do not name the models or datasets).
findings.bears_on: Label-free estimation in classification: whether the misfit (computable without ground truth) quantifies the W2S gain.

passages.text:
misfit between the strong and weak model. We generalize such a characterization to learning tasks whose loss
functions correspond to arbitrary Bregman divergences when the strong class is convex. This extends the
misfit-based characterization of performance gain in weak-to-strong generalization to classification tasks, as
the cross-entropy loss can be expressed in terms of a Bregman divergence. In most practical scenarios, however,
the strong model class may not be convex. We therefore weaken this assumption and study weak-to-strong
generalization for convex combinations of k strong models in the strong class, in the concrete setting of
classification. This allows us to obtain a similar misfit-based characterization of performance gain, upto
an additional error term that vanishes as k gets large. Our theoretical findings are supported by thorough
experiments on synthetic as well as real-world datasets.

Finally, while the plots in Figure 2 and Figure 3a, 3b do illustrate that the gain in performance is directly proportional to the misfit as expected, our theory would also additionally suggest that the gain should quantitatively
be at least the misfit (up to an error term decreasing in k). This does not quite hold in the plots—we can
observe that the misfit is consistently larger than the difference between the weak model and strong model loss.
One significant reason for this is that our result assumes realizability; namely, the target task should be exactly
representable by the strong model. We verified that this does not actually hold in our experiments—even if we
train the strong models on data with ground-truth labels, we see a non-trivial test loss at the end of training.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2412.03881v2: Weak-to-Strong Generalization Through the Data-Centric Lens
findings.claim: The authors propose that weak-to-strong generalization tracks the overlap density, the number of points containing both easy patterns (learnable by a weak model) and challenging patterns (only learnable by a stronger model), present a theoretical result showing that the generalization benefit is a function of the overlap density, and detect overlap points by thresholding weak-model confidence and using absolute inner products as overlap scores, with thresholds set by a change point detection technique. In their experiments, strong model performance improves as the overlap proportion increases, which they describe as providing evidence for the overlap density mechanism's role.
findings.setting: Theory and an overlap-detection algorithm on a stylised data model x = [x_easy, x_hard]; experiments following EleutherAI's replication of Burns et al., with Qwen1.5 0.5B as weak and Llama3 8B as strong model trained by linear probing (not full finetuning) on 19 datasets, and a weak-supervision setting (9 WRENCH datasets, Snorkel label model as weak model, 4-layer MLP as strong model).
findings.bears_on: First half: what properties of the data make weak-to-strong learning of a concept easy or hard.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2605.05710v1: On the Blessing of Pre-training in Weak-to-Strong Generalization
findings.claim: Across Pythia-6.9B and OLMo-7B pretraining checkpoints on reward-modeling tasks, the authors find a statistically significant positive correlation between a checkpoint's linear-probe accuracy and its final weak-to-strong performance (e.g. R2 about 0.90 for Pythia on CAI-Harmless), and report linear decodability as a more predictive indicator than pretraining evaluation loss; they suggest W2S becomes viable when the target concept is sufficiently linearly separable.
findings.setting: Empirical: Pythia-6.9B (154 checkpoints) and OLMo-7B (317 checkpoints) as strong students, weak supervisors such as Pythia-1B and OLMo-1B, reward modeling on HH-RLHF and CAI-Harmless, linear head on a frozen backbone, one epoch. Correlational; linear-probe accuracy uses ground-truth labels.
findings.bears_on: First half: what makes a concept easy to elicit, and an operational notion of salience (linear decodability in the pretrained representation).

passages.text:
Experimental Setup. Consistent with established W2SG benchmarks [Burns et al., 2024, Yang
et al., 2025], we evaluate performance on reward modeling tasks covering two primary alignment
dimensions: Harmlessness (CAI-Harmless [Bai et al., 2022a]) and Helpfulness (HH-RLHF [Bai
et al., 2022b]). To comprehensively trace the evolutionary dynamics of W2SG, our study spans an
extensive range of intermediate pre-training checkpoints from two distinct model families: Pythia6.9B (154 checkpoints) and OLMo-7B (317 checkpoints). For each task, we partition the data into
ground-truth, weak supervision, and test sets. Strong ceiling models are fine-tuned on ground-truth
labels, while weak-to-strong models are trained on labels generated by a weak supervisor (e.g.,
Pythia-1B and OLMo-1B) for a single epoch to mitigate overfitting. We report the test accuracy using
a linear projection head attached to the frozen backbone. Detailed configurations regarding dataset
partitioning and optimization hyperparameters are provided in Appendix C.5.

Mechanistic Insights via Linear Representation Hypothesis. To further explore the geometric
evolution accompanying these macroscopic trends, we investigate the linear separability [Park et al.,
2024, Jiang et al., 2024] of the model’s internal representations during pre-training. As extensively
detailed in Appendix C.7, we find a statistically significant positive correlation between the linear
probe accuracy of the pre-trained checkpoints and their ultimate W2SG performance (e.g., achieving
an R2 ≈ 0.90 for Pythia on CAI-Harmless, see Figure 13 and Table 1). Furthermore, our quantitative
analysis in Table 2 demonstrates that this linear decodability serves as a more predictive indicator
of W2SG feasibility than standard pre-training evaluation loss. This suggests that the emergence of
W2SG is closely associated with the linear decodability of the pre-trained manifold: the capability
to properly mitigate supervision noise and surpass the weak supervisor becomes empirically viable
when the latent geometric structure of the target concepts becomes sufficiently linearly separable.

questions.question: Which other combinations of scalable oversight and weak-to-strong generalization work?
questions.asked_by: Lang et al., Debate Helps Weak-to-Strong Generalization
questions.remaining_question: Does task decomposition combined with weak-to-strong training (a strong model trained on weak supervision of decomposed subtasks, testing part-to-complete generalization) recover more of the performance gap, measured against held-out ground-truth or expert labels, than plain W2SG or debate+W2SG, on verifiable tasks and on tasks without an automatic verifier?

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2608.17776v1: Debate Training Reduces Reward Hacking in RLAIF
findings.claim: A stronger Gemini 2.5 Flash-class policy was trained by RL from a frozen, weaker Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite judge on math tasks with checkable final answers. Debate worked better than a single-player RLAIF baseline: the baseline hacked the judge, while debate kept judge performance and reached a higher peak validation accuracy (45% performance gap recovered); in the results section this is about 2 percentage points above baseline, roughly 45% of the gap to the RLVR roofline, and the authors call the absolute effect small. The authors set this apart from Lang et al.: here the weak judge stays frozen and trusted, and the strong policy is trained on its signals, with the debate protocol relied on to improve signal correctness.
findings.setting: Experiment (RL fine-tuning). A Gemini 2.5 Flash-class policy trained through debate, a generator-critic game adjudicated by a frozen, weaker Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite judge, compared with a single-player RLAIF baseline; mathematics tasks whose verifiable final answers let the authors measure reward hacking. The 45% is the share of the gap between the baseline and an RLVR roofline recovered at peak validation accuracy. Unlike Lang et al.'s set-up, the weak judge stays frozen and its signals train the strong policy; verifiable domain only.
findings.bears_on: A combination other than Lang et al.'s debate-improved weak supervisor: debate as the reward protocol through which a frozen weak judge trains a stronger policy.

passages.text:
We demonstrate that RL finetuning an LLM using debate, a two-player adversarial game between a
generator and a critic adjudicated by a weaker LLM judge, reduces reward hacking compared to a

RLAIF: as training progresses, the policy learns to exploit systematic errors in its AI judge, degrading task

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2606.00424v2: Weak Critics Make Strong Learners: On-Policy Critique Distillation for Scalable Oversight
findings.claim: A weak model provides critiques in on-policy critique distillation (OPCD) training of a strong model; in the alignment scenario the weak model is supervised fine-tuned to follow Burns et al.'s weak-to-strong setting. The authors report that OPCD improves strong-model performance during training: Phi-4-14B on IFEval from 61.60 to 68.74 mean@8 (75.97 to 80.41 pass@8), and Qwen3-4B-base on GPQA from 38.22 to 42.67 mean@8 (70.25 to 76.86 pass@8). Critiques are checked both by whether the revised answer is correct (outcome check) and by whether the critique is relevant and useful as revision guidance (rubric check).
findings.setting: Experiment. Reasoning scenario: weak Qwen3-1.7B-base, strong Qwen3-4B-base, GPQA. Alignment scenario: weak Phi-4-mini-instruct, supervised fine-tuned and used as critic (following Burns et al.), strong Phi-4-14B, IFEval. Reported numbers are training-time performance. The outcome check uses whether the revised answer is correct.
findings.bears_on: Critique combined with weak-to-strong training. The outcome check uses ground-truth correctness, a confound for a 'weak supervision only' reading.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2601.20299v1: Truthfulness Despite Weak Supervision: Evaluating and Training LLMs Using Peer Prediction
findings.claim: Peer prediction, which the authors draw from mechanism-design research, rewards honest and informative answers using a metric based on mutual predictability and without requiring ground-truth labels. Training an 8B model with a peer prediction-based reward produced by a 0.135B language model with no finetuning recovered most of the drop in truthfulness due to prior malicious finetuning. The authors report that peer prediction with the 135M-parameter expert outperforms LLM-as-a-Judge with even the 7B-parameter judge, which they say suggests robustness against optimization pressure.
findings.setting: Experiment. Participants are four Llama-3.1-8B clones (one instructed to deceive); the expert is SmolLM-135M. 37,079 questions from MATH, MMLU, MMLU-PRO, ARC, OpenBookQA and RACE/MCTest subsets, with ground-truth labels used only to compute accuracy for plotting. Malicious (deceptive) finetuning, then training with the peer-prediction reward. Baseline: LLM-as-a-Judge, including a 7B-parameter judge.
findings.bears_on: An incentive-compatible oversight mechanism combined with training a stronger model from a much weaker supervisor. The task is recovering truthfulness after malicious finetuning, not Burns et al.'s W2SG set-up, and the paper does not frame itself as W2SG.

passages.text:
underutilized in LLM research, a wealth of mechanism design research focuses
on game-theoretic incentive compatibility — eliciting honest and informative answers with weak supervision. Drawing from this literature, we introduce the peer
prediction method for model evaluation and post-training. It rewards honest and
informative answers over deceptive and uninformative ones, using a metric based
on mutual predictability and without requiring ground truth labels. We demonstrate the method’s effectiveness and resistance to deception, with both theoretical
guarantees and empirical validation on models with up to 405B parameters. We
show that training an 8B model with peer prediction-based reward recovers most
of the drop in truthfulness due to prior malicious finetuning, even when the reward
is produced by a 0.135B language model with no finetuning. On the evaluation

Models We use four clones of Llama-3.1-8B (Dubey et al., 2024) as participants, one of which is
instructed to respond deceptively to all questions (Appendix D.2). We use SmolLM-135M (Allal
et al., 2024) as the only expert. Models are instruction-tuned.
Dataset (Free-Form Response) By combining MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021b), MMLU
(Hendrycks et al., 2021a), MMLU-PRO (Wang et al., 2024), ARC (Clark et al., 2018), OpenBookQA (Mihaylov et al., 2018), subsets of RACE (Lai et al., 2017) and MCTest (Richardson et al.,
2013), we obtain a dataset of 37079 questions spanning 85 domains, including math, natural sciences,
engineering, social sciences, medicine, humanities, philosophy, law, professional skills, common
knowledge, and general reasoning skills. This includes a mixture of multiple-choice questions (e.g.
MMLU) and free-form questions (e.g. MATH), all with rule-based verification mechanisms. However,
We discard the ground-truth labels/verification rules except when calculating accuracy in plotting,
and only use the questions as input to the peer prediction method. We also transform question
statements to always require free-form responses. We employ cross validation with a 50-50 split.

Result: Recovery of Truthfulness Figure 1 indicates that the most of the accuracy drop from
deception training is recovered. Notably, peer prediction with the 135M-parameter expert outperforms
LLM-as-a-Judge with even the 7B-parameter judge. The finding suggests that peer prediction is
robust against optimization pressure, consistent with Theorem 2.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2602.04210v2: Steering LLMs via Scalable Interactive Oversight
findings.claim: The authors trained a Qwen3-30B-A3B interaction policy with a variant of GRPO; in training rollouts it interacts with a simulated user node by node until all nodes are resolved to yield a PRD, with gemini-2.5-pro as the doc generator and o4-mini updating the requirement tree. With a reward that encourages minimizing the frequency of the user's DontCare responses, they report that 'the interaction could be optimized with the signal from the non-expert user only': as the training reward increased, the alignment score also increased, which they call 'a weak-to-strong optimization effect, where non-experts' feedback at interaction time is sufficient to guide stronger models'.
findings.setting: Experiment (RL training). A Qwen3-30B-A3B interaction policy trained with a GRPO variant resolves the nodes of a requirement tree with a simulated user to produce a PRD (gemini-2.5-pro doc generator, o4-mini tree updates); the reward is based on how often the user answers DontCare. The user simulator is deepseek-R1 emulating non-expert behaviour, conditioned on the ground-truth intent. The alignment score is the fraction of requirements satisfied in the generated PRD, judged in large-scale evaluation by a Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct LLM judge. Differs from the question's W2SG framing: the weak supervisor is an LLM simulating a non-expert user, there is no weak-labels-to-strong-student fine-tuning in Burns et al.'s sense, and no PGR.
findings.bears_on: Task decomposition (a requirement tree resolved node by node) plus training from weak, non-expert feedback, the pairing Lang et al. name: one such combination reported to work, in a narrower setting (PRD writing, an LLM-simulated non-expert user, an LLM-judged alignment score) that is not standard W2SG.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2503.13621v1: Superalignment with Dynamic Human Values
findings.claim: The authors sketch a roadmap for a framework that trains a superhuman reasoning model to decompose complex tasks into subtasks that are still amenable to human-level guidance. It relies on a 'part-to-complete generalization hypothesis' (alignment of subtask solutions generalizes to alignment of complete solutions), and, for high-level summaries of complete solutions that a human-level AI can evaluate only imperfectly, on the planner model possibly learning the true intent through weak-to-strong generalization. They state that its success hinges on part-to-complete generalization, which must be empirically validated.
findings.setting: Roadmap sketch of an algorithmic framework (a superhuman reasoning model decomposing tasks into subtasks for human-level guidance, with a human-level AI judging solution summaries); the passages report no results.
findings.bears_on: Task decomposition + W2SG: the paper confirms the pairing is proposed and names the property to measure (part-to-complete generalization), but gives no result.

passages.text:
Two core challenges of alignment are 1) scalable oversight and 2) accounting for
the dynamic nature of human values. While solutions like recursive reward modeling address 1), they do not simultaneously account for 2). We sketch a roadmap
for a novel algorithmic framework that trains a superhuman reasoning model to
decompose complex tasks into subtasks that are still amenable to human-level
guidance. Our approach relies on what we call the part-to-complete generalization hypothesis, which states that the alignment of subtask solutions generalizes
to the alignment of complete solutions. We advocate for the need to measure this
generalization and propose ways to improve it in the future.

(3) Solution Summarization A third approach involves generating high-level summaries of complete solutions for human-level AI judgment. While the human-level AI may not comprehend all
implementation details, it can provide an imperfect evaluation of whether the summary adequately
reflects the intended composition of subtasks and maintains desired safety properties. Despite the
imperfect evaluation, the planner model may learn the true intent through weak-to-strong generalization.

Although our framework addresses many key alignment challenges, significant work remains. While
it addresses the outer-alignment problem, it does not directly address the alignment of a model’s
internal objectives (inner alignment). Moreover, its success hinges on the extent of part-to-complete
generalization, which must be empirically validated across different domains and task complexities.
New methods to improve part-to-complete generalization need to be developed. These challenges,

entries.label: Proved
entries.statement: In the idealized black-box model (2506.13609v2 Section 7, 2610.02557v1 Section 5), naive recursive debate on a depth-d, width-q AND decomposition with one uniformly hidden flawed leaf catches the dishonest debater with probability at most (m+1)/q^d, for any Bob making m adaptive oracle queries; 1/q^d is attained at m = 0. The model assumes Alice's visible argument does not depend on where the flaw is. Theorem 5.3 of 2610.02557v1 holds in packing form for randomized checkers that are finite mixtures of deterministic decision trees, with Alice folded in as oracle-independent: some root-flipping block changes the acceptance probability by at most m/R. For AND trees with one flaw this gives m >= (1 - 2 eps) q^d. Lemma 5.4 of that paper (local fbs >= rho implies global >= rho^d) is not re-proved; the AND case does not need it.
entries.evidence: 10 of 10 Lean statements checked as faithful (Q21:L1, Q21:L2, Q21:L3, Q21:L4, Q21:L5, Q21:L6, Q21:L7, Q21:L8, Q21:L9, Q21:L10); data/maths/formal/
entries.remains: (1) The question as posed (2311.08702v1 p14 L12-13) is empirical: whether obfuscated arguments appear in harder free-text debates. Nothing here bears on that. (2) Computational form F3: whether any recursive protocol with Bob's cost polynomial in Alice's avoids computationally obfuscated arguments beyond stable / low-FBS decompositions (2610.02557v1 p14 L47-56; 2311.14125v1 p9 L40-46); in the black-box model the answer is negative by F2. (3) Not formalized here: Lemma 5.4 of 2610.02557v1 (local to global fractional block sensitivity, needed beyond AND trees), debaters that query the oracle themselves, and any complexity model (so 'efficient' is an abstract class in Q21_conjecture_computational). (4) Which natural 'harder questions' admit low-FBS decompositions (the stability questions Q51/Q47, handled by another worker).

entries.label: Proved
entries.statement: For the repository's protocol in the Lean model with a flawed verifier oracle (debaters use the true oracle): (1) small uniform verifier errors cost at most δ(106000k²+1) of completeness and soundness, independent of the computation length t, because only verifier queries are charged and the verifier makes O(k²) expected queries; (2) random errors drawn independently of the debaters' strategies cost at most ε(106000k²+1) on average, which answers a precise version of the paper's second sub-question ('arbitrary errors on a randomly selected subset of queries') positively when ε is small compared with 1/k²; (3) in general the loss is the expected number of verifier queries that land on wrong answers in the debate actually played; (4) a precise version of the paper's first sub-question fails for this protocol: one adversarially placed wrong answer lets a dishonest debater win with probability ≥ 49/50, for every t and every k ≥ 1, on either side; in the soundness instance that query is never sent to the verifier under honest play, and for t ≥ 1 changing it does not change the computation's answer; uniform errors of order 1/k also break the protocol; (5) if all parties share a flawed oracle that is itself k-Lipschitz, the repository's theorem transfers with the 2/3 margin raised by kδ.
entries.evidence: 17 of 21 Lean statements checked as faithful (Q22:L1, Q22:L2, Q22:L3, Q22:L4, Q22:L5, Q22:L6, Q22:L7, Q22:L8, Q22:L9, Q22:L10, Q22:L11, Q22:L12, Q22:L13, Q22:L14, Q22:L19, Q22:L20, Q22:L21); data/maths/q22/
entries.remains: (i) Whether some debate protocol, not the repository's, can verify a natural class of K-Lipschitz computations when the verifier's oracle errs adversarially on an arbitrary set of at most k queries (the paper's first sub-question). In the repository's protocol and in Figure 1 the verifier's check at the aborted round decides the debate, so a protocol would have to check more than the disputed query, for example by exploiting robustness of the computation as Chen, Kalai and Xi do for single-prover proofs. (ii) The exact tolerance of the default protocol to uniform verifier error: robust at δ < 1/(10(106000k²+1)), broken at δ = 3/(100k); whether retuned parameters tolerate δ = Θ(1/k) is open. (iii) Random errors whose realised locations the dishonest debater can see. Informally (not proved here) such a debater can follow the honest path until it reaches an erroneous query and lie there, so once errors along a path become likely, the same attack applies. (iv) Errors in the debaters' own oracle (the paper's separate 'Power of the Provers' question), and a shared flawed oracle that is not Lipschitz. (v) Transfer of all statements to the paper's Turing-machine model, with cross-examination coin flipping and its constants.

entries.label: Proved
entries.statement: In a finite one-message model, a training procedure that can evaluate every prover of the class on training instances yields, with probability >= 1 - |V|(1 - eps)^m, a verifier whose completeness plus soundness error against every prover of the class is <= eps, whenever it is consistent on the data; m >= ln(|V|/delta)/eps suffices. The bound depends on the verifier class size but not on the prover class size. If training only sees a weaker prover class than deployment, no sample size and no learner suffices in general: in an explicit two-world example with a perfect verifier available in each world, every learner's expected deployment soundness errors in the two worlds sum to 1/2 for every m. A verifier class that cannot separate a dishonest message on a false instance from the honest message on a true instance has completeness plus soundness error at least the smaller of the two instances' probabilities, whatever the data: the verifier's ability sets a floor that data cannot remove.
entries.evidence: 7 of 10 Lean statements checked as faithful (Q37:L1, Q37:L2, Q37:L3, Q37:L4, Q37:L5, Q37:L6, Q37:L7); data/maths/formal/
entries.remains: (1) Q37_conjecture (prover ability must enter a proper verifier's sample complexity) and Q37_conjecture_improper are open. (2) Q37_agnostic is standard (Hoeffding plus union bound) but not proved in Lean here. (3) Multi-round protocols (nip, mnip, debate) and joint training: in neural interactive proofs the prover is itself learned from data, so its ability is a hypothesis class plus an optimiser; nothing here covers training dynamics or equilibrium finding. (4) Model differences: the nip loss in 2412.08897v2 is worst-case over inputs (Q37-p8, Q37-p9), while our errors are probabilities under P; they coincide only up to the minimum instance mass. (5) Computational abilities (circuit size, compute) rather than hypothesis classes, e.g. relative-complexity results like the soundness construction of 2506.13609v2, are not addressed.

entries.label: Proved
entries.statement: Q47: in Figure 2, a coherent estimator makes every intermediate consistency reward 0 whatever the prover does; the only signal against a coherent dishonest estimator is the leaf reward, bounded by the largest leaf error.
entries.evidence: 2 of 2 Lean statements checked as faithful (Q47:L1, Q47:L2); data/maths/stability/
entries.remains: (1) Exact characterization of completeness for Figure 2 on a fixed tree: an unstable sensitive cut is sufficient for failure (derived) and all-nodes-stable is sufficient for success (Theorem 6.1); the conjecture that 'no unstable sensitive cut' is also sufficient for success (exact for all q = 2, d = 2 trees computed) needs a proof and tests for q >= 3; a closed form for Val(x,T,1/rho) on non-uniform trees is open. (2) Adaptive provers: our necessity results fix the prover's tree; whether a prover that changes decomposition in response to B's estimates can beat the barrier min(r^(d+1), 1/fbs_alpha(F_T)) of its realised tree is not settled here. (3) Beyond black-box judges and unbounded opponents: 2610.02557v1 settles the query lower bound for black-box judges (fixed revealed tree, distinct leaves); protocols with structured or partly transparent judgments, and opponents that cannot find sensitive blocks, remain open, as that paper also states (p14 L47-56). (4) Q51(b) converse: does a decomposition with small global fbs_alpha(F_T) <= R imply one of depth O(d) with local fbs <= C R^(1/d)? And which natural problem classes (beyond weighted thresholds, Lipschitz aggregators, AND-like proofs) have small global fbs for some A-provable decomposition? (5) Q47: a protocol that provably elicits coherent, leaf-calibrated reports with an fbs-independent incentive gap, and a useful notion of honesty whose conversion to correctness costs less than fbs_alpha(F_T), are open; the unstable-to-stable transformation route (M to M*) is not addressed here. (6) General-q proofs of the phi-uniform closed form and of the unstable-cut statement (both only derived and checked for q = 2, 3).

entries.label: Proved
entries.statement: Q51, depth 1: in the Figure 2 game with r = 1/rho (rho >= 1) on one instance, the honest bound (exists A, for all B, E[payoff] >= 1/rho^2) holds iff the root is rho-stable, i.e. iff fbs_z(f) <= rho; the exact value is 1/(rho max(rho, fbs)). Q51, any depth, Figure 2 with r = 1/rho: if the root node of the prover's tree is not rho-stable, every prover strategy is held below the Theorem 6.1 bound 1/rho^(d+1) by some estimator. So root stability is necessary for the conclusion of Theorem 6.1 on that tree. Q51, margin barrier: for every reward ratio r >= 0, every tree T and every prover using T, some valid estimator holds the expected payoff to <= min(r^(d+1), 1/W) for every fractional packing of sensitive blocks of the path-indexed composed function F_T with total weight W; at the LP optimum, <= min(r^(d+1), 1/fbs_alpha(F_T)). So no choice of the protocol parameter gives the honest prover more than 1/fbs_alpha(F_T), and the conclusion of Theorem 6.1 on T forces fbs_alpha(F_T) <= rho^(d+1). Q51(b), sufficient classes with constants: weighted-margin functions are (sum w)/m-stable; weighted-Lipschitz score thresholds with margin delta are (sum w)/delta-stable; [#true >= theta] is t/(t - theta + 1)-stable at t >= theta true inputs and (q - t)/(theta - t)-stable below (exact: equals fbs for q <= 5); every function is q-stable. Q51(b), lower bounds and one-level composition: k disjoint sensitive blocks rule out rho < k (AND of q bits: best constant exactly q); if inner functions are rho2-stable and the outer function is rho1-stable, the composition is rho1 rho2-stable (inner functions may share inputs).
