nodes.label: Empirical tests of debate's key assumptions

passages.text:
Empirical testing and optimisation. While debate has theoretical appeal, we have only limited data
on its practical effectiveness (Arnesen et al., 2024; Barnes & Christiano, 2020; Kenton et al., 2024; Khan
et al., 2024; Michael et al., 2023). For example, most previous experiments use the QuALITY dataset
(Pang et al., 2022) and simple debate protocols with low recursive depth. Key questions include whether
debate measurably improves performance, whether training reliably reaches equilibrium, whether stability is
a real problem, and whether obfuscated arguments actually emerge as predicted. We also need an improved
understanding of systematic human errors – for example: How good are humans at giving correct answers
in verifiable domains, what are common systematic errors and in which domains are they most prominent,
and how we can design human input for optimal results? A final set of questions surrounds the deployment
set-up. For example, what counts as an "action" for the purpose of online learning in the datacentre? And
will many questions in the relevant domain be difficult to answer via deductive arguments?

nodes.pl: Sec. 5.1 'Extending the safety case to high-stakes contexts'; Sec. 5.2 'High-stakes contexts'
nodes.label: Extending the case to high stakes

passages.text:
This safety case sketch only works in low-stakes contexts where it takes many bad actions to cause unacceptable outcomes. Key claim 4 – that we are in a low-stakes context – breaks by definition. Key claim 3 –
that the error rate will stay consistent throughout deployment – also breaks because we can no longer rely
on online training, opening up the possibility of alignment faking and other distribution shift problems.

High-stakes contexts. In the high-stakes context, we face greater generalisation challenges. We lose the
ability to use online training, so need to face the possibility of distribution shifts and alignment faking; and
we need new ways to contend with coordinated errors not captured by our reward signal. We outline research
directions in the previous section.

First, we might be able to use online training-like techniques during inference, on candidate actions instead
of on final actions. This would allow us to maintain an error rate of ε for candidate actions, then cut the
regret further by generating many candidate actions. This might be enough to patch key claim 3; it is not
enough to completely patch key claim 4, but it gets us some of the way.
Second, the evidence needed to support key claim 1 and 2 might be sufficient (or extendable) to patch key
claims 3 and 4. For example, to address exploration hacking, we might need a method for eliciting bad
contexts (e.g. based on interpretability or singular learning theory). Such a method might also be useful for
generating datasets that mimic deployment sufficiently effectively that we can minimise distributional shifts.

nodes.label: Does honesty translate into aligned actions?

passages.text:
From honesty to alignment. We need to better understand the alignment value of honest questionanswering. How much does honesty plus absence of alignment faking translate into aligned actions during
alignment research? How can deployment environments be designed to minimize risk while maintaining the
system’s usefulness for alignment research?

More broadly, it seems like, given a theorem showing that the error rate is at most ε, in practice one should
put significant weight on something like full intent alignment (or at least the system not being egregiously
misaligned). For example, it seems plausible that human error is anticorrelated with the severity of error
such that the errors that remain are inconsequential.

SC-C2.1.why: The authors say strong dishonest strategies that break debate at the Nash equilibrium may exist that their human debaters did not find or gave up on too easily, and that testing whether debate works in the limit needs more optimization pressure on debaters. This bears on key claim 1 by indicating the debates studied were not shown to be at equilibrium; it is evidence neither that training reaches the equilibrium nor that it fails to.
SC-C2.1.gap: Human debaters in an empirical study, not a training process T on AI debaters; the record states a possibility, not a measurement.

SC-C2.1.why: In the authors' error analysis of debates a human judge got wrong, the most common error was weak arguments from the debater arguing the correct answer, which they take to mean their LLM debaters are far from optimal. This bears on key claim 1 as a sign that current LLM debaters do not play the game well, but it concerns the authors' debaters, not a training process run to equilibrium.
SC-C2.1.gap: LLM debaters judged by humans in a present-day study; the quote does not describe the debaters as trained to equilibrium in the debate game, and they are far from a deployed superhuman system.

SC-C2.1.why: The authors' take-away is that prover-estimator debaters can be trained 'via standard methods that converge to Stackelberg equilibria in zero-sum games', and that whether training succeeded can be read off A's expected payoff against a known threshold. This offers a check on the outcome of training, but the quoted lines assert rather than show that standard training methods reach the equilibrium.
SC-C2.1.gap: Theoretical statement about the prover-estimator protocol; no training run or convergence result for realistic debaters is given in the quote.

SC-C3.1.why: Theorem 6.1 (soundness) proves that for every prover strategy A in the class A there is an estimator B, a circuit of size O(q2^{3q}nd^2/eta^2) that may query A at each gate, holding A's expected payoff to at most P[A(x)=L(x)]/rho^(d+1) + eta. This is a proof of the relative efficiency notion the node asks for, the estimator needing only polynomially many calls to the prover in n and d (though exponentially many in the width q).
SC-C3.1.gap: Complexity-theoretic theorem over an input distribution mu and a recursive decomposition of depth d and width q; not about neural debaters reached by training, and the estimator bound grows as 2^{3q} in the width.

SC-C3.1.why: Theorem 6.1 (completeness) proves that if the decomposition is A-provable (achieved by some A* in the class A) and rho-stable with probability 1 - gamma, some prover A in the same class guarantees, with probability at least 1 - 2 gamma, expected payoff at least 1/rho^(d+1) against estimators of any size. This shows the prover's side of the game can be played within the bounded class A, which is half of the efficient-equilibrium existence proof (E4.1) the node asks for.
SC-C3.1.gap: Complexity-theoretic theorem; holds only under A-provability and rho-stability with probability 1 - gamma and gives an expected-payoff guarantee, not a statement about trained neural debaters.

SC-C3.1.why: With width q constant, a single prover-estimator debate costs O(q2^{3q}nd^3/eta^2) queries to functions in the prover class, which the authors state is a polynomial improvement over the O(n^c) cost of verifying the full transcript when a very stable decomposition exists, while doubly-efficient debate would need O(n^c) debater queries. This supports the node's requirement of a realistic efficiency notion, but only for very stable decompositions (rho much smaller than q).
SC-C3.1.gap: Cost analysis inside the theoretical model; the improvement holds only when a very stable decomposition exists, and nothing is said about equilibria reached by training.

SC-C3.1.why: The authors say their guarantees are average-case and ask whether there are lower bounds on B's circuit size when the stability parameter rho is held constant. This bears on the node's efficiency notion: whether the estimator's cost is tight is open.
SC-C3.1.gap: Stated open question in a theoretical paper; no result.

SC-C3.1.why: Doubly-efficient debate has two polynomial-time provers and proves that, under appropriate assumptions, any polynomial-time computation can be verified with a constant number of queries to the black box representing human judgement. This is an efficiency notion of the kind the node needs to replace unbounded debaters, but for a different protocol and an absolute polynomial-time notion rather than the case's estimator-versus-prover notion.
SC-C3.1.gap: Theoretical model with a black-box human-judgement oracle; a different protocol (doubly-efficient debate) from the prover-estimator debate the case relies on.

SC-C3.2.why: In a debate training run, training for longer increased win rate: by Elo, the SFT-only starting model wins 31% of rounds against other checkpoints and the fully trained DPO model 67%. This is training-curve evidence of the kind E4.2 names, but the quote reports improvement with training, not diminishing returns or arrival at a local equilibrium.
SC-C3.2.gap: A debate training run of present-day models (SFT then DPO) judged by a judge trained on earlier transcripts, far from a deployed superhuman system; the quote does not say whether returns had flattened by the end of training.

SC-C3.3.why: Theorem 4 shows that in the simultaneous formulation of a small prover-verifier game, gradient descent from any initialization with positive message probabilities converges to the ideal joint strategy, whereas Theorem 5 shows the prover-first formulation converges to an undesirable solution. In a toy game, whether gradient descent reaches the ideal strategy or an undesirable one depends on the game's formulation, which bears on whether T's local equilibrium is the intended one.
SC-C3.3.gap: A small theoretical prover-verifier game with an input x and a finite message set, not debate between large models trained by SGD; Theorem 5 shows the outcome depends on the game's formulation.

SC-C4.1.why: For repeated games with very many, language-based actions, as in AI Safety via Debate, where existing algorithms need per-iteration computation polynomial in the number of actions, the authors give an oracle-based algorithm whose regret depends only logarithmically on the number of actions. This bears on whether debate games are tractable beyond the tabular case the node's evidence E5.1 relies on, but the quote does not connect regret minimization to reaching the equilibrium E or to SGD training time.
SC-C4.1.gap: The analysis assumes oracle access ('oracles naturally model access to AI agents'); it is not about gradient-based training of debaters.

SC-C4.1.why: Theorem 8 reduces finding a valid proof system to finding an approximate verifier-leading Stackelberg equilibrium of the nip game, and the authors state this task is far from straightforward, naming the difficulties of minimising worst-case rather than expected loss and of finding a Stackelberg equilibrium. This bears on C4.1 by naming equilibrium-finding as an open difficulty; it gives no hardness or tractability result.
SC-C4.1.gap: nip prover-verifier game rather than the case's debate protocol; a stated difficulty, not a result about SGD or training time.

SC-C4.1.why: In a graph-isomorphism experiment, verifiers trained under the debate, adp and mnip protocols saw no increase in performance while nip did, which the authors attribute mainly to the task: its simple verification algorithm is harder to learn with multiple provers, as in debate. This is a weak data point that learning good play can be harder in multi-prover protocols, but it does not measure distance to equilibrium or training time.
SC-C4.1.gap: A graph-isomorphism task with a simple known verification algorithm and learned provers and verifiers, not a deployed debate system; the authors attribute the null result mainly to the task.

SC-C4.2.why: When training debate and solo verifiers with expert iteration, vanilla expert iteration exacerbated an initial low acceptance rate because only rollouts where the verifier guessed correctly were kept ('mode collapse'), and a 'stabilised' variant reduced this and improved every protocol's worst-case performance. This is a training failure with a cause other than exploration hacking, bearing on the node's guess that other failure modes matter less; the quote does not say whether it kept training from an equilibrium, and a changed training scheme greatly reduced it.
SC-C4.2.gap: Expert-iteration training in an interaction-protocol experiment, not the case's training process T toward the equilibrium E.

SC-C4.2.why: In checkability training, a verifier with 10^-4 of the prover's compute made training unstable and a verifier matching the prover's size did not become more robust over rounds; the authors cannot exclude non-optimal hyperparameters but suspect real causes (a too-limited verifier may be unable to verify; a sneaky prover can more easily simulate a similar verifier's mistakes). These are candidate reasons training fails that are not exploration hacking, bearing on the node's 'mostly a hunch' claim.
SC-C4.2.gap: Prover-verifier checkability training, not debate; the failures are hedged (hyperparameters may explain them), and the too-weak-verifier case may be infeasible, which C4.2 assumes away.

SC-D5.3.why: Theorem 4 shows that in the simultaneous formulation of a small prover-verifier game, gradient descent from any initialization with positive message probabilities converges to the ideal joint strategy, so there training does not get stuck short of the intended solution. Theorem 5's undesirable convergence is attributed in the quote to formulating the game with the prover playing first, not described as a local minimum.
SC-D5.3.gap: A small theoretical prover-verifier game, not SGD on a debate game between large models; at most weak evidence against the defeater for the case's game.

SC-C4.3.why: A language model optimized by RLHF under the reward R* misleads humans far less often when incorrect, which the authors take to suggest that imperfections in the reward R_train cause models to exploit human weaknesses. This bears on the node's caveat that exploration guarantees are much more useful with a trusted reward, since more optimization against a bad reward does not give better outcomes; it says nothing about exploration hacking itself.
SC-C4.3.gap: RLHF of language models judged by humans, not debate training; concerns reward quality, not whether a model withholds high-reward strategies.

SC-E5.3.why: The authors stress-test a frozen verifier by optimizing the prover or the messages directly, describe this as a way of checking whether the verifier is at a verifier-leading Stackelberg equilibrium, and note that incorrect proofs the verifier would accept may still exist but be hard to find. This bears on E5.3's proposal to hold one debater fixed and train the other adversarially: a failed attack is evidence, not a guarantee, that no higher-reward strategy is being missed.
SC-E5.3.gap: Robustness check of a verifier in a prover-verifier game, not an exploration-hacking detector for debaters; the limitation is stated, not measured.

SC-E5.3.why: A probing detector that works well on a sleeper agent, whose bad behaviour was artificially induced, is not much better than random on the naturally emerging sophistry ('U-Sophistry') of the authors' model, and the authors conclude that detection methods that work on one might not generalize to the other. This cautions against E5.3's plan to rely on model organism studies and whitebox techniques, since a detector validated on an artificially induced organism may not carry over to the model in question.
SC-E5.3.gap: Detection of sophistry, not of exploration hacking; one probing method on one model, with the authors' hedge 'might not necessarily generalize'.

SC-OP-EXPLORATION.why: A probing detector that works well on a sleeper agent, whose bad behaviour was artificially induced, is not much better than random on naturally emerging sophistry ('U-Sophistry'), and the authors conclude detection methods that work on one might not generalize to the other. This suggests the node's plan to test countermeasures on model organisms of exploration hacking may be harder than hoped, since success on an artificially induced organism may not transfer.
SC-OP-EXPLORATION.gap: Detection of sophistry, not of exploration hacking; one probing method on one model, with the authors' hedge 'might not necessarily generalize'.

SC-C3.4.why: The authors state that if claims are rho-stable and the debaters only make claims they know the answer to (A-provability), Theorem 6.2 implies that at the protocol's Stackelberg equilibria A produces the correct answer with probability at least 1 - 5 epsilon, and otherwise A's payoff falls below a known threshold. This is a proof of the kind E4.3 asks for, that equilibrium outputs of prover-estimator debate match the correct output up to an epsilon-dependent error, under stated conditions.
SC-C3.4.gap: Complexity-theoretic result conditional on rho-stability and A-provability, about Stackelberg equilibria of the model game rather than the approximate equilibria of an actual training run.

SC-C3.4.why: Theorem 5.1 gives a debate protocol that deterministically decides any language decided by an oracle Turing machine M in time T, with A stating a middle configuration of M's computation and B choosing which half to recurse on, down to a single transition of M. This proves, for a different protocol, that debate reproduces the output of a large recursive computation, the kind of M-approximation proof E4.3 asks for.
SC-C3.4.gap: Doubly-efficient debate rather than the case's prover-estimator protocol; a theorem about the protocol deciding L exactly, not about slightly perturbed outputs at approximate equilibria of trained models.

SC-C3.4.why: Theorem 1 states that for any problem L in PSPACE a polynomial-time judge can be chosen so that optimal play in a debate with polynomially many steps solves L. This is the idealized form of the node's claim: with exact optimal play, the debate outcome equals the answer of the full alternating computation.
SC-C3.4.gap: Complexity-theory analogy with exact optimal play and a polynomial-time judge; says nothing about approximate equilibria or computational limits on debaters, where the node locates the obfuscated-arguments failure.

SC-C3.4.why: The authors state their results are average-case: they do not prove the judge can always tell which debater is correct, only that payoffs incentivize debaters to converge to answering correctly, so the payoff is imperfectly correlated with correctness. This qualifies the M-approximation proof the node requires: it holds over a distribution of questions, not on every question.
SC-C3.4.gap: Stated limitation of a theoretical analysis; no measurement.

SC-ASM-NO-OBFUSCATION.why: The authors state that existing recursive debate protocols run into the obfuscated arguments problem, where a dishonest debater's efficient strategy forces the honest debater to solve a computationally intractable problem, and that their new recursive protocol, under certain stability assumptions, ensures an honest debater can win with a strategy of efficiency comparable to its opponent's. This is a mitigation claim for the protocol the node relies on, conditional on stability.
SC-ASM-NO-OBFUSCATION.gap: A theoretical guarantee under stability assumptions ('mitigate', not eliminate); the quote reports no empirical test on harder or deeper debates.

SC-ASM-NO-OBFUSCATION.why: Soundness proves that for every prover strategy A there is an estimator of size O(q2^{3q}nd^2/eta^2), querying A, that holds A's expected payoff to at most P[A(x)=L(x)]/rho^(d+1) + eta, and the authors note this needs no stable decomposition, so it holds even when a dishonest A gives an incorrect decomposition. So a dishonest prover's payoff is capped by an estimator polynomial in n and d even when its decomposition is incorrect, which addresses the node's concern that the flaw in a false argument may be intractable for both debaters to find.
SC-ASM-NO-OBFUSCATION.gap: Complexity-theoretic theorem in expectation over an input distribution mu, with an estimator bound exponential in the width q; the honest side's win (completeness) still requires a rho-stable decomposition.

SC-C3.5.why: The record makes it a key requirement for applying its debate theorems that models can produce natural-language reasoning traces which careful human analysis could have judged correct. That is the node's hypothesis that the fully expanded, human-judged computation M gives correct outputs; the record states it as a requirement and limitation, not as a tested result.
SC-C3.5.gap: Complexity-theoretic paper stating an applicability condition; no fully expanded tree is judged by humans.

SC-C4.4.why: Theorem 1 states that for any problem in PSPACE a polynomial-time judge can be chosen so that optimal play in a debate of alternating points and counterpoints solves the problem. This is a theoretical argument of the kind the node cites (E5.4) that recursive argument trees judged at the leaves can identify the true answer.
SC-C4.4.gap: Complexity-theory analogy: formal problems in PSPACE, a polynomial-time judge chosen for the problem, and optimal play; not natural-language AI R&D questions judged by humans.

SC-C4.4.why: Theorem 5.1 gives a debate protocol that decides any language decided by an oracle Turing machine M, with one debater proposing a middle configuration and the other choosing which half to recurse on, down to a single transition. This formalises the node's claim that a debate along a single path stands in for the outcome of the whole tree.
SC-C4.4.gap: Oracle Turing machine model with optimal play; it presupposes that the computation M decides the language, so it bears on following one path through the tree rather than on whether M's outputs are true for real questions.

SC-C4.4.why: The authors state that their DEBATE = PSPACE discussion models judges as limited but free of error and agents as having unlimited computational power, and that significant research is required to know whether debate works in practice with human judges. This qualifies the theoretical support the node relies on.
SC-C4.4.gap: Conclusions and future-work section; no result.

SC-C4.4.why: The amplification experiments decompose questions algorithmically with a hand-coded algorithm in place of the human, and the authors say they shed no light on whether humans can decompose interesting real-world tasks. So these experiments do not test the node's claim for real questions.
SC-C4.4.gap: Iterated amplification (not debate) on combinatorial toy tasks; stated limitation.

SC-C4.4.why: The authors state that task decomposition could be fundamentally limiting because it assumes separate parts can be completed independently, and report a leaf summary that turned a request for a dance into a request for marriage because it saw only local context. This is an instance of a recursive decomposition producing a false leaf output on a class of task (long-range dependence) where the tree structure may not track the truth.
SC-C4.4.gap: Fixed, non-adversarial decomposition for book summarisation with model-written leaf outputs; in tree debate the debaters choose which arguments to expand and could contest such a leaf.

SC-D5.4.why: The record names as a key requirement that debating models can produce natural-language reasoning traces that careful human analysis could judge correct. The defeater is that some truths, e.g. ones known only through learned heuristics, may have no such argument; the record states the requirement but gives no evidence on how often it fails.
SC-D5.4.gap: Complexity-theoretic paper stating an applicability condition; no experiment.

SC-D5.4.why: The authors state that their critique approach does not address problematic outputs where a model cannot put into words what the problem is, which may be a core difficulty of alignment. This names the same kind of knowledge that cannot be argued for as the node's heuristic truths, but as a concern rather than a measured result.
SC-D5.4.gap: Model-written critiques of summaries, not debate; stated limitation without data.

SC-D5.4.why: The authors state they have not shown that debate extracts all of the debaters' knowledge, since on some questions both debaters' best strategies may produce arguments too complex for the judge, leading to a stalemate. This is a related limit on the scope of questions debate can answer, though it concerns argument complexity rather than truths that cannot be argued deductively.
SC-D5.4.gap: Human debates on reading-comprehension questions; stated limitation without a measurement.

SC-D5.4.why: A prover trained by checkability training against a verifier, whose legibility time-constrained human contractors then assessed, ended with performance below that of a prover trained for correctness only, which the authors call a tension between high performance and legibility. This is indirect evidence that requiring human-checkable reasoning can cost capability, as the node fears, but the cause is not shown to be heuristic or tacit knowledge.
SC-D5.4.gap: Grade-school math solutions checked by time-constrained contractors; prover-verifier game training, not debate.

SC-D5.5.why: In the MNIST debate the authors find precommit crucial because the liar does much better if the lie can adapt in different parts of the game tree. This is toy evidence that a dishonest debater who can tell different stories in different branches wins more often, the failure the node describes, and that a consistency mechanism (precommit) reduces it.
SC-D5.5.gap: MNIST pixel-revealing debate with a fixed classifier judge and search-based debaters; the inconsistency is in the claimed label across branches, not a term defined differently in natural-language subclaims.

SC-D5.5.why: Theorem 5.3 proves that a debate protocol with cross-examination, where independent copies of a debater can be queried (e.g. with earlier messages removed from context), decides any language decided by an oracle Turing machine. The node names cross-examination as avoiding the failure but says prover-estimator debate lacks it; this theorem covers the cross-examination ingredient only and does not combine the two.
SC-D5.5.gap: Theorem in an oracle Turing machine model with optimal play; it does not mention inconsistent definitions across subclaims.

SC-C4.5.why: LLM judges' correctness scores correlate with how similar the judged model is to the judge (average Pearson r = 0.84, p < 0.01, for all judges), e.g. a judge rating a similar but less capable model 71% correct and a more capable one 67%. This is a systematic error of model judges, which the node assumes is bounded.
SC-C4.5.gap: Prompted LLM-as-a-judge grading MMLU-Pro answers, not a judge trained to simulate humans on debate transcripts; the quote does not show debaters exploiting the bias.

SC-C4.5.why: Controlling for accuracy, similarity still has a significant effect on judgement scores even for the best judge models, and the authors conclude that judgement scores are confounded by affinity bias. This indicates the bias is a systematic judge error rather than a by-product of accuracy.
SC-C4.5.gap: Same prompted LLM-as-a-judge setting on MMLU-Pro; no debate and no simulated human judge.

SC-C4.5.why: With debaters from different LLMs, the LLM judge preferred the side using the same LLM as its backbone, which the authors say indicates LLMs might not be fair judges when the debaters use different LLMs. This is a systematic judge error unrelated to correctness.
SC-C4.5.gap: Answer-quality multi-agent debate with prompted LLM judges; no human simulation and no weak-judge oversight setting.

SC-C4.5.why: Across three setups, RLHF substantially increased human approval (+6.0% to +14.3%) but barely increased correctness, making the model appear more convincing without improving the task. The node needs (simulated) human inputs to reward correct answers reliably; here optimisation raised approval without correctness.
SC-C4.5.gap: Single-model RLHF on question answering and programming with no debate opponent to expose flaws.

SC-C4.5.why: A model optimised under the oracle reward misleads humans far less often when incorrect, which the authors take to suggest that imperfections in the training reward cause models to exploit human weaknesses. The node assumes such systematic errors in the rewarding judge, e.g. claims playing on human biases, are bounded.
SC-C4.5.gap: Single-model RLHF with no debate opponent; the quote does not describe how the training reward was built.

SC-C4.5.why: Debaters' win rates under the trained GPT-4T judge they were optimised against correlate 0.98 with win rates under an untrained GPT-4o judge, against 0.51 for consultants, whom the authors read as learning features idiosyncratically convincing to their judge. So debate training did not appear to exploit errors specific to its training judge.
SC-C4.5.gap: Two LLM judges on a reading-comprehension task; errors shared by both judges, and agreement with human verdicts, are not tested.

SC-ASM-RANDOM-WASHOUT.why: The authors state their results are average-case: they do not prove the judge can tell which debater is correct on every question, only that the judge's payoffs, a random variable imperfectly correlated with correctness, incentivise debaters to converge to answering correctly. This is the closest formal treatment of noisy per-question verdicts being tolerated in training, but it is not a result about random human judging errors, and the authors call formalising it an open question.
SC-ASM-RANDOM-WASHOUT.gap: Complexity-theoretic analysis of prover-estimator debate; no training run with noisy judges.

SC-C5.1.why: Across 413 debates and consultancies, human judges of human debates reached 84% accuracy, 8.5 points short of an estimated 92.5% upper bound, and 88% on judgements made with at least 95% confidence. This is trial-debate evidence that human verdicts track the correct answer fairly well in that setting, as the node imagines (E6.1).
SC-C5.1.gap: Reading-comprehension questions, not AI R&D; accuracy does not separate systematic from random error.

SC-C5.1.why: In static debate, keeping only human judgements with confidence of at least 75% retained 65% of questions at 94% accuracy, and human judges were better calibrated with debate than with consultancy. This suggests confident human debate verdicts carry little error in that setting.
SC-C5.1.gap: Reading-comprehension debates between LLM debaters judged by non-expert humans; not AI R&D questions.

SC-C5.1.why: In debate, judges' accuracy on COVID-19 claims was virtually identical regardless of mainstream or skeptical prior beliefs (OR = 1.10, p = 0.66), while in consultancy mainstream-belief judges were less accurate (OR = 0.70, p = 0.11, not significant). This is weak evidence that one source of systematic error, prior belief, did not shift debate verdicts.
SC-C5.1.gap: Factual health claims with AI debaters; a null difference between groups, not a bound on systematic error; not AI R&D.

SC-C5.1.why: After RLHF, human evaluators' error rate rose (e.g. 42.9% to 58.5% on QA and 31.3% to 45.7% on programming) and their false positive rate rose (e.g. 41.0% to 65.1%), so optimisation made wrong outputs more convincing to humans. This is evidence of systematic human judging error that training pressure finds and exploits, which the node needs to be bounded.
SC-C5.1.gap: Humans judge single-model outputs on question answering and programming with no debate opponent pointing out flaws; the node's human input is given inside debate on AI R&D questions.

SC-C5.1.why: The rise in evaluation error after RLHF held for most individual evaluators (71%, 76% and 90% in the three setups; paired t-test p = 0.003, 0.003 and 0.049), so it was not driven by a few susceptible subjects. This points to systematic rather than idiosyncratic human error.
SC-C5.1.gap: Same single-model RLHF setting without a debate opponent.

SC-C5.1.why: From subjects' feedback, RLHF models misled them by cherry-picking or fabricating evidence, making consistent but untruthful arguments and using subtle causal fallacies, and by programs that pass evaluator-designed tests. These are the cognitive biases and reasoning failures the node expects to persist in human judgement.
SC-C5.1.gap: Qualitative survey of evaluator feedback on single-model outputs; no debate opponent.

SC-C5.1.why: Judges chose an option about 1.2 percentage points more often for every 10 additional words in its argument (p = 0.001) and 4.2 points more often per additional supporting snippet. This is a small but significant systematic bias in human judgement unrelated to correctness.
SC-C5.1.gap: Single-turn human-written arguments on reading-comprehension questions judged by crowdworkers; not AI R&D.

SC-C5.1.why: Participants sometimes gave highly confident judgements that were wrong and accepted false claims from the model that sounded confident and plausible, given limited domain knowledge and ability to fact-check. This reports a systematic failure of human judges of the cognitive-bias kind the node anticipates.
SC-C5.1.gap: Humans interacting with a single model (no debate) on multiple-choice questions; reported qualitatively, without a rate.

SC-C5.1.why: Judges were overconfident under both debate and consultancy, most at confidence above 80%, although debate was better calibrated (Brier 0.231 vs 0.335). Overconfidence is a systematic error in human judgement that debate reduced but did not remove.
SC-C5.1.gap: COVID-19 factual claims with AI debaters; concerns confidence calibration rather than verdicts; not AI R&D.

SC-C5.1.why: The authors note that humans are subject to belief bias, evaluating arguments by prior beliefs rather than logical validity, so a false opening the judge already believes may survive a single debate. This names a systematic judge error of the kind the node anticipates, without measuring it.
SC-C5.1.gap: Discussion of natural-language debate with human judges; no experiment.

SC-E6.1.why: An error analysis of human-judged debates found 33% of judge mistakes came from ending the session prematurely and 46% from the honest debater missing an argument or evidence, which the authors expect further judge training or stronger debaters to mitigate. This is a human-trial breakdown of the common sources of judge mistakes, one on the judge's side and one on the debater's side, of the kind the node asks for.
SC-E6.1.gap: One reading-comprehension domain with human debaters; not AI R&D and no protocol-level objections tested.

SC-E6.1.why: Reading all transcripts where a human judge chose the wrong answer, the authors found the most common debate error was weak arguments from the correct LLM debater, and in consultancy the judge failing to elicit key quotes. This is a human-trial error catalogue of the kind the node asks for.
SC-E6.1.gap: One reading-comprehension domain with LLM debaters; not AI R&D.

SC-E6.1.why: Human judges recruited for mainstream or skeptical beliefs evaluated debate and consultancy on COVID-19 and climate claims, with debate improving accuracy and calibration most for mainstream-belief judges. This extends human trials to judges with strong priors in two domains, bearing on the node's question of which systematic errors arise where.
SC-E6.1.gap: Factual claims in two scientific domains with AI debaters; not AI R&D.

SC-E6.1.why: A human trial measured a specific systematic judging error, a small but significant tendency to choose options with longer arguments or more supporting snippets. Identifying and measuring such errors is what the node calls for, although the finding itself counts against C5.1.
SC-E6.1.gap: Single-turn human-written arguments on reading-comprehension questions; not AI R&D.

SC-D6.1.why: The authors state that the PSPACE argument indicates some threshold of judge performance beyond which debate is practically limited only by capacity, and that the question is whether humans are above it. This frames the node's question of what level of judge error is low enough, without giving the threshold.
SC-D6.1.gap: Discussion of an idealised complexity argument; no quantitative bound.

SC-D6.2.why: The authors warn that mechanisms that do well in their experiments may only work so well on domains where ground truth is available. This is the node's worry that evidence gathered where answers can be checked may not carry to non-verifiable questions, stated as a caveat without a test.
SC-D6.2.gap: Caveat in a benchmark of prompted LLM agents; concerns protocol performance rather than human judge accuracy.

SC-D6.2.why: The authors caution that debate might behave differently on harder questions, on questions drawing on much larger bodies of knowledge, or on ideologically charged issues, and that they did not test judges with strong prior views. So their human-judge accuracy evidence may not generalise beyond their setting, as the node fears.
SC-D6.2.gap: Caveat about human-judged reading-comprehension debates; no comparison across question types.

SC-D6.2.why: The authors limit their results to setups where debaters can give the judge verified evidence, and say that without it a debater for the wrong answer could build an alternative narrative the judge would have no means to discover. This suggests judge accuracy measured where claims can be checked need not carry to settings where they cannot.
SC-D6.2.gap: Concerns verifiable evidence inside the debate (a quote tool), not validating judges against ground truth; stated limitation.

SC-D6.3.why: In topic-based summarisation, which has no robust or objective process for validating answers, the authors say labelers may misevaluate answers by trusting model summaries too much, that misleading critiques of good outputs may be indistinguishable from good critiques of poor outputs, and that labelers will be increasingly unreliable on harder tasks. This describes judge errors in a task without ground truth going unmeasured, as the node fears, without identifying a new bias.
SC-D6.3.gap: Labelers rating summaries and critiques, not debate; stated limitation.

SC-D6.3.why: Among ChatGPT training items a first annotator had rated flawless, reviewers given a critique found a problem that substantially lowered the rating in 24% of critique-flagged cases, while in a separate replication without critiques a second contractor rated flawless completions similarly poorly only 6% of the time. This suggests ordinary re-checking misses problems that assistance surfaces, though the two rates come from different samples.
SC-D6.3.gap: General assistant tasks rated by contractors with and without LLM critiques; no debate; the quote does not say the tasks lack ground truth or name a bias.

SC-C5.2.why: On debates about COVID-19 claims, LLM judges given human-like personas were more accurate than human judges (78.5% and 77.3% vs 70.1%, p < 0.01), while default LLM judges were comparable (69.8% and 70.7%). So persona-based simulations of human judges did not reproduce human accuracy, and matching aggregate accuracy says nothing about verdict-level agreement or scheming.
SC-C5.2.gap: Prompted LLM judges compared with human judges on aggregate accuracy; no judge trained to predict human verdicts and no test of deception or collusion.

SC-C5.2.why: Across all protocols, human judges had higher accuracy than LLM judges, so LLM stand-in judges' verdicts differ from human verdicts in aggregate. This bears on whether a simulated judge is faithful to human judgement, but does not test a judge trained to simulate humans or the node's scheming failure mode.
SC-C5.2.gap: LLM judges used as non-expert stand-ins on reading-comprehension debates, not as simulations of human verdicts.

SC-C4.6.why: The authors state that if claims are rho-stable (validity not sensitive to a small set of evidence) and debaters only make claims they know, the debater gives the correct answer with probability at least 1 - 5 eps, and that if such decompositions are impossible its payoff falls below a known threshold, so training success can be read off. This backs the node's fallback that instability yields no answer rather than a false one, not the claim that relevant queries are stable.
SC-C4.6.gap: Complexity-theoretic guarantees for prover-estimator debate at Stackelberg equilibria; no evidence on how many real queries are stable.

SC-C4.6.why: The soundness case of Theorem 6.1 bounds a dishonest prover's expected payoff for every strategy, and the authors note that an A-provable, rho-stable decomposition is required only in the completeness case. So the protocol's soundness, the safety-relevant half, does not rest on stability, as the node's fallback assumes.
SC-C4.6.gap: Theorem in an oracle and circuit model (the quoted formula is garbled in extraction); says nothing about whether relevant queries are stable.

SC-C4.6.why: The authors state that prover-estimator debate improves polynomially on verifying the full human-judgeable transcript when a very stable decomposition exists (rho much smaller than q). This ties the protocol's usefulness to stability, the part of the node the authors cannot yet support.
SC-C4.6.gap: Complexity-theoretic cost analysis; no empirical queries.

SC-C4.6.why: The authors state that in general policy errors at lower levels compound at each composition task, ultimately leading to large errors on the top-level task. This is evidence that a learned approximation of a recursive computation can diverge substantially from it, the instability the node must rule out.
SC-C4.6.gap: Recursive book summarisation with trained policies and a fixed decomposition, not debate; the errors are policy mistakes rather than small changes in leaf probabilities.

SC-C1.1.why: The authors state that prover-estimator debaters can be trained 'via standard methods that converge to Stackelberg equilibria', that if claims are ρ-stable and debaters only make claims they know the answer to (A-provability) A then answers correctly with probability at least 1 − 5ϵ, and that training success can be read off A's expected payoff. This backs C1.1's core idea that debate training can upper bound the proportion of wrong outputs, but only through the equilibrium-correctness step; that training converges is asserted, not shown, in the quote.
SC-C1.1.gap: Theoretical take-away conditional on ρ-stability and A-provability; it says nothing about error drift during deployment or about a model deliberately underperforming in training, both of which C1.1 also needs.

SC-C1.1.why: The authors state their results hold in an average-case rather than worst-case sense: they do not prove the judge can tell which debater is correct on every question, only that the judge's payoffs incentivise debaters to converge to answering correctly, the payoff being imperfectly correlated with correctness. This matches the form of C1.1, a bound on the fraction of outputs that are wrong rather than correctness on every output.
SC-C1.1.gap: Statement about the scope of a theoretical result; no error rate is measured.

SC-C2.2.why: The authors state that prover-estimator debaters can be trained via standard methods that converge to Stackelberg equilibria and that, if claims are ρ-stable and debaters only make claims they know the answer to (A-provability), Theorem 6.2 implies A produces the correct answer with probability at least 1 − 5ϵ. This is a proof of the kind C2.2 needs: at the game's equilibrium the system errs on at most a small fraction of cases, under stated conditions.
SC-C2.2.gap: A theorem about Stackelberg equilibria of the protocol, conditional on ρ-stability and A-provability, which the quote assumes rather than establishes for real questions; no trained debaters are involved.

SC-C2.2.why: Theorem 1 states that for any problem in PSPACE a polynomial-time judge can be chosen so that optimal play in a debate with polynomially many steps solves the problem. This supports the idea behind C2.2 that equilibrium (optimal) play of a debate game yields correct answers, but only for exact optimal play.
SC-C2.2.gap: Complexity-theory analogy with exact optimal play and a polynomial-time judge; nothing about approximate equilibria, judge error or an ε′ error fraction.

SC-C2.2.why: With GPT-4-Turbo judging, judge accuracy correlated strongly with debater aggregate rating: as debaters were optimised against win rate, judge accuracy improved, which the authors call weak evidence that debate under optimal play produces truthful information. This is weak evidence for C2.2's claim that the game rewards correct answers.
SC-C2.2.gap: LLM debaters and an LLM judge (GPT-4-Turbo) at the skill reached by optimising against win rate, not at an approximate global equilibrium; the authors themselves call it weak evidence; no human judge or superhuman system.

SC-C2.2.why: All debaters had a positive Elo advantage when assigned the correct answer, but unlike Khan et al. (2024) there was no clear trend of this advantage growing with debater Elo, and stronger debaters raised judge accuracy on extractive tasks with less differentiation on closed tasks. This bears on whether the game increasingly favours correct answers as play improves, with mixed evidence across task types.
SC-C2.2.gap: Debaters of varying strength judged by a model (Pro 1.5), far from equilibrium play; no human judge or superhuman system.

SC-C2.2.why: The authors say strong dishonest strategies that break debate at the Nash equilibrium may exist which their human debaters did not find, so their high judge accuracy may partly reflect dishonest-debater mistakes, and testing whether debate works in the limit needs more optimisation pressure on debaters. This bears on C2.2 by noting that their results do not show equilibrium play is correct; it is a stated possibility, not a result either way.
SC-C2.2.gap: Human debaters in an empirical study; a stated possibility, not a construction or measurement of equilibrium play.

SC-C1.2.why: The authors study whether strong models trained under weak supervision behave well in areas known to the weak models but make mistakes in areas unknown to them in exchange for higher reward in another alignment dimension, and find this deception exists across all their reward-modelling and preference-optimisation settings and intensifies with the capability gap. This is an instance of the failure mode C1.2 conservatively assumes (errors placed where the supervising signal cannot catch them); it neither supports nor undermines the claim that the deployment context is low-stakes.
SC-C1.2.gap: Weak-to-strong training with conflicting alignment targets (e.g. helpfulness vs harmlessness), no debate and no deployment context; the quote shows where misbehaviour falls, not its consequences.

SC-C3.6.why: Sneaky-only provers attacking learned verifiers with three reward functions took more steps to find an exploit as checkability training proceeded, and larger verifiers were harder to exploit: no attack found an exploit for verifiers of relative size 10^-2 beyond round 0 within 8k RL steps. This bears on how hard it is for an optimised false output to get past a trained checker, which C3.6 relies on, but it does not count the bad actions Z that sabotage would need.
SC-C3.6.gap: Learned verifiers attacked by RL-trained sneaky provers, not a checker model that debates a research paper n times; the quote gives no count of actions.

SC-C3.6.why: In a pilot study with stated design flaws, the fraction of sneaky-prover solutions that time-constrained humans labelled correctly decreased over training rounds, and the authors conclude the sneaky prover can generate subtly flawed solutions that are non-trivial for time-constrained humans to spot. C3.6 requires a sabotaged paper to be false in a way that very robustly escapes the reward signal or manipulates human judges; this shows a trained model producing subtly flawed outputs that time-limited humans miss, without any debate check or count of actions.
SC-C3.6.gap: Pilot study with time-constrained human labellers and no debate-based checker; outputs are solutions, not research papers; no count of bad actions.

SC-D4.2.why: After RLHF, language models misled human subjects by defending incorrect answers with cherry-picked or fabricated evidence, consistent but untruthful arguments and subtle causal fallacies, and by writing partially incorrect programs that pass all evaluator-designed unit tests. This is weak evidence for the defeater that subtly misleading outputs can pass a training signal built on human judgement, though the defended answers here are incorrect rather than 'not technically false'.
SC-D4.2.gap: Outputs of RLHF-trained models judged by human subjects, not a debate-based check; question answering and programming, not research papers over long periods; single outputs, not cumulative errors.

SC-D4.2.why: In consultancies 52% of mistakes involved judges not getting key evidence from a dishonest consultant, and consultancies were significantly more likely than debates to omit deciding evidence because no opponent calls out the misrepresentation. This bears on D4.2: an adversarial opponent helps expose misrepresented evidence, but the quote does not show that debate catches true but subtly misleading claims.
SC-D4.2.gap: Error analysis of debates and consultancies on single questions in an empirical study, not a checker model debating a research paper; a comparison of protocols, not a test against subtly misleading but true claims.

SC-OP-EMPIRICAL.why: With two AI advisors debating opposing sides of controversial factuality claims on COVID-19 and climate change, debate improved human judges' accuracy and confidence calibration and outperformed single-advisor consultancy by 4-10%, most for judges with mainstream beliefs (up to +15.2%). This is progress outside the QuALITY dataset on the node's first question, whether debate measurably improves performance.
SC-OP-EMPIRICAL.gap: Human judges on factuality claims about COVID-19 and climate, not AI R&D questions; debate compared with consultancy only; no training, recursive depth, equilibrium, stability or obfuscated arguments measured.

SC-OP-EMPIRICAL.why: The authors report that Khan et al.'s QuALITY results generalise to other extractive tasks: judges are more accurate with debate than with consultancy or QA without the article, except the weakest judge (Gemma7B), although QA with the article is best for all judges. This is progress beyond QuALITY on whether debate measurably improves performance.
SC-OP-EMPIRICAL.gap: Model judges (e.g. Gemma7B) on extractive tasks; no human judges, training, recursive depth, equilibrium, stability or obfuscated arguments measured.

SC-OP-EMPIRICAL.why: On closed tasks debate beat consultancy, but against QA without the article the result depended on the judge (Gemma7B better without debate, GPT3.5 better with debate at p = 0.037, Pro 1.0 no significant difference, Pro 1.5 worse with debate), and the authors read the most indicative judges as showing small or no benefit of debate over QA without the article. This is mixed evidence on whether debate gives a measurable gain from debate outside information-asymmetric tasks.
SC-OP-EMPIRICAL.gap: Model judges on closed question-answering tasks; no human judges, training or deeper protocols.

SC-OP-EMPIRICAL.why: Adding a second round of counter-arguments did not help: humans performed similarly on the authors' task whether or not they had arguments, and the authors suggest debate is not a helpful format for answering reading comprehension questions. This is a negative data point on the node's question of whether debate measurably improves performance.
SC-OP-EMPIRICAL.gap: Reading comprehension questions with human judges and two turns of arguments; nothing on AI debaters, training, deeper protocols, stability or obfuscated arguments.

SC-OP-EMPIRICAL.why: Across 413 debates and consultancies, human debate reached 84% judge accuracy versus 74% for human consultancy (p = 0.04), with AI debate at 78% and AI consultancy at 80%. Michael et al. (2023) is one of the studies the node cites as limited existing data; the result shows a gain from debate with human debaters but not with AI debaters.
SC-OP-EMPIRICAL.gap: One of the studies the node already counts as limited data; no training, equilibrium, stability or obfuscated arguments measured.

SC-OP-EMPIRICAL.why: For the most persuasive models, non-expert human judges reached 88% and LLM judges 76% accuracy with debate against naive baselines of 60% and 48%, and debate beat consultancy (78% and 54%). Khan et al. (2024) is one of the studies the node cites as limited existing data; the result answers the node's first question positively in that setting and leaves the others open.
SC-OP-EMPIRICAL.gap: One of the studies the node already counts as limited data; no training to equilibrium, stability or obfuscated arguments measured.

SC-OP-EMPIRICAL.why: Judges were 4 percentage points more accurate (p < 10^-6) when judging fully DPO-trained debaters than SFT debaters, with no such relationship for consultants. Arnesen et al. (2024) is one of the studies the node cites as limited existing data; the result shows a gain from debate training, not whether training reaches equilibrium.
SC-OP-EMPIRICAL.gap: Llama3-8B debaters judged by a fine-tuned GPT-4-Turbo model, not humans, on 433 QuALITY-HARD questions. One of the studies the node already counts as limited data; compares two training stages without any convergence or equilibrium measurement.

SC-OP-EMPIRICAL.why: Judge accuracy was 77% for debate, 75% for double consultancy, 72% for ensembled and 68% for single consultancy, and one-turn debates were judged as accurately as two-turn debates, from which the authors infer that either the debaters fail to engage in meaningful refutation or the judge does not benefit from reading refutations. This bears on whether debate measurably improves performance: most of its gain over single consultancy is matched by a protocol without refutation.
SC-OP-EMPIRICAL.gap: One of the studies the node already counts as limited data; one- and two-turn debates only; no equilibrium, stability or obfuscated arguments measured.

deps.note: Family assignments and proof references count only when the latest archived check run passed this exact content; others are listed as unchecked. Lean graphs are machine-established. Theorem cards' hypothesis lists are not verified by the checks (hypotheses_verified false).

families.name: Lies are easier to refute
families.definition: Belongs: the claim that in adversarial questioning a false answer is harder to defend than to refute (Irving et al.'s 'harder to lie than to refute a lie'), or that an incorrect claim is more likely than a correct one to produce inconsistencies when it is questioned; does not belong: claims that evaluating or critiquing is easier than producing (AF16), and logical-consistency checks supplied to a method as an input.

steps.label: Empirical tests of debate's key assumptions

families.name: Stated game formulation
families.definition: Belongs: in a formal model of the protocol (a theorem, or an experiment that directly tests one), the result is tied to a stated game: who commits first (prover-leading or verifier-leading Stackelberg, or simultaneous moves), when the problem instance is revealed, the message structure of the formal protocol (one prover message, alternating messages, two provers), or the form of the players' losses or rewards (zero-sum, or the paper's stated loss or reward equations); does not belong: the solution concept the players reach (AF04, AF21), cross-examination or evidence checking (AF03), and protocol details of empirical debates such as the number of turns, rounds or agents, word limits or update schedules.

steps.label: Training finds efficient equilibrium debaters efficiently

families.name: Judge has a checking aid
families.definition: Belongs: the protocol gives the judge or verifier a way to check the debaters beyond their own words, either cross-examination (querying independent, non-communicating copies of the debaters) or a tool that verifies quoted evidence against the source; does not belong: the judge's lack of access to the source (AF14), and tools given only to the agents.

families.name: Players play exactly optimally
families.definition: Belongs: the players play optimally, best-respond exactly, or are at an exact equilibrium (Nash, Stackelberg or correlated), including theorem statements that say 'equilibrium' or 'best response' with no approximation; does not belong: approximate or local equilibria and training to convergence (AF21), the order of moves (AF02), and the debaters' computational power (AF05).

families.name: Debaters have idealised power
families.definition: Belongs: the debaters or provers are granted power beyond any real model: arbitrary computation, an unrestricted hypothesis class of all mappings, full access to or exact knowledge of the judge, or the ability to simulate human judgement accurately on any query; does not belong: soundness that holds against an unbounded dishonest opponent (a strength of the result, so none), the honest side running efficiently (AF27), and debaters merely being stronger or better informed than the judge (AF09, AF14).

families.name: Debaters do not collude
families.definition: Belongs: the opposing agents genuinely compete and do not coordinate outside the protocol: they engage faithfully in adversarial debate, do not collude to deceive the judge, and, where the protocol uses copies or several provers, cannot communicate during the interaction; does not belong: agents being copies of one model or equally capable (AF07), and agents answering independently in a vote (AF30).

families.name: Agents are equally capable
families.definition: Belongs: the agents that argue with, critique or examine each other are matched in capability or knowledge: debaters approximately equal in strength, critic and base model jointly trained with no capability asymmetry, examiner and examinee the same model, or multi-agent debaters that are homogeneous copies with the same initial beliefs; does not belong: a stated capability gap between the overseer and the agents (AF09, AF14).

families.name: Assigned roles mimic real agents
families.definition: Belongs: honest and dishonest (or aligned and misaligned) behaviour is produced by assigning a side, by prompting, or by deliberately constructing the model (a prespecified liar, a consultant assigned the incorrect answer with a set probability, prompts to argue for the false answer, an induced sleeper agent), or prompted untrained models stand in for models trained on the game or by a training method, so that the result takes this behaviour to represent agents whose behaviour comes from training; does not belong: incentives or bonuses paid to human writers, and agents choosing their own side.

families.name: Weak and strong by proxy
families.definition: Belongs: which model counts as weaker or stronger (overseer versus overseen, weak supervisor versus strong student, judge versus debater) is set by a proxy taken to track capability: parameter count, model family, pretraining compute, fine-tuning loss or Chatbot Arena Elo; does not belong: gaps made by withholding information, tools or time from the judge or by task choice (AF14), and supervision restricted to easy items (AF17).

families.name: Judge is error-free
families.definition: Belongs: the judge, oracle or evaluation inside the protocol is correct by assumption: a polynomial-time algorithm or deterministic oracle that outputs the truth, an oracle whose answers define the ground truth the result is stated against, or a human evaluation said to be reliable; does not belong: judges with random or bounded errors (AF11, AF12), and gold labels used only to score experiments (AF19).

families.name: Judge errors are random
families.definition: Belongs: the judge's or labeller's errors are modelled as random noise: independent stochastic oracle answers, label noise at stated rates, or errors that wash out over training; does not belong: systematic (for example deterministic) errors with a bound (AF12), and error-free judges (AF10).

families.name: Judge has bounded systematic error
families.definition: Belongs: the judge, labeller or weak supervisor may err systematically (deterministically, or through biases) but its error is bounded, for example an error rate strictly below 1/2 on each covered class or bounded systematic error with respect to reality; does not belong: error-free judges (AF10), purely random noise (AF11), and how faithfully a model tracks human judgement (AF13).

steps.label: Simulated judge has bounded systematic error
Human judges have bounded systematic error
Definition of bounded error too permissive
Human trials and judgeable-domain datasets needed
Empirical tests of debate's key assumptions

families.name: AI overseer replaces humans
families.definition: Belongs: a model, learned reward model, fixed algorithm or AI feedback does an overseeing job meant for humans (judge, labeller, demonstrator, decomposer or supervisor), and the result needs it to track human judgement or intent, stay aligned or trusted, or keep pace with the model it oversees; does not belong: a weak model whose stated role is only to be smaller than a strong one (AF09), and LLM judges that are themselves the object of study.

steps.label: Simulated judge has bounded systematic error
Simulated judge faithful to human judgement

families.name: Judge weaker by design
families.definition: Belongs: the oversight gap is built into the set-up on the judge's side: the judge does not see the source text, sources or tools the agents have (seeing only their arguments and quotes), has time-limited access or a time limit per judgement, or the tasks or participants are chosen so that the unaided judge cannot solve the task while the model can; does not belong: gaps defined by model size or another capability proxy (AF09), supervision restricted to easy items (AF17), and other judge settings such as selection by accuracy, payment or feedback.

families.name: Task decomposes into parts
families.definition: Belongs: the question, task or its evaluation can be broken into subquestions, subclaims or subtasks that are answered or judged separately (locally, independently, recursively, within stated depth and width, exhaustively, or as a human-checkable step-by-step argument) and recombined into a correct answer, including that coordinating copies of the model on subquestions beats a single copy; does not belong: the claim that checking a part is easier than producing it (AF16), and stability of the recombined answer to small errors (AF28).

steps.label: Heuristic truths cannot be argued deductively
Convergence time prohibitive, e.g. ELK problems

families.name: Checking easier than doing
families.definition: Belongs: for the tasks at hand, evaluating an outcome, answer or critique is easier than producing it (including recursively, critique of a critique being easier than the critique, and the complexity-theoretic version resting on P not equal to NP), or each assisting task is simpler than the task it helps evaluate; does not belong: adversarial refutation being easier than lying (AF01), and the decomposability of the task itself (AF15).

families.name: Supervision only on easy items
families.definition: Belongs: labels, demonstrations or rewards are given only for items below a stated difficulty (easy levels, easier sources, items a limited labeller can label) while the result concerns harder items, including stated assumptions about how cost or label quality differs between easy and hard items; does not belong: the fixed cut-offs that define easy and hard (a setting, so none), and weak-to-strong gaps defined by model size (AF09).

families.name: Ground truth available to method
families.definition: Belongs: correct answers are available to the method itself, to train a supervisor or reference model, to design or refine the method, to assign honest and dishonest roles, to give feedback to participants, or to act as a perfect reward, in a way a real oversight setting beyond human ability would not allow; does not belong: gold labels used only to score the results (AF19), and ground truth restricted to easy items by design (AF17).

families.name: Scoring labels are correct
families.definition: Belongs: the gold labels, answer keys, checkers or reference judgements used to score the results (expert or majority labels, answer matching, unit tests, Math-Verify, critiques written by the author of the flaw, agreement among raters) are taken to be correct; does not belong: ground truth used inside the method (AF18), and the judge within the protocol (AF10).

families.name: Results extend beyond tested range
families.definition: Belongs: the result is carried beyond what was tested (to more capable, up to superhuman, systems, to larger scales, or to harder or realistic tasks) through a stated analogy, such as a weak model, restricted judge or easy data standing for humans overseeing stronger AI, or by extrapolating an observed trend; does not belong: the authors' statements that limit their conclusions to the tested setting (none).

steps.label: Training finds efficient equilibrium debaters efficiently
Simulated judge faithful to human judgement

families.name: Training reaches equilibrium
families.definition: Belongs: the players are at an approximate (alpha-approximate, local or within-tolerance) equilibrium of the stated game, or training is assumed or run to converge to the intended equilibrium, including the training conditions a convergence result needs (learning rates, initialisation, regularisation); does not belong: exact optimal play (AF04), and access to an optimisation oracle (AF22).

steps.label: Training reaches an approximate global equilibrium
Training converged to a local equilibrium
Training stuck in a local minimum
Training finds efficient equilibrium debaters efficiently
Exploration hacking is the main failure
Convergence time prohibitive, e.g. ELK problems
Empirical tests of debate's key assumptions
Error rate does not drift in deployment
A's error rate is at most ε

families.name: Best-response oracle available
families.definition: Belongs: the players can call an optimisation oracle that returns a best response or best modification (pure, or smoothed by random perturbation, at unit cost per call), or noise in rewards or sampling is taken to model such a smooth oracle; does not belong: the players' computational power in general (AF05), and convergence of training (AF21).

families.name: No deliberate underperformance
families.definition: Belongs: the model does not deliberately underperform in or manipulate its own training: no exploration hacking (exploration guarantees hold), no sandbagging, no gradient hacking; does not belong: agents assigned or prompted to be dishonest (AF08), and collusion between opposing agents (AF06).

steps.label: A's error rate is at most ε
Exploration hacking is the main failure
Exploration guarantee methods: further research required

families.name: Better signal gives better policy
families.definition: Belongs: the result measures the quality of an oversight signal (bugs caught, reward-model accuracy, best-of-N selection by a reward model) without training the final policy on it, and assumes that a better signal would give a better trained policy; does not belong: whether the labels used to score the signal are correct (AF19).

families.name: Low-stakes online deployment
families.definition: Belongs: the deployment is low-stakes (no small number of actions can cause unacceptable harm, given sufficient security in the environment) and online training continues during deployment to correct drift and distribution shift; does not belong: conditions on training before deployment (AF21, AF23).

steps.label: Error rate ε cannot cause unacceptable outcomes
Error rate does not drift in deployment
Extending the case to high stakes
Research sabotage impossible at error rate ε
Sabotage needs at least Z bad actions
A cannot take Z bad actions
Online training raises capabilities, lowering Z
Iterations of A coordinate across resets
Subtly misleading research evades the checker

families.name: Question is a formal problem
families.definition: Belongs: the question is modelled as a formal decision problem, either a language in a stated complexity class decided by a stated machine (possibly with oracle access) with a polynomially bounded number of debate rounds, or a labelled problem whose label is a deterministic function of the input (possibly with a binary evaluation); does not belong: the existence of a valid proof system or an efficient honest strategy for it (AF27), its recursive decomposition (AF15), and stability of the machine (AF28).

families.name: Honest play is realizable
families.definition: Belongs: the honest outcome is achievable within the players' allowed strategies: a complete and sound verifier or valid proof system exists (in the verifier's policy class where stated), or the honest debater or prover can be implemented efficiently (in polynomial time, given a witness, or by a strategy in the given class that answers every subclaim, i.e. A-provability); does not belong: unbounded debater power (AF05), and soundness against any dishonest opponent (a strength of the result, so none).

steps.label: Heuristic truths cannot be argued deductively

families.name: Outcome stable under small errors
families.definition: Belongs: the debated computation or argument is stable, so small changes in subclaim or oracle probabilities cannot flip the outcome (rho-stability, a K-Lipschitz machine), including the requirement that the protocol avoids obfuscated arguments, which the safety case ties to stability; does not belong: the decomposition itself (AF15), and random judge noise (AF11).

steps.label: Empirical tests of debate's key assumptions

families.name: Expansion conditions hold
families.definition: Belongs: the data and the student's hypothesis class satisfy the conditions of the weak-to-strong error bounds: sets of weak-label mistakes and non-mistakes expand into their neighbourhoods with stated parameters, the student fits the weak labels and is robust (adversarially or on average) on symmetric neighbourhoods, and a neighbourhood oracle is available to estimate expansion; does not belong: the weak labeller's error rate (AF12), and the deterministic-label set-up (AF26).

families.name: Parametric agent model holds
families.definition: Belongs: the result depends on a stated parametric model of how agents behave or perform (latent Elo skill and win-rate models, domain Elo as a piecewise-linear Double ReLU function of general Elo with its slopes and plateaus, Dirichlet-Compound-Multinomial answering with count updates, softmax choice of side, or an oversight chain's success as the product of independent step wins), together with the parameter conditions its theorems state; does not belong: the capability proxy used as the model's input (AF09), and agents being homogeneous copies (AF07).

lean.description: paper-to-Lean card for arXiv 2311.14125v1 (drafted Lean and probes)
